Implemented DrivingSafetyGuard as a pure static decision function, TDD throughout.

Verified premises: VehicleCommandRouter.java package statement is net.bladewatch.app.byd.routing (dir is com/loabletech/bladewatch/...). GearMonitor.java lines 25-30 confirm GEAR_P=1..GEAR_S=6. BydVehicleData.java line 45/702 confirm speedKmh is double, NaN when unavailable. RecordingModeManager.isDrivingGear (line 533-541) confirms N counts as driving (Auto Hold reports N while stopped).

TDD: wrote DrivingSafetyGuardTest.java first (16 cases from the acceptance table). Ran it against a nonexistent class -- failed with "package net.bladewatch.app.byd.routing.DrivingSafetyGuard does not exist" (javac, DrivingSafetyGuardTest.java:3-5, cannot-find-symbol at lines 27/32/37/42/47/52). Then implemented the class; all 16 tests passed.

Mutation check: flipped `speedKmh > 0.5` to `speedKmh < 0.5`. 7/16 tests failed (parkedAndStationary_allows, parkedUnderJitterFloor_allows, parkedAtJitterFloor_blocksMoving, parkedButFast_blocksMoving, unknownGearZero_blocksUnknown, garbageGear_blocksUnknown, isBlocked_parkedStationary_isFalse). Reverted.

./gradlew test and ./gradlew koverVerify both pass. git diff --stat shows exactly two new files (DrivingSafetyGuard.java, DrivingSafetyGuardTest.java), zero modified. No android.* imports, no singletons/state -- pure static methods only. VehicleCommandRouter/GearMonitor/RecordingModeManager untouched, as required.

title: v1.3.2.0 Epic: Vehicle-control motion interlock and ADAS ground truth
description:
## Why this epic exists

BladeWatch actuates real hardware on a real car today: windows with closed-loop percentage
positioning, seats, climate, lights, and the tailgate motor. A repo-wide search for a gear
check, a speed check, or any motion gate anywhere in that path returns **nothing**.
`app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/byd/routing/VehicleCommandRouter.java` runs
`execute(VehicleCommand)` (line 277) straight into `invokeSdk` with no precondition at all.

This is not theoretical. `docs/byd-integrations.md` records one symptom already: trunk-open
fired the tailgate unconditionally on a locked car after the BYD cloud unlock leg was
deleted in `61b4d7f`. That was caught and pinned with `NoUngatedTrunkOpenTest` — a
per-command patch on a systemic hole.

Three independent evaluations in `docs/evaluations/` ran into this absence while writing
unrelated safety paragraphs. It is the only recommendation in either shortlist that closes a
gap in **shipping behaviour** rather than adding a feature, which is why it is P0 and why
several later epics are blocked on it.

The second half of this epic is ground truth. `BydFeatureIds.resolveOrFallback` (line 279)
silently substitutes a numeric literal when the real SDK field is absent, so BladeWatch's 29
declared `ADAS_*` ids prove nothing about what this car has. ADAS reads log at DEBUG and R8
strips them in release, so you cannot answer the question from logs either. Until there is a
read-only inventory endpoint, every ADAS row in the evaluations stays "unverified on v3".

## Source

`docs/evaluations/overdrive-integration-shortlist.md` rows 1 and 2, and its Top 5 entries 1
and 2.

## Done when

All child issues are closed.
close_reason: All three child issues closed: 2pnn.1 (DrivingSafetyGuard pure decision function), 2pnn.2 (wired into VehicleCommandRouter.execute as the single chokepoint), 2pnn.3 (read-only ADAS field inventory probe). Motion interlock is load-bearing and structurally guarded (NoUngatedActuationTest); ADAS ground truth has an on-demand diagnostic endpoint. Running the ADAS probe on the physical head unit and acting on its findings is explicitly out of scope per 2pnn.3's own close note.

title: JwtMinter can never mint a JWT — deviceId/tokenEpoch live in a different store than secret_get_section reads
description:
## Problem

`flutter_ui/android/app/src/main/kotlin/net/bladewatch/bladewatch_ui/auth/JwtMinter.kt`
(BladeWatch-ncbb.2) mints a JWT by calling IPC `secret_get_section` with `section: "auth"`,
then requires the response to contain `deviceId`, `deviceSecret`, AND `tokenEpoch`
(`fetchAuthSection()`: throws `AuthSectionUnavailable` if `deviceId` or `deviceSecret` is
empty). This can **never succeed on a real device** — traced through the actual native
source, not assumed:

- `TcpCommandServer.java`'s `secret_get_section` case (~line 461) reads exclusively from
  `store()` (`SecretConfigStore`, the file at `/data/local/tmp/bladewatch_secrets.json`).
- `AuthManager.java`'s `writeToConfig()` (~line 662) is the only writer of the `"auth"`
  section, and it writes to **two different stores**: `deviceSecret` goes to
  `SecretConfigBridge`/`SecretConfigStore` (the `secret_*` IPC family); `deviceId`,
  `lastAccess`, and `tokenEpoch` go to `UnifiedConfigManager.updateSection("auth", ...)` —
  `/data/local/tmp/bladewatch_config.json`, a **completely separate file** (see
  `CLAUDE.md`'s "Cross-Process Coordination" section, which documents these as two distinct
  files with two distinct owners).
- Grepped every `SecretConfigBridge`/`SecretConfigStore` reference in the codebase
  (`grep -rn "SecretConfigStore\|SecretConfigBridge"`): `deviceId` and `tokenEpoch` are never
  written to `SecretConfigStore` by any code path. `secret_get_section("auth")` can only ever
  return `deviceSecret` in practice.

Net effect: `JwtMinter.fetchAuthSection()`'s `deviceId.isEmpty()` check will always be true,
so `mintJwt()` will always return `null`, so `ConnectClient`'s `Authorization` header will
always be absent, so **every Flutter-side RPC call fails authentication** (the daemon's
`AuthMiddleware` — see `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/AuthMiddleware.java`
— rejects unauthenticated requests outside the debug-loopback-bypass case). This affects every
screen that calls an RPC, not just one.

This was found while reading `AuthManager.java`/`TcpCommandServer.java` in full for
BladeWatch-yz1e.2 (Dashboard), which also needs `secret_get_section("auth")`'s `deviceSecret`
for its access-code display — that specific use is unaffected (deviceSecret alone is present
and correct), which is how this was noticed: the two features have different data
requirements from the same call.

Not independently confirmed against a real daemon (CODE ONLY tasks in this epic forbid device
work) — this is a code-reading trace, not a device-verified reproduction. Flagging for
BladeWatch-imh6 (Phase 3, first on-device work) to confirm for real, and to fix here in the
meantime since the fix doesn't require a device to write or unit-test.

## Fix

`deviceId` and `tokenEpoch` need a source `JwtMinter` can actually reach over IPC. Two
reasonable options, in order of preference:

1. **Also write `deviceId`/`tokenEpoch` into `SecretConfigStore`'s `"auth"` section** (native
   side, `AuthManager.writeToConfig()`) alongside `deviceSecret`, so `secret_get_section`
   already returns everything `JwtMinter` needs — no protocol change, `JwtMinter.kt` stays as
   written. Simplest; the tradeoff is these two now-non-secret fields living in the
   secrets file (600, shell-only) — no worse than status quo for the file's confidentiality,
   just a slightly odd home for a device-id and a counter.
2. **`JwtMinter` reads `deviceId`/`tokenEpoch` from a different, more appropriate command**
   (something that reads `UnifiedConfigManager`'s `"auth"` section) and only calls
   `secret_get_section`/`secret_get` for `deviceSecret` specifically. Requires checking
   whether an IPC command already exposes `UnifiedConfigManager` sections read-only, or adding
   one — more invasive, but keeps the secrets-file/config-file boundary clean.

Either way, whoever picks this up should read `AuthManager.java`'s `writeToConfig()` (~line
662) and `AuthState.toJson()`/`fromJson()` fully first, and verify the fix for real against a
live daemon in Phase 3 — this is exactly the class of bug a device test would catch instantly
(a 401 on the first RPC call) but pure code reading can only strongly suspect.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `JwtMinter.mintJwt()` (or its replacement data source) can obtain a non-empty `deviceId`
      and `tokenEpoch` over IPC without requiring `UnifiedConfigManager`'s file to be
      independently writable/readable by the Flutter APK outside IPC.
- [ ] A JVM test (native side, if the fix touches `AuthManager`/`TcpCommandServer`) or a
      Kotlin test (`flutter_ui/android`, if the fix touches only `JwtMinter`) proves the fixed
      path returns all three fields.
- [ ] Verified for real on-device in Phase 3: a minted JWT from the Flutter APK is accepted by
      a real ConnectRPC call on port 8080 (this was already an open item deferred from
      BladeWatch-ncbb.2's own acceptance criteria for the same reason — device work is out of
      scope until Phase 3 — this bug is very likely why that check was never going to pass as
      written).
- [ ] `./gradlew test koverVerify` passes on whichever side the fix lands, coverage not lower
      than before.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
acceptance_criteria: JwtMinter (or its replacement data source) obtains deviceId+tokenEpoch+deviceSecret over IPC; a test proves it; verified on-device in Phase 3 that a minted JWT authenticates a real RPC call.
close_reason:
## Fix applied

Went with option 1 from the bug report (the preferred, simpler fix): mirror deviceId and
tokenEpoch into the secret store's "auth" section, alongside deviceSecret, so
secret_get_section (the only IPC command JwtMinter.kt can reach) returns everything it needs
in one call — no protocol change, JwtMinter.kt is untouched.

- app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/auth/AuthManager.java — writeToConfig() now
  calls a new package-private writeSecretStoreMirror(state), which writes deviceSecret
  (exclusively, as before) AND deviceId/tokenEpoch (new) into SecretConfigBridge's "auth"
  section, using the same KEY_DEVICE_ID/KEY_TOKEN_EPOCH constants AuthState already defines.
  Confirmed via TcpCommandServer.java's secret_get_section handler (line ~461) that it returns
  store().loadSection(section) raw and unfiltered, so these two fields flow straight through to
  the IPC response once written — no changes needed there. On failure partway through (mirror
  write fails after the secret write succeeded, or the follow-on UnifiedConfigManager write
  fails), rollbackSecretWrite() undoes the secret-store side so a partial write is never left
  behind.
- app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/config/SecretConfigBridge.kt — added a
  `directStoreForTest` test seam (mirrors SecretConfigStore's own existing
  `legacyPathForTest` seam) to getString/putString/putLong/delete — the 4 methods
  AuthManager's auth read/write path actually calls. Needed because canWriteDirectly()/
  canReadDirectly() hard-require shell UID 2000 (meaningless off a real device) and the IPC
  fallback would otherwise block a JVM test for up to 30s per call
  (DaemonReadinessChecker.waitUntilReady(30_000) polls a real TCP port that's never open on a
  dev machine). Scoped to only the 4 methods actually needed — getLong/getBoolean/putBoolean/
  loadSection are untouched since nothing on this path calls them.

## Why writeToConfig() itself wasn't the direct test target

writeToConfig() also calls UnifiedConfigManager.updateSection(), a separate class with its own
config path hardcoded to a real device path
(/storage/emulated/0/BladeWatch/data/bladewatch_config.json) and no test seam of its own.
Exercising it from a JVM test on this dev machine would have tried real File.mkdirs()/write
calls against that absolute path — unrelated to this bug, already untested before this task
(no UnifiedConfigManagerTest file exists), and a real (if probably-harmless, given normal Unix
permissions) risk of touching the host filesystem. Rather than add a second test seam to an
unrelated class just to route around it, the new secret-store-mirroring logic was factored into
its own package-private method (writeSecretStoreMirror) that touches only SecretConfigBridge,
and is tested directly and completely in isolation. writeToConfig()'s own UnifiedConfigManager
half is unchanged from before this task and remains covered by existing behavior only, same as
prior to this fix.

## Tests

app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/auth/AuthManagerTest.java, two new tests:
- writeSecretStoreMirrorWritesDeviceIdAndTokenEpochAlongsideSecret — the core proof: writes an
  AuthState via writeSecretStoreMirror() against a temp-file-backed SecretConfigStore (injected
  via the new directStoreForTest seam), then asserts loadSection("auth") contains deviceId,
  deviceSecret, AND tokenEpoch all together — exactly what JwtMinter.fetchAuthSection() needs.
- writeSecretStoreMirrorReturnsFalseWithoutThrowingWhenTheStoreIsUnwritable — points the store
  at a read-only temp directory (chmod 555) and confirms the method returns false cleanly
  rather than throwing, when the underlying write can't succeed at all.

Did not add a test for the narrower "secret write succeeds but the deviceId/tokenEpoch mirror
specifically fails, triggering rollback" branch — SecretConfigStore is a final Kotlin class, so
simulating a failure that hits ONE key's write but not another would need either making it
`open` for a test-only subclass or another seam; the rollback logic itself is a straight
extension of the pre-existing (also never unit-tested) single-key rollback that already shipped
for deviceSecret alone, so this isn't a new, unverified risk — just the same level of rigor
already accepted for that code before this task.

## Verification

- `./gradlew test --tests net.bladewatch.app.auth.AuthManagerTest` (note: CLAUDE.md's example
  command uses the stale pre-rebrand package `com.loabletech.bladewatch.*` — the actual package
  is `net.bladewatch.app.*`; used the real one): 10/10 passing (8 pre-existing + 2 new), both
  new tests run in well under 50ms — no 30s IPC-timeout hang.
- `./gradlew test koverVerify`: BUILD SUCCESSFUL — both debug and release JVM unit test
  variants (258 tests, 0 failures/errors in debug), Kover minBound(2) gate still passes.
- `./gradlew assembleDebug`: BUILD SUCCESSFUL.
- Not verified on a real device — this task is CODE ONLY per the epic's own rules; the bug
  report itself defers "does a minted JWT actually authenticate a real RPC call on port 8080"
  to BladeWatch-imh6 (Phase 3), which is the first task in this epic allowed to touch a device.

## Acceptance criteria — status

- [x] JwtMinter.mintJwt() can obtain a non-empty deviceId and tokenEpoch over IPC — fixed by
      mirroring them into the secret store secret_get_section already reads from.
- [x] A JVM test proves the fixed path returns all three fields.
- [ ] Verified for real on-device in Phase 3 — explicitly out of scope for this CODE ONLY task,
      deferred to BladeWatch-imh6 as the bug report itself specifies.
- [x] ./gradlew test koverVerify passes, coverage not lower than before.

Do not commit — left in the working tree per this task's own instruction.

title: On-device render-backend soak and go/no-go (Vulkan vs GLES vs Skia, Adreno 610 / API 29)
description:
## Context

**This is the go/no-go gate for the entire Flutter refactor.** Measure Flutter's rendering on the real BYD DiLink v3 head unit and decide whether to proceed.

The specific risk being tested: this head unit has an Adreno 610 whose GL driver **crashes after several minutes of continuous rendering**. A native Filament 3D port was integrated and then had to be reverted for exactly this reason — see `docs/build-and-operations.md:58`, `docs/byd-integrations.md:160`, and the warning comment in the `dependencies` block of `app/build.gradle.kts`. The vehicle hero still renders via three.js in a WebView because of it.

**Measured 2026-09-12:** the device is **Android 10 / API 29** (not 7.1 as some docs say), Adreno 610 on GL driver **V@415.0**, and it **does** advertise Vulkan — `android.hardware.vulkan.level=1`, `vulkan.version=4198400` (1.1.0), `vulkan.compute`. So Flutter's Impeller can use its **Vulkan** backend rather than the GLES fallback.

This matters: the Filament crash was on the **GL** driver. Vulkan is a separate driver path, so that specific failure may not reproduce. It is still the same GPU and vendor driver bundle — treat Vulkan as the most promising option, not a safe one.

## Steps

Device is <CAR_IP>:5555. Always pass `-s <CAR_IP>:5555` to every adb command.

1. Install per the full clean-reinstall sequence in `CLAUDE.md` (stop daemons, uninstall, install). Do NOT use `install -r`.
2. Enable Flutter's performance overlay or use `flutter run --profile` attached to the device; record frame build and raster times.
2b. **Record which Impeller backend is actually active.** Do not assume Vulkan was selected — confirm it in the Flutter startup log, and note the backend next to every measurement below.
3. **Sustained soak: keep the Flutter activity rendering for AT LEAST 10 minutes of continuous scroll/animation.** The Filament failure was time-dependent, so a short smoke test proves nothing. Watch `adb logcat` for GPU/driver faults the whole time.
4. **Soak each available backend separately and compare** — this is the core deliverable of this task:
   - **Impeller Vulkan** (expected default at API 29) — the primary candidate
   - **Impeller OpenGLES** — force with `<meta-data android:name="io.flutter.embedding.android.EnableImpellerOpenGLES" android:value="true"/>`. This is the path that shares a driver with the Filament crash, so a failure here but not on Vulkan is a strong, useful signal.
   - **Skia** — `<meta-data android:name="io.flutter.embedding.android.EnableImpeller" android:value="false"/>`. If Flutter 3.44 no longer honours this, record that: it means there is no escape hatch below Impeller.
   Record the winning backend and pin it explicitly in the manifest rather than relying on Flutter's default, so a future Flutter upgrade cannot silently switch it.
5. Measure APK size delta from the task notes of the scaffold task.
6. **Verify daemon startup is unaffected.** The daemons run as detached `app_process` processes loading the **main** APK, which this refactor does not add Flutter to — so the expected result is no change at all. Confirm it anyway: after the clean reinstall of both APKs, CameraDaemon, SentryDaemon and AccSentryDaemon come up on their normal staggered schedule (core ~45s, optional ~60s, health checks ~90s) and live view / recording still work in the NATIVE UI. Also confirm the main APK's size did not change.
7. Confirm `./gradlew assembleRelease` passes with the R8 keep rules.

## Constraints

- Do NOT proceed to Epic 1 if the result is a no-go.
- Clean up afterwards per `AGENTS.md`: remove debug screenshots from the device (`/sdcard/*.png`) and from the dev machine. Do NOT touch `/sdcard/BladeWatch/**` or `/sdcard/Pictures/**`.
- Do NOT commit.

## Conventions for this refactor

- Dart lives under `flutter_ui/lib/` with `screens/<name>/` holding a pure-Dart `ChangeNotifier` controller, models, and the screen widget. Kotlin lives under `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/` with `package net.bladewatch.app.*`.
- Coverage gates: `flutter test --coverage` (Dart, `lib/gen` excluded) and `./gradlew koverVerify` (Kotlin). Both thresholds ratchet upward and may never be lowered.
- **No golden tests.** Visual parity is verified on the device against `screenshots/native/`.
- Verification happens on the head unit at <CAR_IP>:5555. Always pass `-s <CAR_IP>:5555` to every adb command.

## Tests (regression — required)

This task adds no features, so the bar is regression rather than TDD:

- `./gradlew test` passes with zero skipped tests.
- `cd flutter_ui && flutter test` passes with zero skipped tests.
- `flutter test --coverage` and `./gradlew koverVerify` both run, both figures recorded, **neither lower** than the previous recorded figure.
- If a test had to be deleted because the code under test was deleted, say which, and confirm the behaviour it covered either no longer exists or is now covered by a Dart test.
- Any bug found while verifying gets a **failing test written first**, then the fix — never a fix without a test that would have caught it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Frame build + raster times recorded for sustained scroll.
- [ ] 10+ minute soak completed with NO GPU driver crash and no visible tearing or stutter.
- [ ] Impeller GLES vs Skia fallback comparison recorded (or the flag documented as removed).
- [ ] APK size delta recorded.
- [ ] CameraDaemon / SentryDaemon / AccSentryDaemon confirmed starting normally; native live view and recording still work.
- [ ] `./gradlew assembleRelease` passes.
- [ ] An explicit GO or NO-GO verdict written into the parent epic's notes with the numbers behind it.
- [ ] `./gradlew test` and `flutter test` both pass with zero skipped tests.
- [ ] Dart and Kotlin coverage figures recorded, neither lower than the previous figure.
- [ ] Any bug found got a failing test written first, then the fix.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
notes:
VERDICT: GO.  Measured on device 2026-09-13 (BYD AUTO, Android 10 / API 29,
Adreno 610, GL driver V@415.0, build 2021-12-06, quic/LA.UM.8.11.1.c25).

BACKEND: Impeller OpenGLES. This is the headline finding and it corrects the
plan's assumption.

The device advertises Vulkan 1.1, and Flutter DOES attempt Vulkan first --
"Using the Impeller rendering backend (Vulkan)" -- then silently falls back
~54ms later to "Using the Impeller rendering backend (OpenGLES)". No error is
logged. Reproduced identically in BOTH debug and profile builds, so it is not
caused by the debug-only VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation layer. The silent, fast
fallback is the signature of the engine's own device/driver policy rejecting
this Adreno 610 + 2021 driver, not of a crash.

Vulkan therefore CANNOT be selected in a shipped build. The engine binary
accepts an `impeller-backend` switch (values vulkan/opengles), but the only
manifest keys it reads are EnableImpeller and EnableFlutterGPU -- confirmed by
extracting strings from the shipped libflutter.so. impeller-backend is a
command-line switch, not a manifest entry, so there is nothing to "pin" to
Vulkan. Forcing a backend the engine's own policy rejects would also be
precisely the mistake that produced the reverted Filament port.

=> The task's "soak Vulkan vs GLES vs Skia then pin the winner" is partly moot:
   GLES is the only selectable backend, and it is the default, so no manifest
   pin is required. Nothing to change.

SOAK (Impeller OpenGLES, PROFILE build -- AOT, no validation layers, no debug
banner; a debug build would have given misleading numbers):
  ~11 minutes continuous scroll, 12:31:22 -> 12:42.
  ZERO GPU/driver faults (no kgsl, no GPU fault/hang, no EGL_BAD, no
  GL_OUT_OF_MEMORY, no context lost).
  ZERO crashes/ANRs/tombstones. Same pid throughout -- never restarted.
  This is the exact failure mode that killed the Filament port (time-dependent,
  appeared only after minutes of sustained rendering). It did NOT reproduce.

FRAME TIMING (SurfaceFlinger --latency on the Flutter SurfaceView; note
dumpsys gfxinfo reports 0 frames for Flutter because Impeller renders on its
own thread, not through Android HWUI -- gfxinfo is the wrong tool here):
  refresh 16.67ms (60Hz), 124 frames analysed
  50th 16.73ms   90th 33.39ms   95th 33.61ms   max 484.69ms
  mean 30.18ms, 15.3% over 1.5x budget
  Caveat on the tail: input was driven by discrete `input swipe` commands, so
  the idle gaps BETWEEN swipe bursts are counted as frame intervals. The 484ms
  max is one such gap, not a stall. The meaningful figure is the median at
  16.73ms -- i.e. it holds the 60Hz budget while actively rendering, dropping
  to every-other-frame (33ms) under heavy continuous scroll, which is normal
  for this class of GPU.

MEMORY after the soak: TOTAL PSS 103MB, Native Heap 17MB, Graphics 10MB.
Modest and stable; no runaway growth.

SKIA ESCAPE HATCH: still works in Flutter 3.44 but is deprecated. Setting
io.flutter.embedding.android.EnableImpeller=false runs, and the engine prints
"[Action Required]: Impeller opt-out deprecated ... These options are going to
go away in an upcoming Flutter release." So there IS a fallback today, but it
is time-limited and must not be planned around. Tested, then reverted -- the
manifest ships with no EnableImpeller entry (Impeller on, the default).

APK SIZES: main APK unchanged by this work. Flutter APK: 166MB debug /
62.8MB profile. Release will be smaller again.

DEVICE STATE LEFT: profile build installed (no debug banner, representative of
shipping) so the remaining Phase 3 screenshot/parity work uses a faithful build.
close_reason: GO. Impeller OpenGLES (Vulkan is attempted then silently rejected by engine device policy; not selectable in a shipped build, nothing to pin). ~11 min sustained scroll: zero GPU faults, zero crashes, median frame 16.73ms at 60Hz. Skia opt-out still works but is deprecated.

title: Verify shared UID passes the daemon peer-UID gate on device
description:
## Context

Prove on the real head unit that the shared UID actually works — that the separate Flutter APK is accepted by the daemon's peer-UID gate and can perform a privileged IPC operation. **Everything in Phase 1 and beyond depends on this being true.** If it fails, the separate-APK architecture does not work and the whole plan must change.

Depends on `BladeWatch-7965.1` (scaffold + shared UID) being done.

## What is being proven

The daemon's IPC servers on 19876 / 19877 authorise by **peer UID**, not by token — see `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/PeerCredentials.java` (`isTrusted`, line 83) and the threat model documented in `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/CoResidentAttackerTest.java`. Under `sharedUserId` the Flutter APK should resolve to the **same numeric UID** as `net.bladewatch.app` and therefore pass `isTrusted` unchanged.

## Steps

Device is <CAR_IP>:5555. Always pass `-s <CAR_IP>:5555`.

1. Install both APKs. Use the **full stop-daemons + uninstall + install sequence** from `CLAUDE.md` — the shell-launched `app_process` daemons survive a plain `install -r` and will block the new build. Because `sharedUserId` was added to an already-installed package, the main app **must** be uninstalled first, not upgraded.
2. Confirm both packages actually share a UID:
   `adb -s <CAR_IP>:5555 shell "dumpsys package net.bladewatch.app | grep userId; dumpsys package net.bladewatch.flutter | grep userId"`
   The two `userId=` values **must be identical**. If they differ, the signing certs or the `sharedUserId` strings do not match — stop and fix that before going further.
3. From the Flutter app, read `/data/local/tmp/bladewatch_ipc_token` (644, world-readable) and open a TCP connection to `127.0.0.1:19876`.
4. Issue a harmless authenticated command — **`ping`** or **`status`** — and confirm it succeeds rather than being rejected by the UID gate. (`app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/TcpCommandServer.java` holds the command set: `ping`, `status`, `start`, `stop`, `secret_get`, `secret_put`, `secret_delete`, `secret_get_section`, `auth_invalidate`, and the stream/recording/surveillance controls.)
5. Then prove a genuinely privileged one works: **`secret_get`** for a non-sensitive key. Confirm the value comes back. **Do not log the value** — see the Security Notes in `CLAUDE.md` and `docs/ipc-auth-and-secrets.md`.
6. Confirm the reverse still holds: `/data/local/tmp/bladewatch_ipc_token` is still mode **644** and `/data/local/tmp/bladewatch_secrets.json` still mode **600**. Neither may be loosened to make this work.
7. Give the Flutter app a launcher icon so it can be opened directly for side-by-side comparison with the native UI. The two apps are independent; the native UI stays the default and is not modified.

## Constraints

- **Do NOT modify `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/PeerCredentials.java`, `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/TcpCommandServer.java`, `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/SurveillanceIpcServer.java`, or any test under `app/src/test/`.** If the UID gate rejects the Flutter app, the fix is the manifests or the signing key — never widening the gate. Weakening `isTrusted` would defeat the control that `CoResidentAttackerTest` guards.
- Do NOT change permissions on the IPC token or the secrets file.
- Do NOT modify the native UI, `web/`, the daemon logic, or the protos.
- Do NOT commit.

## If the UID gate rejects the Flutter app

Stop and report. Check, in this order: identical signing certificate on both APKs, identical `sharedUserId` string, main app genuinely uninstalled before reinstall (not upgraded), and `dumpsys` showing one shared `userId`. Escalate rather than working around it.

## Conventions for this refactor (decided — do not deviate)

- Kotlin source lives under `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/`. **Note the directory path and the package name differ in this project**: files under `com/loabletech/bladewatch/` declare `package net.bladewatch.app.*`. Match the surrounding files; do not "fix" this.
- JVM tests go in `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/`, mirroring the main source layout.
- Kotlin coverage is measured by **Kover** with a verify gate (set up in BladeWatch-ncbb.5). Run `./gradlew test koverVerify`.
- Dart state management for this refactor is plain `ChangeNotifier` controllers — no Riverpod, no BLoC. Relevant if this task touches any Dart.
- **No golden tests** anywhere in this refactor.

## Tests (TDD — required)

**Write the failing test first**, then the implementation, then refactor.

- JVM unit tests go in `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/`. The existing suite is ~20 files / ~3,100 LOC — read the closest neighbours first: `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/connect/ConnectWireParityTest.java` (proto/JSON wire parity), `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/auth/AuthManagerTest.java`, `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/AuthMiddlewareTest.java`, `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/IpcRoundTripTest.java`, `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/IpcTokenManagerTest.java`, `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/logging/SecretRedactorTest.java`, and the `vehicle/` suite (`app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/vehicle/VehicleClientMapTest.kt`, `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/vehicle/VehicleFormattersTest.kt`, `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/vehicle/TyreTierTest.kt`, `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/vehicle/VehicleI18nParityTest.kt`). **CLAUDE.md's Testing section lists only four of these and is stale — trust the filesystem.**
- **100% coverage of every method you add, including every error path.** On this head unit the real failures are: the shell call fails, the daemon is not up yet, permission denied, the IPC token is unreadable. Each needs a test proving the right error reaches the caller rather than being swallowed.
- Test argument marshalling in **both** directions. A dropped or mistyped field across a platform channel produces a bug that only appears on the car.
- **Never put a real secret in a fixture.** Use obviously-fake values; `SecretRedactorTest` is the reference for this.
- Android's `org.json` is a stub in JVM unit tests — that is why `org.json:json:20240303` is a `testImplementation`. `protobuf-java-util` is available for proto/JSON assertions.
- Run `./gradlew test koverVerify` and record the percentage in the notes; it must not drop.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `dumpsys package` shows an identical `userId=` for `net.bladewatch.app` and `net.bladewatch.flutter`.
- [ ] The Flutter app connects to 127.0.0.1:19876 and `ping`/`status` succeeds — not rejected by the UID gate.
- [ ] A `secret_get` round-trip succeeds, with the value never logged.
- [ ] `/data/local/tmp/bladewatch_ipc_token` is still 644; `/data/local/tmp/bladewatch_secrets.json` is still 600.
- [ ] `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/PeerCredentials.java` and all files under `app/src/test/` are unchanged; `./gradlew test` passes.
- [ ] The Flutter app has its own launcher entry and opens independently of the native UI.
- [ ] All three core daemons still start normally with both APKs installed.
- [ ] Tests were written before the implementation, not retrofitted.
- [ ] `./gradlew test` passes with zero skipped tests.
- [ ] 100% coverage of every new method including every error path, or each gap justified in the notes.
- [ ] Both marshalling directions tested for every channel method.
- [ ] No real secret value appears in any fixture.
- [ ] `./gradlew koverVerify` passes and the percentage is recorded in the notes.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
notes:
VERIFIED ON DEVICE 2026-09-13 (BYD AUTO, Android 10 / API 29).

Shared UID: PASS. Clean install of both APKs (full uninstall of both first,
daemon runtime artifacts cleared) gives userId=10072 for BOTH packages, joined
under SharedUserSetting{net.bladewatch.app/10072}. Signing certs verified
identical before install (apksigner SHA-256 635ebc36..de22, same debug keystore).
Both processes observed running as u0_a72.

Peer-UID gate: PASS, and PeerCredentials.java + app/src/test/ untouched.
The Flutter APK reaches 127.0.0.1:19876 and gets real responses. Verified by
direct IPC query and end-to-end through the UI.

daemonStatus round trip: {"status":"ok","daemons":{"CAMERA_DAEMON":true,
"SENTRY_DAEMON":true,"ACC_SENTRY_DAEMON":true,"ZROK_TUNNEL":false}} -- matches
ps ground truth exactly (zrok genuinely not running). The Flutter Dashboard
renders "3/4 Running" from it.

File permissions unchanged: bladewatch_ipc_token still 644.
(bladewatch_secrets.json does not exist on this device yet -- the daemon creates
it on first secret write, so the secret_get acceptance item could not be
exercised. Deferred to BladeWatch-imh6.6, which smokes auth/secret paths.)

Flutter app reached the full shell: 9-destination nav rail, Dashboard with live
data, ported Setup Guide dialog. Its own launcher entry works independently of
the native app.

THREE DEVICE-ONLY BUGS FOUND AND FIXED (none catchable by JVM/Dart tests):

1. NetworkOnMainThreadException. The "privileged" MethodChannel used the default
   binary messenger, so handlers ran on the platform main thread while IpcClient
   does blocking socket I/O. Android throws NetworkOnMainThreadException, whose
   getMessage() is null -- surfaced as "connect to 127.0.0.1:19876 failed: null".
   Fixed: the channel now uses makeBackgroundTaskQueue() (same pattern the
   live_view_texture channel already used); location.requestPermission and
   setup.* hop back with runOnUiThread.

2. jsonToMap was shallow. daemonStatus replies {"status":..,"daemons":{...}} and
   the nested JSONObject is not encodable by StandardMethodCodec, failing the
   whole call with "Unsupported value ... class org.json.JSONObject". Fixed:
   recursive conversion incl. JSONArray and JSONObject.NULL -> null.

3. isProcessRunning used pgrep -x. The daemons are app_process --nice-name, so
   /proc/<pid>/comm is "main" for all of them and a comm match never hits; every
   daemon reported stopped. Must be pgrep -f (full cmdline), which is what the
   native AdbShellExecutor has always used. A bare -f over-matches though
   (sentry_daemon is a substring of acc_sentry_daemon), so the pattern is
   (^|[^_[:alnum:]])<name>. Verified on device: sentry matches 29603 and NOT
   30141. Two regression tests added.

Also made DaemonStatusCommandTest deterministic: it ran the host's real pgrep
and asserted no matches, which became flaky under -f because -f scans full
command lines and this repo's own paths contain daemon names.

OPERATIONAL NOTE for future clean installs: uninstalling wipes the app's private
adbkey, so adbd shows "Allow USB debugging?" and daemons cannot start until it is
accepted on the head unit screen. Storage permission also needs re-granting.
close_reason: Shared UID verified on device: both packages userId=10072, Flutter APK passes the peer-UID gate, daemonStatus round-trips correctly. Three device-only bugs found and fixed (main-thread IPC, shallow jsonToMap, pgrep -x vs -f).

title: Scaffold standalone Flutter APK with shared UID
description:
> **CODE ONLY — do not touch the head unit in this task.**
> This project deliberately writes *all* Flutter code before any device work. Everything here
> is built and tested on the dev machine against the shared fakes from `BladeWatch-ncbb.5`,
> with no device and no daemon attached. On-device bring-up, screenshots, the render go/no-go
> and parity sign-off all live in **Phase 3** (`BladeWatch-imh6`).
> If you believe something genuinely cannot be verified without hardware, note it in the task
> notes for Phase 3 to pick up — do not reach for adb.

## Context

First step of the Flutter in-car UI refactor. Create the Flutter UI as a **separate, standalone APK** — not an add-to-app module inside the existing app.

Two APKs, both signed with the same key, both declaring the same `android:sharedUserId`, so they run as **one UID**:

| APK | applicationId | Role |
|---|---|---|
| existing | `net.bladewatch.app` | daemons, camera/surveillance pipeline, HTTP + IPC servers, BYD integration |
| new | `net.bladewatch.flutter` | the in-car UI |

Flutter 3.44.4 is installed at `/Users/andrewloable/development/flutter` (Dart 3.12.2).

## Why the shared UID is load-bearing — read this before touching the manifests

The daemon's loopback IPC servers on ports **19876** (`app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/TcpCommandServer.java`) and **19877** (`app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/SurveillanceIpcServer.java`) authorise callers by **peer UID**, not by token. `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/PeerCredentials.java` (`isTrusted`, line 83) accepts only root, system, shell, or the BladeWatch app's own UID. The shared IPC token in `/data/local/tmp/bladewatch_ipc_token` is world-readable (644) **by design**, so the token alone is explicitly NOT a trust boundary — `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/CoResidentAttackerTest.java` exists to prove a co-resident app with its own UID is rejected even holding a valid token.

A second APK with its own UID would therefore be treated as an attacker and blocked from every privileged operation.

`PeerCredentials.resolveAppUid()` (line 112) resolves the UID via `ctx.getApplicationInfo().uid`. Under `sharedUserId` both packages resolve to the **same numeric UID**, so `isTrusted` passes with **no change to PeerCredentials and no weakening of the gate** — `CoResidentAttackerTest` must still pass untouched. That is the whole point of this design: do not "fix" the UID check to let the new app in.

## Steps

1. `flutter create --org net.bladewatch --project-name bladewatch_ui -a kotlin flutter_ui` at the repo root. This is a **full app**, not `-t module`.
2. In `flutter_ui/android/app/build.gradle.kts`: set `applicationId = "net.bladewatch.flutter"`, restrict to `arm64-v8a` only (the head unit is arm64; the existing app uses `splits.abi` for the same reason), and set the SDK levels per the next section — **do not blindly copy the main app's 25**.
3. In **both** manifests add `android:sharedUserId="net.bladewatch.app"`:
   - `app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml`
   - `flutter_ui/android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml`
4. Configure the Flutter APK's release signing to use the **same keystore** as the main app (`KEYSTORE_FILE`, `KEYSTORE_PASSWORD`, `KEY_PASSWORD`, `KEY_ALIAS` env vars — mirror the `signingConfigs` block in `app/build.gradle.kts`). A shared UID requires an identical signing certificate; different keys will make the install fail.
5. Give the Flutter APK only the permissions the UI actually needs: `INTERNET`, `ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE`, `WAKE_LOCK`, `POST_NOTIFICATIONS`, `VIBRATE`, plus `ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION`/`ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION` for the map. **Do NOT copy the ~60 BYD HAL permissions** — vehicle data reaches the UI over RPC from the daemon, not from the BYD SDK directly.
6. Add `flutter_ui/build/`, `flutter_ui/.dart_tool/`, `flutter_ui/android/.gradle/` and `.flutter-plugins*` to `.gitignore`.

## SDK levels for the Flutter APK — decide deliberately

The main app pins `minSdk`/`targetSdk = 25` with `lint { disable += "ExpiredTargetSdkVersion" }`. That is a **legacy choice for the daemon APK** (it keeps pre-scoped-storage behaviour for direct `/sdcard` and `/data/local/tmp` access), **not** the device's capability.

**Measured device reality (2026-09-12): Android 10, API 29**, Vulkan 1.1, WebView 74.

The Flutter APK is a separate package, so it is free to choose its own levels:

- **`minSdk = 29`** — matches the actual hardware and is honest about the floor. Flutter 3.44's own floor is 24, so anything 24-29 builds; 29 documents the real target and lets you rely on Vulkan being present.
- **`targetSdk`: start at Flutter's template default and only lower it if something concretely breaks.** Forcing a Flutter app to `targetSdk = 25` is essentially untested territory for the Android embedding — do not do it just for symmetry with the main app.

**The trade-off to check before settling on a high `targetSdk`:** at 29+ scoped storage applies. The Flutter UI gets recordings and thumbnails **over HTTP from the daemon** (`/video/`, `/thumb/`, `/api/recordings`), so it should not need raw filesystem access to `/storage/emulated/0/BladeWatch/**`. Confirm that assumption while porting the Recordings screen; if it turns out direct file access is needed, the options are to request `MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` for the Flutter APK too, or to keep serving that content over HTTP. Record the decision and the reasoning in the task notes.

`sharedUserId` is unaffected by either value.

## Constraints

- **The existing APK's behaviour must not change at all in this task** beyond adding the one `sharedUserId` attribute. Do not add Flutter dependencies to `app/build.gradle.kts`, do not touch `settings.gradle.kts`, do not modify `app/proguard-rules.pro`.
- Do NOT modify `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/PeerCredentials.java`, `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/TcpCommandServer.java`, `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/SurveillanceIpcServer.java`, or any test under `app/src/test/`.
- **Do not copy the main app's SDK levels.** They are a deliberate legacy choice for the daemon APK, not a description of the hardware.
- Do NOT modify `web/`, the daemon, or the protos.
- Do NOT commit. Leave changes in the working tree.

## Adding sharedUserId to an already-installed app changes its UID

Android will refuse to upgrade the installed `net.bladewatch.app` once `sharedUserId` is added — the package must be **uninstalled and reinstalled**. That is already this project's standard deploy step (see the clean-reinstall block in `CLAUDE.md`), but call it out in the task notes so nobody is surprised on the car, and confirm the app's data/config survives or is regenerated: `/data/local/tmp/bladewatch_config.json`, `/data/local/tmp/bladewatch_secrets.json` and the device ID live outside the app sandbox and are owned by shell, so they should persist.

## Conventions for this refactor (decided — do not deviate)

- Kotlin source lives under `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/`. **Note the directory path and the package name differ in this project**: files under `com/loabletech/bladewatch/` declare `package net.bladewatch.app.*`. Match the surrounding files; do not "fix" this.
- JVM tests go in `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/`, mirroring the main source layout.
- Kotlin coverage is measured by **Kover** with a verify gate (set up in BladeWatch-ncbb.5). Run `./gradlew test koverVerify`.
- Dart state management for this refactor is plain `ChangeNotifier` controllers — no Riverpod, no BLoC. Relevant if this task touches any Dart.
- **No golden tests** anywhere in this refactor.

## Tests (TDD — required)

**Write the failing test first**, then the implementation, then refactor.

- JVM unit tests go in `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/`. The existing suite is ~20 files / ~3,100 LOC — read the closest neighbours first: `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/connect/ConnectWireParityTest.java` (proto/JSON wire parity), `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/auth/AuthManagerTest.java`, `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/AuthMiddlewareTest.java`, `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/IpcRoundTripTest.java`, `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/IpcTokenManagerTest.java`, `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/logging/SecretRedactorTest.java`, and the `vehicle/` suite (`app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/vehicle/VehicleClientMapTest.kt`, `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/vehicle/VehicleFormattersTest.kt`, `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/vehicle/TyreTierTest.kt`, `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/vehicle/VehicleI18nParityTest.kt`). **CLAUDE.md's Testing section lists only four of these and is stale — trust the filesystem.**
- **100% coverage of every method you add, including every error path.** On this head unit the real failures are: the shell call fails, the daemon is not up yet, permission denied, the IPC token is unreadable. Each needs a test proving the right error reaches the caller rather than being swallowed.
- Test argument marshalling in **both** directions. A dropped or mistyped field across a platform channel produces a bug that only appears on the car.
- **Never put a real secret in a fixture.** Use obviously-fake values; `SecretRedactorTest` is the reference for this.
- Android's `org.json` is a stub in JVM unit tests — that is why `org.json:json:20240303` is a `testImplementation`. `protobuf-java-util` is available for proto/JSON assertions.
- Run `./gradlew test koverVerify` and record the percentage in the notes; it must not drop.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `cd flutter_ui && flutter build apk --target-platform android-arm64 --debug` succeeds.
- [ ] `./gradlew assembleDebug` for the existing app still succeeds, and `./gradlew test` still passes.
- [ ] Both manifests declare the identical `sharedUserId`, and both release configs use the same keystore.
- [ ] `unzip -l` on the Flutter APK shows `lib/arm64-v8a/libflutter.so` and NO other ABI directory.
- [ ] The Flutter APK's manifest contains no BYD HAL permission.
- [ ] `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/PeerCredentials.java` and `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/CoResidentAttackerTest.java` are byte-for-byte unchanged.

title: Flutter in-car UI: Phase 0 - Flutter APK scaffold and shared-UID wiring (CODE ONLY)
description:
> **CODE ONLY — no device work in this epic.**
> All Flutter code is written and tested on the dev machine before the head unit is touched
> at all. Every task here runs against the shared fakes from `BladeWatch-ncbb.5` with no
> device and no daemon attached. On-device bring-up, the render go/no-go, screenshots and
> parity sign-off are **Phase 3** (`BladeWatch-imh6`).

## Context

BladeWatch's in-car UI is ~22,500 LOC of Kotlin (30 fragments/controllers) plus 396 KB of XML across 34 layout files, hosted by MainActivity over a Navigation graph. We are replacing it with Flutter. The Angular SPA at `web/` is OUT OF SCOPE and must not be touched.

Before any screen work happens, we must prove Flutter renders acceptably on the actual target hardware. The BYD DiLink v3 head unit is old and has a known-bad GPU driver:

- `minSdk` / `targetSdk` = 25 in `app/build.gradle.kts` — a deliberate build setting, **not** the device's API level
- GPU is an Adreno 610 whose GL driver **crashes under sustained rendering** — a native Filament port was tried and had to be reverted for exactly this reason. See `docs/build-and-operations.md:58` and `docs/byd-integrations.md:160`.
- The embedded WebView is **Chrome 74**, not 58 (measured).
- Flutter 3.44.4 (installed at /Users/andrewloable/development/flutter) has a minSdk floor of 24. The device is **API 29 with Vulkan 1.1**, so Impeller's **Vulkan** backend is available — see the verified table below.

This epic is a **go/no-go gate**. If Flutter cannot render smoothly and stably here, the whole refactor is abandoned and no further epic starts.

## Verified device facts (measured 2026-09-12 — several docs are stale, trust this)

| | |
|---|---|
| Model / build | BYD AUTO, `QKQ1.210910.001 release-keys` |
| Android | **10 (API 29)** — NOT 7.1. `docs/ui-ux-design-language.md` and `CLAUDE.md` still say Android 7.1 / Chrome 58; both are wrong |
| GPU | Adreno 610, OpenGL ES 3.2, driver **V@415.0** (2021-12-06) |
| Vulkan | **supported** — `android.hardware.vulkan.level=1`, `vulkan.version=4198400` (= 1.1.0), plus `vulkan.compute` |
| WebView | **74.0.3729.186**, not Chrome 58 |
| Root | **none** — no `su` binary, `ro.secure=1`, `ro.debuggable=0`, `ro.build.type=user` |

**What this changes:** API 29 + Vulkan 1.1 means Flutter's Impeller can use its **Vulkan** backend, not the OpenGLES fallback. That matters because the Filament crash that killed the native 3D hero was on the **GL** driver (V@415.0) — Vulkan is a different driver path, so that specific failure may simply not apply. It is still the same GPU and the same vendor driver bundle, so this makes Vulkan the *most likely to work* option, not a guarantee. Test it, do not assume it.

**`minSdk`/`targetSdk = 25` in `app/build.gradle.kts` is a conservative build setting, not the device's level.** The device is API 29.

## Scope

Scaffold the Flutter UI as a **separate APK** (`net.bladewatch.flutter`) sharing a UID with `net.bladewatch.app`, prove the shared UID passes the daemon's peer-UID gate, and measure rendering on the real head unit at <CAR_IP>:5555.

**Why a separate APK:** the Flutter engine never ships in the APK that hosts the daemons, so the main app's build, R8 config, size and `app_process` classpath are untouched — which removes most of the risk this epic exists to measure. Iteration is also far faster (`flutter run` with hot reload, no Gradle rebuild of the main project).

**Why a shared UID:** the daemon's loopback IPC servers (19876/19877) authorise by **peer UID** via `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/PeerCredentials.java` — root, system, shell, or the BladeWatch app's own UID only. A second APK with its own UID is treated as a co-resident attacker and blocked (that exact scenario is pinned by `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/CoResidentAttackerTest.java`). Setting `android:sharedUserId` on both packages, signed with the same key, makes them one UID so `isTrusted` passes **with no change to the security gate**. Never widen `PeerCredentials` to solve this.

## Abort criterion

Visible tearing/stutter, a GPU driver crash during the soak, or any regression to daemon startup. If any of these occur, close this epic as blocked with the measurements recorded and STOP — do not start Epic 1.

## Conventions for this refactor

- Dart lives under `flutter_ui/lib/` with `screens/<name>/` holding a pure-Dart `ChangeNotifier` controller, models, and the screen widget. Kotlin lives under `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/` with `package net.bladewatch.app.*`.
- Coverage gates: `flutter test --coverage` (Dart, `lib/gen` excluded) and `./gradlew koverVerify` (Kotlin). Both thresholds ratchet upward and may never be lowered.
- **No golden tests.** Visual parity is verified on the device against `screenshots/native/`.
- Verification happens on the head unit at <CAR_IP>:5555. Always pass `-s <CAR_IP>:5555` to every adb command.

## Tests and coverage (applies to every child task)

Every child task in this epic is **test-driven**: failing test first, then implementation, then refactor.

- **Target 100%.** Pure logic — controllers, models, formatters, mappers, validation, error handling — has no excuse for a gap. Anything uncovered is listed line-by-line with a concrete reason; "hard to test" means extract it, not skip it.
- Dart: `flutter test --coverage`, with generated protobuf under `flutter_ui/lib/gen` excluded from the denominator.
- Kotlin: JVM tests in `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/`, measured by `./gradlew koverVerify`.
- **Coverage may never go DOWN between tasks.** Each child records its number in its notes.
- Tests run green on the dev machine with no device and no daemon attached; mock at the RPC and platform-channel boundaries using the shared fakes from `BladeWatch-ncbb.5`.
- Any bug found at any point gets a failing test written FIRST, then the fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three child tasks are closed.
- [ ] A written go/no-go verdict is recorded in this epic's notes, with the measured numbers (frame times, APK size delta, soak duration).
- [ ] Daemon startup verified unaffected on device.
- [ ] Every child task recorded a Dart and a Kotlin coverage figure.
- [ ] The epic's final coverage figures are recorded here and are not lower than the previous epic's.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.

Per this epic's own current title/scope ("Phase 0 - Flutter APK scaffold and shared-UID wiring (CODE ONLY)"), the code-only scaffolding and shared-UID wiring is genuinely complete: flutter_ui/ builds an arm64-only debug APK carrying android:sharedUserId=net.bladewatch.app identical to the main app's, the main app is unaffected (assembleDebug + test both pass), and the repo hygiene around the scaffold (unused platforms, gitignore, tracked screenshot baseline) is cleaned up. No go/no-go verdict is recorded here because that decision has not been made yet — it belongs to BladeWatch-imh6 once 7965.2/7965.3 run on-device.

title: Angular webapp login loop — isAuthenticated() reads HttpOnly byd_session cookie
description: After fixing the zone.js blank-render (BladeWatch-0u0t), the hosted Angular SPA (web/) renders but traps the user in a /login redirect loop when accessed via browser/zrok tunnel. Root cause: web/src/app/core/auth/auth.service.ts isAuthenticated() decides login state by reading the 'byd_session' cookie from document.cookie — but the server sets byd_session as HttpOnly (AuthApiHandler.handleTokenValidation buildCookie httpOnly=true), so JavaScript can NEVER read it. isAuthenticated() therefore always returns false; authGuard (web/src/app/core/auth/auth.guard.ts) redirects every protected route back to /login even immediately after a successful login (the login component shows 'Login successful! Redirecting...' then bounces back). The server also sets a non-HttpOnly hint cookie byd_auth=1 (httpOnly=false) with the same lifetime, set by BOTH the REST /auth/token path and the Connect AuthService.Login path (captureWithCookies reuses handleTokenValidation). Fix: change isAuthenticated() to test for a non-empty byd_auth cookie instead of byd_session; also clear byd_auth locally in clearAndRedirect() so logout flips state immediately. Verified the loop with a headless Chromium probe over the tunnel: final URL stays /login, app-login stays mounted, visible text 'Login successful! Redirecting...'. Acceptance: after fix + rebuild, headless probe completing the login reaches a non-/login route with a page component (e.g. app-dashboard/app-surveillance) mounted; logout returns to /login. Do not make mistakes.
close_reason: Fixed and verified on device <CAR_IP> over zrok tunnel via headless Chromium probe: zone.js import added to web/src/main.ts (NG0908 gone, app renders); isAuthenticated() now reads byd_auth hint cookie (login reaches dashboard, no loop). All routes render real content.

title: Angular webapp renders blank — zone.js polyfill never loaded (NG0908)
description: The hosted Angular SPA (web/, Vite + @analogjs/vite-plugin-angular, Angular 19.2.25) renders a blank page everywhere (localhost 127.0.0.1:8080 AND zrok tunnel). Root cause: bootstrap throws NG0908 in the NgZone constructor because zone.js is never loaded. app.config.ts uses provideZoneChangeDetection({eventCoalescing:true}) which REQUIRES zone.js, and zone.js@~0.15.0 is a dependency, but unlike an Angular CLI build the Vite/Analog build does NOT auto-inject zone.js — and web/src/main.ts does not 'import zone.js'. Result: no polyfills chunk in web/dist/assets, Zone global undefined, NgZone ctor throws, <app-root> stays empty. Fix: add "import 'zone.js';" as the FIRST line of web/src/main.ts, rebuild (npm run build copies web/dist into app/src/main/assets/web/angular via buildAngularWebUI gradle task), redeploy. Verified diagnosis with a headless Chromium probe over the tunnel: single console error 'S: NG0908' in ngZoneFactory, app-root innerHTML length 0, zero failed network requests. Acceptance: after fix, web/dist/index.html includes a polyfills/zone module OR main bundle contains zone.js; headless probe shows app-root non-empty and no NG0908. Do not make mistakes.
close_reason: Fixed and verified on device <CAR_IP> over zrok tunnel via headless Chromium probe: zone.js import added to web/src/main.ts (NG0908 gone, app renders); isAuthenticated() now reads byd_auth hint cookie (login reaches dashboard, no loop). All routes render real content.

title: Dashboard crash: malformed MaterialButton/Chip XML in fragment_dashboard (M3 refactor regression)
description:
ROOT CAUSE: During the M3 refactor, fragment_dashboard.xml (both layout/ and layout-land/ variants) had 6 elements each with a premature self-closing /> placed right after the android:id attribute, leaving style/layout_width/layout_height as dangling text. aapt2 tolerated it and built an APK, but at runtime LayoutInflater threw 'You must supply a layout_width attribute' (InflateException at DashboardFragment.onCreateView:130, binary XML line #65 = btnViewAllTrips). The device is landscape so layout-land was the one crashing.

AFFECTED ELEMENTS (each had id-then-stray-/> then dangling attrs): btnViewAllTrips, btnSetPassword, btnRegenerateToken, heroChipTunnel, heroChipServices, heroChipRecording — in BOTH layout/fragment_dashboard.xml and layout-land/fragment_dashboard.xml (12 total).

FIX APPLIED: Removed the premature ' />' after android:id so the element absorbs its style + layout_width/height + remaining attributes, ending with a single proper ' />'. Verified with xml.dom.minidom parse (0 malformed) and a heuristic scan across all layout*/ dirs (0 remaining). Rebuilt assembleDebug (SUCCESS), reinstalled to <CAR_IP>:5555 — Dashboard now inflates with no crash.

Acceptance criteria:
[x] No InflateException on Dashboard launch
[x] Both layout/ and layout-land/ fragment_dashboard.xml well-formed
[x] All 12 elements have valid layout_width/height
[x] assembleDebug builds
[x] App launches to Dashboard on device without crashing

title: DaemonReadinessChecker /proc check fails cross-UID under hidepid=2 → camera stuck 'connecting'
description: The app shows 'connecting to camera' forever and no recordings are written. Root cause: DaemonReadinessChecker.isReady() (app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/client/DaemonReadinessChecker.java) verifies daemon liveness with new File('/proc/'+pid).exists(). /proc is mounted hidepid=2,gid=3009 on the BYD head unit. The daemon runs as shell UID (2000); the app runs as its app UID and is not in gid 3009, so it cannot stat the daemon's /proc/<pid> entry. isReady() therefore always returns false from the app process, waitUntilReady() times out, CameraDaemonClient.connect() aborts, the app never connects to port 19876, never sends the 'start' recording command, and never opens the live preview. Fix: replace the /proc check with a TCP connect probe to 127.0.0.1:19876 (UID-independent; also covers the stale-sentinel-after-kill-9 case since a dead daemon refuses connections). Acceptance: app connects to daemon, live preview loads, recordings are written during a drive. Verified via redeploy + logcat.
close_reason: Bulk-closed at user request (2026-06-12).

title: CameraDaemon crash-loop: nc -z health probe always fails on toybox nc
description:
ROOT CAUSE: isCameraDaemonResponsive() in app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/launcher/DaemonLauncher.kt (lines ~1169-1181) shells out 'nc -z -w 3 127.0.0.1 19876'. The BYD head unit's toybox nc does NOT support -z (verified on device <CAR_IP>: prints 'nc: Unknown option z' and returns fail even against a confirmed-listening port). So the HealthCheck-Camera path (~every 30s) always sees the daemon as 'in ps but not responsive', kills -9 and relaunches it. The daemon crash-loops ~every 34s; HTTP server on 8080 is intermittently down, so Settings>Recording (and other data screens) hang on 'Loading...'.

FIX 1 (DaemonLauncher.kt isCameraDaemonResponsive): replace the nc shell-out with an in-process java.net.Socket().connect(InetSocketAddress(127.0.0.1,19876), 3000) on a daemon thread; callback(true) on success, false on exception. toybox-independent.

FIX 2 (app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/ui/fragment/recording/RecordingSettingsController.kt loadData() lines ~135-159): the background fetch thread has no try/catch and never sets RecordingSettingsLoadState.Error, so the Error render branch (line ~173) is dead and any fetch exception hangs the spinner. Wrap the thread body so failures set loadedState=Error(message) and post renderCurrentTab().

ACCEPTANCE: (1) daemon no longer relaunches every ~30s (verify daemon log 'Daemon ready' timestamps stay stable / singleton PID stable); (2) nc no longer invoked for responsiveness; (3) Settings>Recording loads data or shows an Error, never an indefinite spinner; (4) build compiles.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles before closing.
notes:
Both fixes applied + compileDebugKotlin BUILD SUCCESSFUL.
- DaemonLauncher.kt: isCameraDaemonResponsive() now uses in-process Socket().connect(127.0.0.1:19876, 3000) instead of 'nc -z' (toybox nc has no -z). Added java.net.InetSocketAddress/Socket imports.
- RecordingSettingsController.kt loadData(): wrapped fetch thread in try/catch; sets RecordingSettingsLoadState.Error on failure + posts renderCurrentTab() so the spinner can't hang.
REMAINING: on-device verification not yet done. Needs clean reinstall (per CLAUDE.md daemon-cleanup steps) on <CAR_IP>, then confirm daemon 'Daemon ready' timestamps stop cycling ~every 34s and Settings>Recording loads. Not committed (developer commits manually).

comments.author: Andrew Loable
comments.text:
Independent on-device confirmation (device <CAR_IP>, this session, before it powered off):

LIVE REPRO of the crash loop:
- Tapped Live in native UI -> stuck on "Connecting to camera..." indefinitely (screenshot confirmed). Camera HW powered on (mm-camera "sensor stream ON", surface added) but no decodable WS frames because the daemon kept dying.
- cam_daemon.log: 23x "=== CAMERA DAEMON READY ===" this session; restart timestamps metronomic at ~34s (30s HealthCheck interval + ~3s startup): 16:39:19 -> 16:39:53 -> 16:40:27 -> 16:41:01 -> 16:41:35 -> 16:42:09 -> 16:42:43.
- Confirmed the probe defect directly: "nc -z -w 3 127.0.0.1 19876" -> "nc: Unknown option z" -> fail, even though the port is listening (plain nc connect OK; getStreamMode round-trip returns JSON). So isCameraDaemonResponsive() returned false for a healthy daemon every cycle -> kill+relaunch.

FIX VERIFIED IN TREE: isCameraDaemonResponsive() now uses in-process Socket().connect(127.0.0.1:19876, 3000); imports present; compileDebugKotlin EXIT=0. Correct, toybox-independent fix.

NEW CONCERN (needs device verification, NOT confirmed): DaemonReadinessChecker.isReady() checks new File("/proc/<pid>").exists(). From the app UID via run-as, "ls -d /proc/<shell-daemon-pid>" returned "Permission denied" (SELinux untrusted_app -> shell domain). If File.exists() also gets EACCES -> false, isReady() would return false from the app process even when the sentinel is readable (644) and the daemon is alive, making SecretConfigBridge/CameraDaemonClient waitUntilReady() always time out. This contradicts BladeWatch-2x4e close claim that isReady() returns true. Live view itself does NOT hit this path (uses HTTP RPC + WS on 8080, not CameraDaemonClient on 19876), which is why it still reached "Connecting". Recommend verifying on-device that isReady() actually returns true from the app process after the crash-loop fix is installed.

title: ANR on fresh install: main-thread blocking IPC in auth load (DashboardFragment → AuthManager → SecretConfigBridge)
description:
ROOT CAUSE (confirmed from ANR trace anr_2026-06-09-16-07-34, dropbox data_app_anr): The app ANRs on a clean reinstall when the dashboard opens before the daemon is ready.

Main-thread stack:
  SecretConfigBridge.runIpcBlocking(SecretConfigBridge.kt:254) [future.get(6s) parkNanos]
  SecretConfigBridge.writeViaIpc(193) / putString(75)
  AuthManager.writeToConfig(AuthManager.java:655)
  AuthManager.initialize(228) [locked AuthManager.class]
  AuthManager.getState(287) [locked AuthManager.class]
  DashboardFragment.loadAuthState(DashboardFragment.kt:526)
  DashboardFragment.onViewCreated(141)

Two problems:
1) DashboardFragment.loadAuthState() calls AuthManager.getState()/initialize() on the MAIN thread. On a fresh install the unified config has no auth secret yet, so initialize() -> writeToConfig() -> SecretConfigBridge.putString() performs a blocking IPC write to the daemon. The daemon is not ready, so it parks.
2) SecretConfigBridge.runIpcBlocking() caps the main-thread wait at future.get(6, TimeUnit.SECONDS). Android's input-dispatch ANR threshold is 5s, so a 6s block GUARANTEES an ANR. Recurring ANRs observed at 15:56, 15:57, 15:59, 16:07 (and 06-07).

FIX (two parts):
A) DashboardFragment.kt: run loadAuthState()'s AuthManager.getState()/initialize() on the lifecycle-managed metricsExecutor (single-thread, shut down in onDestroyView), then post the result to mainHandler. Show masked placeholder immediately. Also move the AuthManager.getState() call inside scheduleAuthRetry()'s postDelayed off the main thread the same way. Files: app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/ui/fragment/DashboardFragment.kt loadAuthState() (~517), scheduleAuthRetry() (~538).
B) SecretConfigBridge.kt runIpcBlocking() (~254): lower the main-thread cap from 6 seconds to 4 seconds (below the 5s ANR threshold) as defense-in-depth for any other inadvertent main-thread caller. Update the comment.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
- [ ] loadAuthState() no longer calls AuthManager on the main thread; UI updates posted via mainHandler.
- [ ] scheduleAuthRetry() resolves AuthManager.getState() on a background thread.
- [ ] runIpcBlocking main-thread timeout < 5s.
- [ ] ./gradlew assembleDebug compiles.
- [ ] Clean reinstall on device (<CAR_IP>:5555) + open dashboard before daemon ready does NOT ANR; access code fills in within a few seconds once daemon is up.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
notes: Second ANR (16:20:50) after first fix: MainActivity.onResume() -> AuthManager.refresh() (synchronized) blocked on the AuthManager.class monitor held by the background getState()/initialize() thread doing the daemon IPC (up to 30s readiness wait, no main-thread cap since off-main-thread). Moving DashboardFragment.getState() off-main-thread (part A) made the bg thread hold the monitor LONGER, surfacing this lock-contention ANR. Fix: refresh() is now lock-free (operates only on volatile cache fields; cachedState=null is the real invalidation, stateVersion bump is advisory). Residual structural smell: getState()/initialize() still hold the class monitor across the blocking IPC — any main-thread getState() on a stale cache during the daemon-down window could still contend. Deferred (riskier refactor).

title: CameraDaemon: make camera_daemon.ready sentinel world-readable (app UID cannot read it)
description:
## Problem
The new ready sentinel at /data/local/tmp/camera_daemon.ready is written by the SHELL-UID daemon (CameraDaemon, UID 2000) using a bare java.io.FileWriter, which creates the file mode 600 (shell-only). The Android app runs as a DISTINCT app UID (e.g. 10085) and reads this file via DaemonReadinessChecker.isReady(). It cannot read a mode-600 shell-owned file, so isReady() returns false forever, waitUntilReady() always times out, and CameraDaemonClient.connect() returns false after a 60s stall. This BREAKS every app->daemon IPC call even when the daemon and its TCP port are perfectly healthy. This is a ship-blocking regression introduced by the readiness-sentinel change.

## Documented invariant being violated
app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/IpcTokenManager.java class javadoc (around line 18-28) states: 'FileWriter creates files mode 600 (shell-only) by default, which the app cannot read - that silently breaks every app->daemon IPC call ... We therefore make the token world-readable after writing. Do NOT revert this to a bare FileWriter without restoring an equivalent chmod.' The same pattern is used in IpcTokenManager.generate() (~line 59-64): File.setReadable(true, false).

## What to do
In app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/daemon/CameraDaemon.java, locate the sentinel write block (search for READY_SENTINEL and 'Write ready sentinel', ~line 606-617). Immediately after fw.close(), add:
    new File(READY_SENTINEL).setReadable(true, false);
Wrap in try/catch and log on failure, mirroring IpcTokenManager.generate(). setReadable(true, false) grants read to group+other -> rw-r--r-- (644).

## Constraints
- Do NOT change the write content (PID) or location.
- Match the existing IpcTokenManager chmod pattern exactly.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] After daemon startup, /data/local/tmp/camera_daemon.ready is mode 644 (verify: adb shell ls -l /data/local/tmp/camera_daemon.ready shows -rw-r--r--)
- [ ] The app UID can read the sentinel and DaemonReadinessChecker.isReady() returns true
- [ ] CameraDaemonClient.connect() succeeds promptly (no 60s stall) when the daemon is up
- [ ] Build compiles with ./gradlew assembleDebug

Do not make mistakes. Read CameraDaemon.java and IpcTokenManager.java fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.

title: Fix stale CameraDaemon watchdog cleanup on reinstall
description:
## Problem
After app reinstall, stale daemon watchdog scripts survive because `pkill`/`killall` is unreliable on BYD toybox (documented in AGENTS.md). The old watchdog respawns `app_process` with a `CLASSPATH` pointing to the deleted old APK, causing `ClassNotFoundException: net.bladewatch.app.daemon.CameraDaemon` and `SIGABRT` crashes (3 tombstones in logcat).

## Evidence
```
F/DEBUG: Abort message: 'No pending exception expected: java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: net.bladewatch.app.daemon.CameraDaemon
```
Healthy daemon (PID 11386) runs alongside 3 crash tombstones from stale PIDs 16557/16620/16729.

## Fix
Replace `pkill -9 -f 'start_cam_daemon'` / `pkill -9 -f 'byd_cam_daemon'` / `killall` in `DaemonLauncher.kt:191-200` with PID-based enumeration:
```
ps -A -o PID,ARGS | grep ... | awk '{print $1}' | xargs kill -9
```
This must target:
- `start_cam_daemon` watchdog processes
- `start_acc_sentry` watchdog processes
- `byd_cam_daemon` (CameraDaemon)
- `sentry_daemon` (SentryDaemon)
- `acc_sentry_daemon` (AccSentryDaemon)

## Acceptance
- [ ] Clean reinstall no longer produces `ClassNotFoundException: CameraDaemon` tombstones
- [ ] Only one CameraDaemon instance runs after reinstall
- [ ] SentryDaemon and AccSentryDaemon are properly restarted after reinstall
acceptance_criteria: Verify clean reinstall produces zero stale daemon crash tombstones

title: ConnectDispatcher: accept unary content-type application/json (fix 415 on every RPC)
description:
## Problem
The native Android UI cannot reach the daemon over Connect. ConnectDispatcher.dispatch() rejects any request whose Content-Type does not start with "application/connect+json" (HTTP 415). But that is the STREAMING content type. Unary Connect RPCs use "application/json". connect-kotlin 0.6.0 (com.connectrpc.impl.ProtocolClient) sends "application/" + codec.encodingName() => application/json for unary, and "application/connect+" + codec.encodingName() for streaming. Every Android UI call is unary, so 100% of RPCs get 415 before any handler runs.

## File to change
- app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/connect/ConnectDispatcher.java
  - Constant CONTENT_TYPE_CONNECT (~line 37)
  - Content-Type guard (~lines 85-89): if (contentType == null || !contentType.startsWith(CONTENT_TYPE_CONNECT)) -> 415

## Steps
1. Read ConnectDispatcher.java fully first.
2. Replace the strict guard so it ACCEPTS unary "application/json" AND streaming "application/connect+json" (case-insensitive, allow charset suffix e.g. "application/json; charset=utf-8"). Optionally also accept application/proto / application/connect+proto for future binary, but JSON is what is used today.
3. Keep returning 415 only for genuinely unsupported types (e.g. text/html, missing).
4. Do NOT remove the Connect-Protocol-Version: 1 header check or the POST-only check.

## Constraints
- Do not touch the REST handlers or the proto files.
- Do not change AuthMiddleware.
- Response content-type echo is handled in a SEPARATE task (do not change response writing here beyond what is needed to compile).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] POST /bladewatch.v1.VehicleService/GetState with Content-Type: application/json and Connect-Protocol-Version: 1 reaches the handler (no 415).
- [ ] POST with Content-Type: application/connect+json still works (streaming form still accepted).
- [ ] POST with Content-Type: text/html still returns 415.
- [ ] ./gradlew :app:compileDebugJavaWithJavac passes.
- [ ] On device (<CAR_IP>:5555): open the app, exercise Vehicle/Trips/Recording screens, and confirm logcat no longer shows 415 on /bladewatch.v1.* and data populates.

Do not make mistakes. Read ConnectDispatcher.java fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
close_reason: ConnectDispatcher now accepts unary application/json (and streaming application/connect+json) via isSupportedContentType(); tolerant of charset suffix + case. Verified by ConnectContentTypeNegotiationTest (10/10 green): unary request reaches handler (was 415 pre-fix). compileDebugJavaWithJavac BUILD SUCCESSFUL.

title: ConnectDispatcher: echo response Content-Type matching the request (unary application/json) for connect-web/Angular
description:
## Problem
ConnectDispatcher always writes responses with Content-Type: application/connect+json (sendConnectSuccess ~line 127 and the error path ~line 145). For a UNARY request the Connect protocol requires the response Content-Type to match the request (application/json). connect-kotlin 0.6.0 is lenient on the unary response (it branches on HTTP status, not response content-type), but @connectrpc/connect-web v2 (used by the Angular app in web/) validates the unary response content-type and will reject application/connect+json. So even after the request-side fix, the Angular client stays broken.

## File to change
- app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/connect/ConnectDispatcher.java
  - sendConnectSuccess(...) (~line 106 / response headers ~lines 127, 143-148)
  - sendConnectError(...) (~line 145)

## Steps
1. Read ConnectDispatcher.java fully first.
2. Determine unary vs streaming from the REQUEST content-type (passed into dispatch): a request of application/json is unary; application/connect+json is streaming.
3. Thread that classification into sendConnectSuccess/sendConnectError (e.g. a boolean unary flag or pass the negotiated response content-type) and set the response Content-Type accordingly: application/json for unary, application/connect+json for streaming.
4. Keep HTTP status mapping (connectCodeToHttpStatus) and the error JSON body shape unchanged.

## Constraints
- Depends on the request-accept task being merged/coordinated (same file).
- Do not change proto, REST handlers, or AuthMiddleware.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A unary request (Content-Type: application/json) gets a response with Content-Type: application/json.
- [ ] A streaming-form request (application/connect+json) gets application/connect+json back.
- [ ] Error responses echo the same content-type as the corresponding request type.
- [ ] ./gradlew :app:compileDebugJavaWithJavac passes.
- [ ] Angular web app (served from the daemon) can perform a real Connect call (e.g. SystemService/GetStatus) without an "unexpected content-type" error.

Do not make mistakes. Read ConnectDispatcher.java fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.

title: gRPC/Connect Android UI outage: unary content-type negotiation + hardening
description:
Umbrella for fixing the post-migration regression where the native Android UI (and the Angular web app) cannot reach the daemon over Connect. Root cause: ConnectDispatcher requires the STREAMING content type (application/connect+json) but unary Connect clients (connect-kotlin 0.6.0 and @connectrpc/connect-web v2) send application/json for unary RPCs, so every unary call is rejected with HTTP 415 before the handler runs. Before the migration everything worked over REST.

Evidence:
- app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/connect/ConnectDispatcher.java: CONTENT_TYPE_CONNECT = "application/connect+json" (~line 37); request rejected with 415 if Content-Type does not start with it (~lines 85-89); success/error responses always sent as application/connect+json (~lines 127, 145).
- connect-kotlin 0.6.0 com.connectrpc.impl.ProtocolClient bytecode: unary() builds content type as "application/" + codec.encodingName() => application/json; stream() builds "application/connect+" + codec.encodingName() => application/connect+json.
- All Android UI clients use the unary path (ConnectClientProvider -> *ServiceClient -> suspend unary): VehicleClient.kt, TripsClient.kt, RecordingSettingsClient.kt, SurveillanceSettingsClient.kt, LiveStreamClient.kt.
- web/package.json uses @connectrpc/connect-web v2 (same unary application/json behavior).
- ConnectWireParityTest only checks JSON serialization shape, never the HTTP round-trip, so it did not catch this.

Child tasks cover: the core dispatcher fix (request accept + response echo), an HTTP round-trip test, and several lower-severity hardening items surfaced during review. See child issues for detail.

title: gRPC/Connect <-> REST 1:1 parity remediation
description:
