   hairpinning reasons, so a same-NAT test measures nothing at all — it is not merely a
   weaker signal, it is no signal.
3. Record, for at least a 10-minute run: sustained throughput (Mbit/s), end-to-end latency,
   dropped and late frame rate, car CPU usage, and thermal throttling if observable.
4. Repeat at each quality setting the producer supports. If a lower setting is required to
   sustain the stream, that is a RESULT — record which one, do not quietly pick it.
5. Measure the IPC boundary specifically: how much of any shortfall is the JS-to-native hop
   versus the network? Instrument the pump if needed. "It is slow" without knowing where is
   not actionable; the fix differs completely between the two.
6. Compare every number against the baselines, especially tor. Tor is the bar — it is what
   owners have today.
7. Record an explicit verdict.

## Constraints

- Do NOT measure on the same NAT as the car and report it as a Pear result.
- Do NOT use a different measurement method than the baseline task. Reproduce its harness.
- Do NOT tune quality mid-run to make a number look better.
- Do NOT run for 30 seconds. Buffer growth and thermal throttling are the two failure modes
  that matter and both need time to appear.
- Do NOT close with "it seemed fine". A close reason without numbers does not discharge the
  gate on the Tor-removal task.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Live-view measurements captured over Pear from a network genuinely different from the
      car's, with the network described.
- [ ] Each run lasted at least 10 minutes.
- [ ] Throughput, latency, dropped-frame rate, car CPU and thermal behaviour recorded.
- [ ] Measured at every supported quality setting.
- [ ] The JS-to-native IPC cost is separated from network cost.
- [ ] Every number is directly comparable to the baseline task's, same harness.
- [ ] An explicit verdict: does live view over Pear sustain an acceptable stream, yes or no,
      and at which quality setting.
- [ ] If no, a follow-up bd issue is filed naming the options (reduce quality over Pear /
      LAN-only live view / keep tor for video) and the Tor-removal task is updated to
      reference it.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
notes:
THROUGHPUT RISK found while implementing .3: pear-end moves connection bytes as BASE64 inside JSON frames (CONNECTION_DATA / CONNECTION_WRITE, index.js lines 183-188 and 705-716), so every video byte is inflated ~33% and JSON-parsed on every BareKit IPC hop, on top of the per-hop IPC copy. When separating IPC cost from network cost (step 5), measure this encoding cost explicitly -- if it is the bottleneck, the fix is FrameType.RAW (schema.js already reserves 0x01, 'no reader yet'), not a quality downgrade.
Measure with tools/throughput/Throughput.java exactly as docs/throughput-harness.md defines (rdtj.9's baselines are in its close reason: loopback and LAN TLS; no tor baseline by owner decision). For Pear the client points at the companion LocalGateway's http://127.0.0.1:<port> with the route forced to Pear from a DIFFERENT network; sampler --procs byd_cam_daemon,pear_daemon.
READY 2026-09-26: runner companion/integration_test/pear_bench_test.dart (docs/throughput-harness.md, Running the Pear path) runs the unchanged harness through the companion's LocalGateway with the route forced to Pear, plus cold start / burst / thumbnails. Smoke-tested end to end on the car's own network (NOT a measurement): paired over Pear, harness rpc and clip through the gateway, burst, thumbnails (outcomes by status: 200s and one 202 thumbnail-pending), 2 cold starts, quality presets logged (ULTRA_LOW, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, ULTRA_HIGH, SMOOTH, ...). One of five smoke runs reported a test failure after all results had printed; not reproduced in two reruns. Session plan: on the car's LAN turn PEAR_PEER on, record meta, start the car sampler (detached, 2400 s); switch the Mac to a phone hotspot; run video MEDIUM 600 s (longer than a foreground command, so it runs detached and is waited on), then rpc/clip/burst/thumbnails/20 cold starts; further presets if time allows; back on the LAN fetch the sample, revoke the pear bench device, PEAR_PEER off. Found while preparing: BladeWatch-qryk (companion announces itself on the car's topic).
RUN 2026-09-26 (Pear, companion on a phone hotspot, genuinely different network: Mac on 10.101.x, the car's LAN unreachable; hotspot HyperDHT firewalled=true randomized=true; hotspot ping to 1.1.1.1 avg 102 ms, 74-151, 0 percent loss; car PARKED WITH THE CAR OFF, head unit awake and recording; build 1.4.0.0 debug of feature/v1.4.0.0, quality MEDIUM 800x600 10 fps 1 Mbit/s, same as the baselines).
LIVE VIDEO, harness video --seconds 600 --probe-every 2, one viewer:
| Path | Duration | fps | Mbit/s | frame gap p50/p95/p99/max ms | stalls >500 ms | first IDR | loaded RTT p50/p95/p99/max ms |
| Pear (hotspot) | 601 s | 12.13 | 0.836 | 0.3 / 327.2 / 1572.3 / 10340.5 | 240 | 2201 ms | 853.7 / 7820.6 / 9437.0 / 10127.0 |
(baselines: loopback 13.09 fps, 0 stalls, RTT p50 4.9; LAN TLS 14.04 fps, 0 stalls, RTT p50 34.0)
Dropped vs loopback: 1 - 12.13/13.09 = 7.3 percent, at the ~7 percent run-to-run noise. The failure mode is jitter, not throughput: per 10 s interval the rate swings between 3.6 fps (gaps to 10 s) and 38-44 fps catch-up bursts; frame gap p50 0.3 ms means frames arrive batched. No trend down over the 10 minutes. Car sampler ran through the video (fetch pending; first sample: CPU 26 percent busy, byd_cam_daemon 43.8 percent of a core, pear_daemon 5.5, 75 C, freq ratio 0.56).
Still to do: IPC-vs-network attribution (plan: the same video over Pear on the car's own LAN -- smooth there means the mobile path, jittery there means the pump), other presets, verdict.
PRESETS from the hotspot (12:13-12:42, same conditions; car on the fixed build):
- HIGH (960x720, 12 fps, 1.5 Mbit/s): NOT sustainable -- 3 of 3 runs ended within ~40 s: the Pear connection itself went {swarm: reconnecting} and the car closed the stream (e.g. 540 messages; first 30 s delivered 15-16 fps at 1.4-1.55 Mbit/s).
- LOW (640x480, 600 kbit/s): smooth -- 555 s at 15.57 fps mean, 0.583 Mbit/s, only 1 of 55 intervals with a gap over 2 s (worst 6.7 s) -- until the Pear connection reconnected at 555 s and the stream closed (8626 messages). Two earlier LOW attempts failed to route (NAT, BladeWatch-idfn).
- MEDIUM (see above): 601 s sustained, 12.13 fps, 0.836 Mbit/s, 240 stalls over 500 ms, loaded RTT p50 854 ms / p95 7.8 s.
ATTRIBUTION (the same MEDIUM run over Pear on the car's own LAN, 11:08, 600 s): 11.47 fps, 0.999 Mbit/s, 10 stalls over 500 ms, gap p99 423 / max 645 ms, loaded RTT p50 41 / p95 109 / max 304 ms (LAN TLS baseline: 14.04 fps, 0 stalls, RTT p50 34). So the pump + BareKit IPC add ~7 ms median and a few short stalls, and cost some frame rate at full bitrate; the hotspot's jitter and drops are the mobile path and the Pear connection's stability, not the pump. Car during the hotspot MEDIUM run: CPU busy 31.0 percent (28.3-36.3), byd_cam_daemon 61.7 percent of a core, pear_daemon 12.2 (1.2-26.9), 75 C flat, freq ratio 0.7 -- no throttling, not CPU-bound.
VERDICT: live H.264 over Pear is viable but not robust from a mobile hotspot behind a randomizing NAT. It is the network path, not the car or the pump. Remote live view should default to LOW (or adapt), must auto-resume after a drop (BladeWatch-tayl; transport-level option BladeWatch-bbvx), and connection reliability from hard NATs remains the open risk (BladeWatch-idfn). No tor baseline by owner decision.
close_reason: Measured 2026-09-26: 10-minute MEDIUM live view over Pear from a phone hotspot (randomizing NAT, car off) with the car sampler (CPU/thermal), the same run over Pear on the car's LAN for the pump-vs-network attribution, and HIGH/LOW presets from the hotspot. Verdict in the notes: viable but not robust from mobile -- the network path and Pear connection drops, not the car or the pump; remote default should be LOW/adaptive with auto-resume (BladeWatch-tayl, bbvx); NAT reliability BladeWatch-idfn. No tor baseline by owner decision.

title: Security review of the new network surface (TLS listener, UDP responder, public DHT peer)
description:
## Problem / context

v1.4.0.0 replaces a single, well-understood remote surface (a tor onion service fronting
loopback) with three new ones, all reachable by parties the owner did not choose:

1. A TLS listener bound to `0.0.0.0:8443` — reachable by everything on the LAN.
2. A UDP discovery responder bound on all interfaces — reachable by everything on the LAN.
3. A Hyperswarm peer on the public DHT — reachable by anyone who learns the topic.

Behind all three sits an HTTP API that includes vehicle control which actuates real
hardware: windows, trunk, lights, climate, ADAS, charge cap. CLAUDE.md requires
conservative treatment of exactly that surface.

This task is a deliberate security review of what v1.4.0.0 added. It runs AFTER the
transport work is functional and BEFORE tor is removed, so that a finding serious enough to
change the design is still cheap to act on.

## Exact locations

New code to review (from this epic):
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/launcher/PearLauncher.kt`
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/PearStreamPump.kt`
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/LanDiscoveryResponder.kt`
- The TLS listener changes in `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/HttpServer.kt`
- The pairing payload mint/redeem/revoke path in `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/TcpCommandServer.kt`
- The companion's transport selector and certificate pinning.

Existing invariants that must survive:
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/AuthMiddleware.kt` line 210 —
  loopback bypass is debug-only.
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/PeerCredentials.kt` — UID-based IPC
  authorisation, pinned by `CoResidentAttackerTest`.
- `docs/ipc-auth-and-secrets.md` — the secret-store and IPC-token model.
- `/data/local/tmp/bladewatch_ipc_token` must stay mode 644; the secret store must stay 600.

## Step-by-step instructions

1. Read `docs/ipc-auth-and-secrets.md` and `docs/networking-and-tunnels.md` first.
2. Review each new surface against at least these questions, and record an answer per
   question rather than an overall impression:
   - TLS listener: can an unauthenticated LAN caller reach any endpoint that is not
     deliberately public? Is the certificate's private key readable by the app UID? Does a
     client that ignores the fingerprint still get served (it will — so what stops a
     man-in-the-middle on the LAN, and is the companion the only client that pins)?
   - UDP responder: does it answer unsigned probes? Can a captured probe be replayed? Does
     the reply leak anything beyond routing data and a public fingerprint? Can it be used
     as a UDP amplification reflector — is the reply larger than the probe?
   - Pear peer: who can connect? Is the topic derivable from anything public, such as the
     device id, a VIN, a serial, or a timestamp? What does an attacker who learns the topic
     get — confirm they still face full JWT auth. Is there any rate limit on connection
     attempts, or can the daemon be exhausted?
   - Stream pump and the Tier 2 loopback bypass. THIS IS THE HIGHEST-RISK ITEM IN THE
     REVIEW; treat a failure here as P0. `AuthMiddleware` lines 174-192 grant
     unauthenticated access to callers from 127.0.0.1 on DEBUG builds when
     `isTunnelActive()` is false — and debug is the build that ships to the car. The Pear
     pump opens a plain loopback connection, exactly like tor did, and removing tor deletes
     the only signal `isTunnelActive()` ever had (`TorLauncher.TOR_PROCESS`).
     Verify, by test and on a real DEBUG build on the head unit:
       * a Pear peer with no JWT gets 401 from a normal endpoint;
       * a Pear peer with no JWT gets 401 from a VEHICLE-CONTROL endpoint;
       * the above still hold with `setLoopbackBypassOverride(true)` and
         `setTunnelActiveOverride(false)` both forced — i.e. the protection is structural
         (the per-listener policy on the remote-origin loopback listener, 127.0.0.1:8081),
         not merely current state;
       * a newly added listener defaults to NOT bypass-eligible.
   - Stream pump resources: can a peer open unbounded connections or buffer unbounded data?
   - Pairing payload: what does a photographed QR grant, and for how long? Is it
     single-use? Does revoking one companion affect others? Can an unauthorised local app
     mint one?
3. Check the whole diff for secrets reaching places they must not: logs, world-readable
   files, the config file, crash reports, or the pairing payload.
4. Run the project's `security-review` skill over the branch diff and record its findings.
5. Re-run `CoResidentAttackerTest` and confirm it passes unmodified.
6. File a separate bd issue for every finding that is not fixed inside this task. Do not
   close this task with unfixed findings recorded only in prose.

## Constraints

- Do NOT weaken `AuthMiddleware`, `PeerCredentials`, or the file modes in
  `docs/ipc-auth-and-secrets.md` to resolve a finding. Those are the invariants; fix the
  new code instead.
- Do NOT change `/data/local/tmp/bladewatch_ipc_token` away from mode 644. The app UID needs
  it and the docs explain why.
- Do NOT close this task before the tor-removal task, and do not let tor removal proceed
  with an unresolved P0 or P1 finding.
- Do NOT treat "auth is required anyway" as a complete answer to a surface-exposure
  question. Record what the surface exposes BEFORE auth: version strings, device
  identifiers, timing, and the mere fact that a BladeWatch car is present.
- Do NOT test only the happy path. Send malformed probes, oversized frames, half-open
  connections, and a client that ignores the certificate.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every question in step 2 has a written, individually recorded answer.
- [ ] The TLS private key and keystore password are unreadable by the app UID — verified on
      device with `run-as`, not assumed.
- [ ] An unsigned UDP probe provably gets no reply; a replayed probe provably gets no reply.
- [ ] The UDP reply is not larger than the probe, or amplification is explicitly ruled out.
- [ ] The swarm topic is provably not derivable from any public identifier.
- [ ] A Pear peer without a valid JWT provably gets 401 from every non-public endpoint,
      including the vehicle-control endpoints — verified on a real DEBUG build on the head
      unit, not only in a unit test and not only on release.
- [ ] That still holds with `setLoopbackBypassOverride(true)` and
      `setTunnelActiveOverride(false)` forced, proving the protection is structural.
- [ ] A newly added `HttpServer` listener defaults to NOT Tier 2 bypass-eligible.
- [ ] The pump provably connects to 127.0.0.1:8081 and never to 8080:
      `grep -n '8080' app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/PearStreamPump.kt`
      returns nothing.
- [ ] Connection-count and buffer limits on the pump are proven by test to be enforced.
- [ ] A pairing payload provably cannot be redeemed twice or after expiry.
- [ ] `CoResidentAttackerTest` passes unmodified.
- [ ] The `security-review` skill has been run over the branch diff and its output recorded.
- [ ] No secret appears in logcat, in any world-readable file, or in the pairing payload.
- [ ] Every unfixed finding has its own bd issue, linked from this task's close reason.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
notes:
From .4: TcpCommandServer's secret_get / secret_get_section / secret_put / secret_delete have NO key allow-list (TcpCommandServer.kt ~line 469). Any caller passing PeerCredentials (the BladeWatch app UID, shared by both APKs) can read EVERY secret-store entry -- deviceSecret, and after this epic pear.topicSeed and the LAN TLS private key too. That is consistent with the current trust model (the owner's app is trusted, and deviceSecret already mints JWTs), but the review should state it explicitly: app-UID compromise = every secret. Decide whether the new Pear/TLS material warrants a read allow-list.
From .7 (2026-09-24), two items for this review: (1) Pear and tor traffic all arrive at HttpServer from 127.0.0.1, so remote clients share ONE AuthApiHandler rate-limit bucket (/auth/token, /auth/pair, /auth/companion): one abusive peer can lock every other remote client out of login for the lockout window (not the car itself). Consider keying the bucket on something per-peer for REMOTE listeners (e.g. the Pear peer key passed out-of-band, which the opaque pump currently cannot do) or accepting the DoS with a shorter lockout. (2) The in-car UI's pre-existing auth.getAccessCode returns the raw device secret to Dart for display (the web login access code IS the device secret). Pairing never uses it, and it goes away with the web app (.13), but until then any Dart-side leak of that value is a full-access credential.
REVIEW ANSWERS, 2026-09-24 (head unit on a DEBUG build of feature/v1.4.0.0; tor not running -- so Tier 2's "bypass allowed + no tunnel" condition held naturally during every device check).

Design note: this task predates the TLS-inside-Pear decision (rdtj.8). The Pear pump now connects to the REMOTE TLS listener 127.0.0.1:8444, not 8081; 8081 is tor's. Criterion "pump never connects to 8080" holds: PearStreamPump.kt contains no "8080" (PearStreamPumpTest pins the 8444 target).

TLS LISTENER (0.0.0.0:8443, opt-in)
- Unauthenticated LAN caller: every request goes through checkAuth with ListenerTrust.REMOTE, so only PUBLIC_PATHS (auth endpoints, static web assets) answer without a JWT; the loopback bypass and vehicle second-factor exemption need LOCAL_APPS. Pre-auth exposure: the port answers and the certificate CN is "BladeWatch" -> the car's presence is visible on the LAN while LAN access is on (BladeWatch-cjhz).
- Private key readable by the app UID: NO. It lives only in the 600 shell-owned secret store (lanTls.privateKeyPkcs8); run-as net.bladewatch.app cat of the store -> Permission denied (on device); the PKCS12 keystore exists only in memory with a random per-run password (nothing persisted). FIXED in this task: the app UID could still fetch it over IPC (secret_get has no allow-list) -- TcpCommandServer now refuses every secret_* command on lanTls/pear/lanDiscovery/companions (DaemonOnlySecretSectionTest, mutation-checked).
- A client that ignores the fingerprint is served; only the companion pins. Browsers that click through the warning are MITM-able on the LAN (BladeWatch-cjhz; moot once web/ is retired).

UDP RESPONDER (18443, opt-in) -- device evidence from rdtj.5 (2026-09-24): forged, corrupted-HMAC, 25 h stale, 25 h future, truncated and exactly-replayed probes all got NO reply; a valid reply is 182 bytes vs the 256-byte probe, and the code refuses any reply >= probe size -> no amplification. Reply content: LAN IP, port, public TLS fingerprint, deviceId -- only to a correctly signed, fresh, unseen probe. Known ceiling: the nonce cache is in memory, so after a daemon restart a probe captured in the last 24 h is answered once more (LAN-only).

PEAR PEER
- Who can connect: anyone who knows the topic. The topic = SHA-256("bladewatch/pear/topic/v1" || 0x00 || 32-byte SecureRandom seed) held in the 600 store -- not derivable from deviceId, VIN, serial or time; the only way to learn it is a pairing QR.
- An attacker with the topic gets: a Hyperswarm connection, then the REMOTE TLS listener -- 401 for everything without a JWT (below). No pre-auth data beyond what the QR already held (/auth/status's deviceId, BladeWatch-6047).
- Exhaustion: Hyperswarm caps peers at 64; the pump caps 16 streams per peer and 64 total, with per-stream credit (overrun loses the stream) and a 5-minute idle sweep (PearStreamPumpTest); pear-end 0.4.3 holds at most 1 MiB per not-yet-tagged connection -> 64 MiB worst case; lowered to 256 KiB upstream (flutter_pear-70b, uncommitted for 0.4.4).

STREAM PUMP + TIER 2 (the P0-class item) -- verified ON THE DEBUG BUILD on the head unit with an invalid JWT:
- 127.0.0.1:8444 (Pear) and 127.0.0.1:8081 (tor): SystemService/GetStatus 401, VehicleService/SetChargeCap 401, RecordingsService/ListRecordings 401, SettingsService/GetQuality 401, /ws upgrade 401, clip listing 401.
- Contrast, 127.0.0.1:8080 (LOCAL_APPS): all 200 and live view streamed -> the protection is the listener, structurally: with the bypass on and no tunnel it still does not reach REMOTE listeners. Unit tests: AuthMiddlewareTest aRemoteListenerNeverGetsTheLoopbackBypass (overrides forced) and onlyTheLocalListenerOnLoopbackIsExemptFromTheVehicleSecondFactor.
- New listener defaults to NOT bypass-eligible: every shorter checkAuth overload passes REMOTE; RemoteLoopbackListenerTest pins exactly one LOCAL_APPS listener.
- FINDING (pre-existing, not the new surface): on debug builds ANY co-resident app gets the full API on 8080 without credentials, vehicle control included -> BladeWatch-g5u7 (P2), with a PeerCredentials-based fix.

PAIRING PAYLOAD: a photographed QR, redeemed within 5 minutes and before the owner's own device, grants a companion credential; after that it is worthless for access (single use, 128-bit code, TTL 5 min, max 4 pending -- CompanionPairingTest; device: a used code was refused). It permanently reveals the topic and probe key (capability data, no credential; no rotation short of re-pairing). Revoking one companion leaves others working (CompanionPairingTest). Minting is in-car only (IPC, PeerCredentials) -- PairingCommandTest.

SECRETS: logcheck on the head unit over 16 files (every world-readable text file in /data/local/tmp, the canonical config, debug_app.log, an 8,193-line logcat dump) -- 0 hits for the Pear topic, topic seed, probe key, TLS private key and device secret. The pairing payload carries no credential (topic/probe key are capability data by design). secret store 600, IPC token 644 (unchanged).

ALSO FIXED IN THIS TASK: login rate limits were keyed on IP:port (InetSocketAddress.toString()) -- a fresh bucket per connection; now the peer IP (HttpServer.rateLimitIdentity, pinned by RemoteLoopbackListenerTest). Remote clients still share 127.0.0.1's bucket and the global lockout is a login DoS -> BladeWatch-rlgv. Stale ListenerTrust KDoc corrected.

OTHER FINDINGS FILED: BladeWatch-6047 (deviceId in /auth/status to loopback-source remote callers + raw device secret to Dart; both web/tor-only, remove with .12/.13), BladeWatch-zmmf (world-readable camera probe images in /data/local/tmp).

GATES: ./gradlew test 914/914 debug+release, koverVerify pass; CoResidentAttackerTest 9/9 unmodified.

OUTSTANDING: the security-review skill over the branch diff (acceptance item) -- not run yet.
close_reason:
All acceptance criteria met (per-question answers and device evidence in the notes).

security-review skill, run 2026-09-24 over the branch's uncommitted/staged diff vs HEAD (owner approved subagents for this run): NO FINDINGS at the >=0.8 confidence bar. It traced the new listeners and ListenerTrust wiring, /auth/pair and /auth/companion, CompanionPairing (128-bit single-use code, HMAC token, constant-time compare), the JWT cid re-check, the IPC pairing commands and the daemon-only secret-section guard, LanTls/LanDiscoveryResponder, the Pear daemon/pump/mux/topic/launchers, the cross-process locks, and the companion transport (pinned TLS checked on the handshake and the negotiated certificate). Considered and not reported (below 0.7): the companion's loopback LocalGateway accepts connections from any app on the owner's phone -- such a caller still needs a JWT for anything beyond the public auth endpoints, so recorded here as a hardening note for rdtj.11 (e.g. a per-launch gateway secret), not a vulnerability.

Fixed in this task: TcpCommandServer refuses every secret_* IPC command on the daemon-only sections lanTls/pear/lanDiscovery/companions (DaemonOnlySecretSectionTest, mutation-checked); login rate limits keyed on the peer IP instead of IP:port (RemoteLoopbackListenerTest); stale ListenerTrust KDoc. Upstream: flutter_pear-70b (hold cap 1 MiB -> 256 KiB).

Unfixed findings, each filed: BladeWatch-g5u7 (P2, pre-existing: debug-build Tier 2 gives any co-resident app the full API incl. vehicle control), BladeWatch-6047 (deviceId in /auth/status to loopback-source remote callers + raw device secret to Dart; remove with rdtj.12/.13), BladeWatch-rlgv (global login lockout DoS), BladeWatch-cjhz (LAN TLS served to non-pinning clients; CN=BladeWatch presence leak), BladeWatch-zmmf (world-readable camera probe images). No P0 or P1 finding is open, so nothing here blocks tor removal.

Gates: ./gradlew test 914/914 debug+release, koverVerify pass; CoResidentAttackerTest 9/9 unmodified.

title: Decide and implement sentry alert delivery to the companion (Web Push does not carry over)
description:
## Problem / context

THIS IS AN UNSOLVED DESIGN PROBLEM, NOT A PORTING TASK. Read it fully before writing code.

Sentry and proximity events are the point of a sentry-mode dashcam, and today they reach
the owner through Web Push. `docs/features.md` line 352: "Surveillance and proximity events
deliver notifications through Web Push. There is no Telegram notification path."

How it works today: `PushSink.kt` hands an encrypted payload to `PushTransport.kt`, which
POSTs it directly to the browser's push subscription endpoint (a public internet URL
operated by the browser vendor — FCM for Chrome, Mozilla autopush for Firefox), signed with
VAPID keys from `VapidKeyStore.kt`. The BROWSER's service worker receives it and raises the
notification. The car needs only outbound internet.

Why this does not carry over to the companion: a Flutter app has no service worker and
cannot receive Web Push. Delivering a background notification to a Flutter app on Android
or iOS requires FCM or APNs, which means a Firebase/Apple project and a central service the
car must authenticate to. That directly contradicts the serverless, no-central-authority
premise that motivated moving to Pear in the first place.

And a live Pear connection is NOT a substitute: flutter_pear's own README documents that
mobile OSes aggressively suspend background apps, that each suspend/resume cycle resets the
swarm to `discovering`, and that a DHT lookup can take 30s or more. A phone in a pocket
cannot hold a swarm connection waiting for an alert.

This task DECIDES the mechanism and then implements it. It is a hard blocker on retiring
`web/`: if alerts cannot reach the companion, the browser PWA remains the only way an owner
learns their car was hit, and retiring it would be a straight functional regression.

## Exact locations

- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/notifications/sinks/PushSink.kt`
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/notifications/sinks/LogSink.kt` (the sink interface to implement against)
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/notifications/push/PushTransport.kt`
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/notifications/push/VapidKeyStore.kt`
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/notifications/push/VapidSigner.kt`
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/NotificationApiHandler.kt`
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/connect/impl/NotificationsServiceImpl.kt`
- Web client side being replaced: `web/src/app/pages/notifications/` and the service worker (`sw.js`)
- flutter_pear's background-execution notes: `packages/flutter_pear/BACKGROUND_EXECUTION.md`
  and `packages/flutter_pear/doc/ios.md`

## Step-by-step instructions

1. Read all the files above, plus `docs/features.md` around line 352 and flutter_pear's
   BACKGROUND_EXECUTION.md, before proposing anything.
2. Evaluate at least these options and write down the trade-offs of each:
   - FCM + APNs. Works reliably, is what users expect, and is what every other dashcam app
     does. Cost: a central service, a Firebase/Apple project, credentials on the car, and a
     dependency the P2P design was meant to remove. Note the car already POSTs to browser
     push endpoints, so "the car talks to a vendor push service" is NOT new — be honest
     about how much this actually changes the threat model versus how much it feels like it
     does.
   - UnifiedPush. Open standard, self-hostable, no Google dependency. Android and desktop
     only; no iOS. Smaller ecosystem.
   - Desktop-only live Pear connection. A desktop companion is NOT suspended
     (`Pear.platformInfo.backgroundExecution` reports `unrestricted` there), so it can hold
     the swarm and alert instantly. Does nothing for phones, which is where alerts matter.
   - Keep the browser PWA purely as the notification channel. Honest, zero new work, but
     means `web/` never fully retires.
   - Local-network-only alerts. Works when parked at home on the same Wi-Fi; silent
     everywhere else, which is when you most want to know.
3. Branch app behaviour on `Pear.platformInfo.backgroundExecution`, NOT on a platform check.
   flutter_pear's README is explicit about this: it reports `unrestricted` on desktop and
   the real constraint on mobile, so the policy is written once.
4. Write the recommendation into this task's notes and GET IT CONFIRMED before implementing.
   This decision changes the project's dependency posture; it is not an implementation
   detail to be chosen silently by an agent.
5. Implement the chosen mechanism as an additional sink beside `PushSink`, not as a
   replacement, so Web Push keeps working for browser clients while `web/` still exists.
6. Add the subscription-management surface to the companion, mirroring what
   `web/src/app/pages/notifications/` offers.
7. Test with the car's screen off and the phone locked and backgrounded for at least 30
   minutes. A notification that only arrives while the app is in the foreground has not
   solved this problem.

## Constraints

- Do NOT silently adopt FCM. It adds a central dependency to a project that just removed
  one; the choice must be explicit and recorded.
- Do NOT remove or break `PushSink`. Browser clients keep using it until `web/` retires.
- Do NOT assume a held Pear connection is a viable mobile alert path. flutter_pear
  documents the opposite.
- Do NOT put push service credentials in `bladewatch_config.json` or any world-readable
  file. They belong in the secret store, mode 600, like every other credential.
- Do NOT log notification payloads. They describe when the owner's car was disturbed and
  where it was parked.
- Do NOT close this task by declaring alerts "out of scope for v1.4.0.0" without also
  updating the `web/` retirement-gate task to record alerts as a permanent blocker.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All options above are evaluated in writing, with trade-offs, in the task notes.
- [ ] A recommendation is recorded AND explicitly confirmed before implementation starts.
- [ ] The chosen mechanism is implemented as an additional sink; `PushSink` still works.
- [ ] Subscription management exists in the companion.
- [ ] A real surveillance event on a real head unit raises a notification on a real phone
      that is LOCKED and BACKGROUNDED, verified over at least 30 minutes.
- [ ] The same is verified from a network different from the car's.
- [ ] Any new credential is in the secret store at mode 600, not in config.
- [ ] `./gradlew test` and `./gradlew koverVerify` pass.
- [ ] `docs/features.md` line ~352's "no Telegram notification path" paragraph is updated to
      describe the actual delivery mechanisms after this change.
- [ ] The `web/` retirement-gate task is updated with this task's outcome, since it is a
      blocker on that decision.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
notes:
OWNER DECISION 2026-09-24: store and forward. No push service (no FCM/APNs/UnifiedPush): the car keeps the alerts and delivers them to the companion only when it connects (LAN or Pear). The companion shows what arrived since its last connection. Consequence recorded honestly: an alert reaches the owner only when the companion next connects, not in real time while the phone is pocketed.
OPTIONS, recorded for the acceptance criteria (the owner chose before implementation):
- FCM+APNs: real-time, reliable, expected; costs a Firebase/Apple project, credentials on the car, and a central dependency. Rejected by the owner.
- UnifiedPush: no Google, self-hostable; no iOS. Not chosen.
- Desktop-only held Pear connection: instant on desktop, useless on phones. Not chosen.
- Keep the PWA as the alert channel: zero work, but web/ never retires; the owner is retiring web/.
- LAN-only alerts: silent away from home. Not chosen.
- CHOSEN (owner, 2026-09-24): store and forward over the companion's own connection (LAN or Pear). No new dependency and no credential. Trade-off: no real-time alert while the phone is pocketed.

IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-24 (uncommitted):
- proto: NotificationsService.ListInbox, InboxEntry, ListInboxRequest{after_id, limit}, ListInboxResponse{entries, latest_id, oldest_id}. Regenerated Kotlin, Dart and TS; only the notifications files changed.
- Car: notifications/CompanionInbox.kt is a NotificationBus sink BESIDE PushSink, which is untouched. It is subscribed in CameraDaemon at Connect registration, so it works even when the push registry fails to load. File /data/local/tmp/bladewatch_inbox.json: mode 600, atomic replace, max 200 entries, 14 days. Ids never reuse (nextId is persisted). A matching tag supersedes. The data extras are never stored. Nothing is logged.
- NotificationsServiceImpl registers ListInbox and reads afterId as either a proto3 JSON string or a number.
- bladewatch_rpc: NotificationsServiceClient.listInbox plus a decode test. Gate 100% (416/416).
- Companion: lib/inbox_sync.dart collectInbox(client, cursor) pages until caught up. It restarts from 0 once if the car's ids went backwards (inbox wiped), and stops on a no-progress page. 4 tests; gate 98.08%.
- Tests: CompanionInboxTest has 9 tests, including a Connect round trip. Mutations killed: tag supersede, nextId restore, file mode, inclusive cursor, page cap, dropping the newest, afterId ignored, limit ignored. debug and release 936/936. koverVerify OK.
- Docs: features.md (the store-and-forward paragraph beside the Web Push one), http-api-reference.md (the ListInbox row and section), data-flow-and-storage.md (the inbox file).
- Review finding, fixed in the same change: the docs claimed file names were never stored, but the click URL carries file= and hero= for clip alerts, as the push payload does. The doc and KDoc were corrected.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA UNDER THE OWNER'S DECISION:
- "Subscription management in the companion": there is no subscription in store and forward. Per-category display filtering belongs to the companion screens (.11), which also DISPLAY the collected alerts and persist the cursor per car.
- "Locked, backgrounded phone for 30 min": does not apply, since the owner chose no background delivery. The replacement device check: a real event raised while the companion is away is collected on the next connection, over LAN AND over Pear from another network. integration_test/car_e2e_test.dart now does this (SendTest through the real bus, collectInbox, exactly once).
- PENDING: the device run of that e2e (lan and pear), in the next install batch.
DEVICE 2026-09-24: car_e2e_test's inbox check passed on the head unit over the LAN and over Pear (same network). SendTest went through the car's real NotificationBus, and collectInbox found 'Test notification' exactly once, with nothing more on the second collect. STILL PENDING: the same over Pear from a DIFFERENT network (a phone hotspot), batched with rdtj.18/.19/idfn.

title: Melos workspace: extract shared RPC package, scaffold the Flutter companion app with flutter_pear
description:
## Problem / context

The companion app is a FLUTTER app using the FLUTTER_PEAR plugin for its P2P transport.
That is a fixed decision, not an option to re-evaluate: flutter_pear
(/Volumes/mandark-1Tb/projects/loabletech/flutter_pear, published on pub.dev at v0.4.0)
puts a typed Dart API over the Pear stack — Bare worklet, Hyperswarm, Hypercore family —
and is the same stack the car-side daemon runs via BareKit. Do not substitute a different
P2P library, a raw socket design, or a hand-rolled DHT.

The companion cannot be a new platform target inside `flutter_ui/`. That project is
Android-head-unit-only by standing decision, and `app/build.gradle.kts` line 1294
(`validateFlutterAndroidOnly`) FAILS THE BUILD if `ios`, `macos`, `windows`, `linux` or
`web` directories appear under `flutter_ui/`. See "Platform Scope" in `BladeWatch/CLAUDE.md`.

So the companion is a separate Flutter project. But it must not fork the RPC layer:
`flutter_ui/lib/rpc/` and `flutter_ui/lib/gen/` are exactly what it needs, and two copies
will drift. Extract them into a shared package consumed by both.

## Exact locations

- Shared code to extract: `flutter_ui/lib/rpc/` (connect_client.dart, connect_error.dart,
  jwt_source.dart, raw_http_sender.dart, rpc_transport.dart, services/) and `flutter_ui/lib/gen/`
- Proto generation config: `flutter_ui/proto/buf.gen.yaml`
- The guard that must keep passing: `app/build.gradle.kts` line 1294
- Reference melos monorepo: `/Volumes/mandark-1Tb/projects/loabletech/flutter_pear/melos.yaml`
- flutter_pear install and per-platform requirements: that project's `README.md`, plus
  `packages/flutter_pear/doc/ios.md`, `doc/macos.md`, `doc/linux.md`, `doc/windows.md`
- flutter_pear error catalog: `packages/flutter_pear/ERRORS.md`
- flutter_pear troubleshooting (install-time failures): `packages/flutter_pear/doc/troubleshooting.md`

## Step-by-step instructions

1. Read `BladeWatch/CLAUDE.md`'s "Platform Scope" section fully, then flutter_pear's README
   Install and Desktop sections. Both contain build-wiring steps that fail loudly and
   confusingly if skipped.
2. Decide and document the workspace layout. Suggested:
   - `packages/bladewatch_rpc/` — the extracted `lib/rpc/` plus `lib/gen/`.
   - `flutter_ui/` — unchanged head-unit app, depending on `bladewatch_rpc` by path.
   - `companion/` — the new multi-platform Flutter app.
3. Add a `melos.yaml` at the repo root wiring these together.
4. Move `lib/rpc/` and `lib/gen/` into `bladewatch_rpc`, update `flutter_ui`'s imports, and
   confirm `flutter_ui` still analyzes, tests and builds with ZERO behaviour change.
5. Update `flutter_ui/proto/buf.gen.yaml` so generated code lands in the shared package.
6. Create `companion/` with `flutter create`, platforms: android, ios, macos, windows,
   linux. This is the one place in this repo where those targets are correct. Flutter SDK
   must be >= 3.24 (flutter_pear's floor).
7. Add flutter_pear with an EXACT version pin, not a caret:
   `flutter_pear: 0.4.0` (confirm the current version first). Its README states minor
   versions may break the API without notice before 1.0. Add `flutter_pear_test` as a dev
   dependency — it ships in-memory fakes for the whole API so P2P logic is unit-testable
   without radios or real peers.
8. Apply flutter_pear's per-platform build wiring. These are NOT optional and the plugin
   cannot do them for you:
   - ANDROID: set `minSdk = 29` in `companion/android/app/build.gradle.kts`. Flutter's
     template default of 24 is too low and the Gradle manifest merger FAILS THE BUILD
     OUTRIGHT below 29. This is the one manual Android step.
   - ANDROID RELEASE: ship only the `arm64-v8a` and `x86_64` splits (or an app bundle).
     Both `--split-per-abi` and appbundle emit an `armeabi-v7a` variant by default that is
     missing the plugin's native libraries entirely; it is not a supported configuration.
   - iOS: add `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription` to `companion/ios/Runner/Info.plist`, with a
     description of this app's ACTUAL local-network use (reaching the owner's car on the
     same network). Apple requires it be accurate. Missing it is the single biggest
     simulator-invisible failure.
   - macOS: run `dart run flutter_pear:doctor --fix` FROM `companion/`, not from inside the
     flutter_pear package. It disables the App Sandbox in BOTH
     `macos/Runner/DebugProfile.entitlements` and `macos/Runner/Release.entitlements`, adds
     `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription` to `macos/Runner/Info.plist`, and raises the
     deployment target to 12.0+. Without the first, spawning the `bare` subprocess is
     unconditionally blocked and the app will not even build.
   - LINUX: host needs clang, cmake, ninja, pkg-config and GTK 3 dev headers.
   - WINDOWS: host needs Visual Studio 2022 with "Desktop development with C++".
9. Run `dart run flutter_pear:doctor` from `companion/` and record its output. It checks
   DHT bootstrap reachability, gives a NAT/firewall estimate, and runs a local loopback

title: Baseline throughput: loopback, LAN TLS and tor (capture BEFORE tor is removed)
description:
## Problem / context

This is the FIRST of three throughput tasks. It captures BASELINES ONLY — loopback, LAN
TLS, and TOR. The Pear measurements are separate tasks (live video, and control/clips).

RUN THIS EARLY. It does not depend on any Pear work, and the tor baseline is DESTROYED the
moment tor is removed. There is no way to recover that number afterwards, and without it the
Pear numbers have nothing to be compared against. It needs only a device and the TLS
listener.

Live view streams H.264 over a WebSocket. Over the Pear path, every video byte crosses the
JavaScript-to-native BareKit IPC boundary twice on the car (worklet to Kotlin) and twice on
the companion (Dart to worklet), on top of Hyperswarm's own encryption and whatever the DHT
path costs. Nobody has measured whether that sustains a live stream on a BYD head unit,
which is a 2019-class arm64 SoC already running camera capture, GPU downscaling, motion
detection and H.264 encoding.

If the answer is "no", the plan is not dead — but the epic must decide consciously between
lowering stream quality over Pear, dropping live view from the Pear path while keeping it
on LAN, or keeping Tor for video. That decision needs data, not a guess.

## Exact locations

- Car pump: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/PearStreamPump.kt`
- Companion pump and selector: the companion package.
- Streaming producer: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/StreamingApiHandler.kt` (349 lines)
- WebSocket framing: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/HttpServer.kt` lines 1283-1332
- Quality settings: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/QualitySettingsApiHandler.kt`

## Step-by-step instructions

1. Read `StreamingApiHandler.kt` and the WebSocket framing above so you know what bitrate
   and frame cadence the stream actually produces at each quality setting. Record the
   configured bitrates before measuring.
2. Measure a BASELINE first, or the Pear numbers mean nothing:
   - Live view over loopback in the car (the in-car Flutter UI).
   - Live view over the LAN TLS path on 8443.
   - Live view over the existing tor tunnel, while it still exists. This is the number Pear
     must beat or match, and it disappears once Tor is removed — so capture it NOW.
3. Do NOT measure any Pear path here. That is the next two tasks.
4. For each path record: sustained throughput (Mbit/s), end-to-end latency (glass to glass,
   or at minimum frame-timestamp to display), dropped/late frame rate over a 10-minute run,
   car CPU usage, and car temperature or thermal throttling if observable.
5. Run each for at least 10 minutes. A 30-second burst hides buffer growth and thermal
   throttling, which are the two failure modes that matter here.
6. Also measure the non-video baseline on each path: a burst of ConnectRPC calls and a
   recorded-clip download.
7. Define the MEASUREMENT HARNESS here — the exact commands, sampling method and units — and
   write it down so the two Pear tasks measure the same way. Numbers gathered by three
   different methods cannot be compared, which would defeat the whole point.
8. Write the results into the bd close reason as a table, with the exact head unit build,
   the quality setting used, and the network conditions.

## Constraints

- Do NOT remove or disable Tor in this task. The tor baseline is the comparison and it must
  still be running to be measured. If tor is already gone when you pick this up, STOP and
  say so — the baseline is unrecoverable and the epic needs to know.

- Do NOT tune quality settings mid-run to make a number look better. If a lower quality is
  needed to sustain the stream, that is a RESULT — record which setting was needed.
- Do NOT close this task with "it seemed fine". A close reason without numbers does not
  discharge the gate on the Tor-removal task.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Baseline numbers captured for loopback, LAN TLS, and TOR, while tor still runs.
- [ ] Each measurement ran at least 10 minutes.
- [ ] Throughput, latency, dropped-frame rate and car CPU recorded for every path.
- [ ] Control-RPC and clip-download baselines measured separately from live video.
- [ ] The measurement harness is documented precisely enough for the two Pear tasks to
      reproduce it exactly.
- [ ] Results written into the bd close reason as a table with head unit build, quality
      setting and network conditions.
- [ ] No Pear measurement is attempted in this task.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
