title: Companion-side Pear pump and LAN/Pear transport selector
description:
## Problem / context

The mirror image of the car-side pump, plus the decision of which transport to use.

The companion exposes the remote car as a LOCAL TCP port. Everything above the transport —
`ConnectClient`, the WebSocket live-view client, video URLs — then talks plain HTTP to
`127.0.0.1:<localport>` and neither knows nor cares whether the bytes are travelling over
Pear or the LAN.

Transport selection, in order:

1. Broadcast a signed LAN discovery probe, ~300ms timeout. If the car answers, connect
   directly to `https://<car-ip>:8443` with the pinned certificate fingerprint. This is
   strictly better when available: lower latency, no DHT, full bandwidth, and it sidesteps
   the JS-to-native IPC throughput question entirely.
2. Otherwise, join the Pear topic and pump through the worklet.

The LAN path exists because Hyperswarm FAILS between two peers behind the same NAT (router
hairpinning), which is exactly the car-in-the-driveway case.

## Exact locations

- New companion package (created by the scaffold task); the pump and selector live there.
- Car-side counterpart to mirror: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/PearStreamPump.kt`
- Probe format defined by: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/LanDiscoveryResponder.kt`
- Client that consumes the result: `flutter_ui/lib/rpc/connect_client.dart` line 43 — `baseUrl`
  is already a constructor parameter defaulting to `http://127.0.0.1:8080`.
- flutter_pear Dart API: `Pear.start()`, `pear.join(topic)`, `swarm.connections`,
  `conn.write(bytes)`, `conn.data.listen(...)` — see the flutter_pear README quick start.

## Step-by-step instructions

1. Add `flutter_pear` to the companion's pubspec with an EXACT version pin, not a caret.
   Its README states minor versions may break the API without notice before 1.0.
2. Implement the LAN prober: open a `RawDatagramSocket`, send the signed probe to the
   broadcast address, wait ~300ms for a unicast reply, verify the reply's signature, and
   return the car's IP, port and fingerprint.
3. Implement the TLS client path: an `HttpClient` with `badCertificateCallback` accepting
   ONLY a certificate whose SHA-256 fingerprint equals the pinned one from pairing. Reject
   everything else. Do not accept any certificate merely because it is self-signed.
4. Implement the Pear path: start the worklet, join the topic from the pairing invite, open
   a local `ServerSocket(0)`, and pump bytes between each accepted local socket and a Pear
   connection using the same framing the car-side pump defines.
5. Implement the selector: probe first, fall back to Pear. Re-evaluate on network change
   (for example the phone leaves Wi-Fi) rather than only at app start.
6. Expose a connection-state stream the UI can render. flutter_pear's README warns that a
   phone whose screen locks mid-handshake looks exactly like a broken connection, and a DHT
   lookup can take 30s or more. The UI must show "still looking" distinctly from "failed",
   or users will think the app is broken.
7. Point `ConnectClient.baseUrl` at whichever endpoint the selector chose.
8. Add Dart unit tests against fakes: selector prefers LAN when the probe answers; falls
   back to Pear when it does not; rejects a reply with a bad signature; rejects a
   certificate whose fingerprint does not match; re-evaluates on network change.
   `flutter_pear_test` ships in-memory fakes for the Pear API — use them, do not require a
   radio in unit tests.

## Constraints

- Do NOT accept a TLS certificate without fingerprint matching. An unconditional
  `badCertificateCallback` returning true is a man-in-the-middle hole on exactly the shared
  Wi-Fi this design is meant to be safe on.
- Do NOT bind the companion's local pump socket to anything but `127.0.0.1`.
- Do NOT reimplement ConnectRPC, HTTP framing or the WebSocket protocol. If you are writing
  H.264 or SPS/PPS handling in this task, the design has been misread — the pump moves
  opaque bytes.
- Do NOT use a caret version constraint on `flutter_pear`.
- Do NOT add iOS/macOS/Windows/Linux directories to `flutter_ui/`. This code lives in the
  separate companion project; `app/build.gradle.kts` line 1294 fails the build otherwise.
- Do NOT log payload bytes, the token, the invite or the fingerprint key material.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `cd <companion> && flutter analyze && flutter test` pass.
- [ ] A test proves the selector picks LAN when a valid probe reply arrives.
- [ ] A test proves it falls back to Pear when no reply arrives.
- [ ] A test proves a probe reply with an invalid signature is ignored.
- [ ] A test proves a certificate with a non-matching fingerprint is REJECTED, by feeding a
      different certificate and asserting the connection fails.
- [ ] A test proves the selector re-evaluates after a simulated network change.
- [ ] On real hardware, the companion reaches the car over the LAN from the same Wi-Fi.
- [ ] On real hardware, the companion reaches the car over Pear from a DIFFERENT network
      (mobile data, not the car's Wi-Fi). Same-NAT testing proves nothing here — flutter_pear
      documents that two peers behind one NAT fail for router reasons.
- [ ] Connection state is observable and distinguishes "discovering" from "failed".

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
notes:
From .4: the LAN TLS certificate is pinned by LanTls.Identity.fingerprintSha256 -- lowercase hex, no colons, SHA-256 over the certificate DER. Pinning must accept on fingerprint ALONE: in badCertificateCallback return true iff sha256(cert.der) equals the pinned value, and ignore every other failure reason (self-signed, hostname mismatch, and EXPIRY). The car never rotates this cert on expiry, on purpose: the head unit's clock jumps at boot, and rotation would silently break pairing. So an expired-but-pinned cert is the expected, valid case. The listener binds 0.0.0.0:8443 only while network.lanHttpEnabled is on, and accepts TLS 1.2/1.3 only.
From .10: flutter_pear 0.4.2 does NOT export PearRpc or PearMethod (package:flutter_pear exports only the high-level API; src/rpc.dart is internal). flutter_pear_test's FakeBareWorklet is documented as PearRpc(FakeBareWorklet(hub: hub)), which therefore requires an implementation import of package:flutter_pear/src/rpc.dart (flagged by implementation_imports). Recommended for this task: define a small companion-owned interface over exactly what the transport needs from Pear (join topic, connection stream, per-peer data stream, write), implement it with the real Pear/PearSwarm/PearConnection API, and unit-test the selector and pump against a hand fake of that interface -- so the companion never depends on flutter_pear internals. Use FakeBareWorklet only where end-to-end Pear semantics matter, with an explicit, justified ignore for the implementation import. Worth raising upstream in flutter_pear: export a supported test seam.
DISCOVERY MUST BE UNICAST (device finding from rdtj.5, 2026-09-24). On the head unit, signed probes sent to the subnet-directed broadcast address and to 255.255.255.255 were NEVER answered (6 tries); the same probes sent unicast to the car's IP were answered every time. Cause: the Qualcomm Wi-Fi firmware filters broadcast/multicast unless a WifiManager.MulticastLock is held (dumpsys wifi shows none), and the daemon (shell uid) lacks CHANGE_WIFI_MULTICAST_STATE; holding a lock from the app process would also keep Wi-Fi awake for all multicast all sentry night. iOS also forbids SENDING broadcast without Apple's multicast entitlement.

So the companion's LAN path must: (1) probe the car's last-known LAN address (from the last successful reply) by unicast; (2) if no reply within ~1 s, sweep the companion's own /24 by unicast with ONE probe (same nonce, one nonce per sweep), 254 datagrams to udp/18443; only the keyed car answers; (3) cap the sweep at /24 even on larger subnets, and fall back to Pear if nothing answers. Do not implement broadcast discovery at all - it cannot work on this car. docs/networking-and-tunnels.md "LAN discovery" has the measurements.
IMPLEMENTED OFFLINE 2026-09-24 (device checks pending). companion/lib/transport/:
- pear_mux.dart / mux_bridge.dart: the companion mirror of PearMux + PearStreamPump (credit windows both ways; local reads pause at zero credit; local writes flushed one frame at a time; a car overrun closes the stream).
- lan_prober.dart: UNICAST discovery per the rdtj.5 finding (last-known address, then own private /24s); reply must pass magic, nonce echo, HMAC, and fp == pin.
- pinned_tls.dart: accepts ONLY the pinned SHA-256 fingerprint (checked in onBadCertificate AND on the presented cert).
- local_gateway.dart: plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1:<ephemeral>, forwarded to LanRoute (pinned TLS to 8443) or PearRoute (TLS through a mux stream). No route = refused, not hung.
- transport_selector.dart: LAN first, then Pear; phases discovering/lan/pear/failed; re-evaluates on address change (5 s poll), on Pear drop, and 30 s after a failure; a superseded evaluation never wins.
- pear_link.dart: PearConnectionLink adapter; findCarOverPear picks the peer that completes pinned TLS (other companions on the topic never answer and are dropped); pearLinks(swarm).
- car_auth.dart: CarAuth.redeem (POST /auth/pair) and login (POST /auth/companion); CompanionJwtSource feeds ConnectClient.

DECISION (owner, 2026-09-24): TLS INSIDE PEAR. pear-end's Hyperswarm key pair is random per start and not exposed, so nothing pins the car's Pear identity, and every companion on the topic can connect to every other. The car now serves a loopback-only TLS listener on 127.0.0.1:8444 (HttpServer.PEAR_TLS_PORT, same LanTls certificate, ListenerTrust.REMOTE, independent of the LAN opt-in); PearStreamPump connects there instead of 8081. 8081 stays for tor only. Docs updated: networking-and-tunnels.md (ports table, listener trust, "Car authentication over Pear", "The companion's side"), daemons-and-processes.md, ipc-auth-and-secrets.md, CLAUDE.md.

Step 7 (ConnectClient.baseUrl): the gateway exposes baseUrl; wiring it into companion screens is rdtj.11. The device harness does it end to end.

Tests: companion 48 tests, all green 3x; coverage 98.03% (299/305) and the gate is ratcheted 83 -> 98. A test over flutter_pear_test's FakeSwarmHub proves find-through-swarm, TLS through it, and that PearConnection.data closing reports the drop (mutation-checked).

DEVICE HARNESS: companion/integration_test/car_e2e_test.dart, skipped without --dart-define=BW_PAIRING. BW_ROUTE=lan|pear. Asserts: the chosen route; 401 with no JWT through the route; redeem + login; GetStatus deviceId equals the QR's deviceId; a used code is refused.

REMAINING ACCEPTANCE: (1) LAN from the same Wi-Fi on real hardware; (2) Pear from a DIFFERENT network (same-NAT proves nothing).
DEVICE 2026-09-24: (1) LAN from the same Wi-Fi: PASSED -- car found by unicast probe in 86 ms, pinned TLS to 8443, 401 without JWT, redeem + login, GetStatus deviceId == QR deviceId, used code refused. (2) Pear, SAME network: PASSED after BladeWatch-ekbp (route 19.9-25 s). REMAINING: Pear from a DIFFERENT network (mobile hotspot) -- same-NAT does not prove hole-punching. Handshake timeout now 60 s (owner), search window 90 s.
DEVICE 2026-09-24, Pear from a DIFFERENT network: FAILED, 2/2 runs. Mac companion on a phone hotspot (mobile data; car LAN unreachable), car on home Wi-Fi with the ekbp-fixed pear-end. The DHT lookup finds the car (45 swarm 'connecting' updates per run) but no connection ever forms: swarm failed CONNECT_TIMEOUT, findCarOverPear times out at 90 s. The hotspot side measured with HyperDHT (pear-end's copy, in Node): firewalled=true, randomized=false -- a CONSISTENT NAT, normally punchable. Next: measure the home network's NAT the same way (a randomized home NAT would explain it), then decide with the owner (relay, port-forward/UPnP, or keep tor as the remote fallback -- this directly gates rdtj.12).
DEVICE 2026-09-24 13:18, Pear from a DIFFERENT network: PASSED on a second hotspot session (Mac at 10.101.x, HyperDHT firewalled=true randomized=true): route pear in 14.8 s, pinned TLS through Pear to the car's 8444 listener, 401 without JWT through it (the harness then failed only at redeem because that QR's code had expired an hour earlier -- redeem/login over Pear were already verified from the home network). A plain HyperDHT dial probe (Node, pear-end's hyperdht) from the same network opened the car in 3.7 s. OPEN QUESTION: the FIRST hotspot session (Mac at 192.168.4.x, firewalled=true randomized=false) failed 2/2 with no connection at all -- cause unknown (asked the owner what differed between the two sessions).
The unexplained first-hotspot failure is tracked as BladeWatch-idfn (blocks rdtj.12), so it does not hold .8 open. .8 closes once BladeWatch-ekbp (flutter_pear release) closes.
close_reason: All criteria met. Companion transport (companion/lib/transport/): unicast LAN discovery, pinned TLS, LocalGateway, TransportSelector (discovering/lan/pear/failed, re-evaluates on network change and Pear drop), findCarOverPear (TLS-inside-Pear car identification), CarAuth pairing/login. Tests 48, coverage 98.03% (gate ratcheted 83 -> 98). On the head unit 2026-09-24: LAN from the same Wi-Fi PASSED (probe 86 ms, pinned TLS to 8443, 401 without JWT, pair + login, GetStatus deviceId == QR deviceId, used code refused); Pear from a DIFFERENT network (phone hotspot, 10.101.x) PASSED (route 14.8 s, pinned TLS through Pear, 401 through it). Pear handshake timeout 60 s (owner), search 90 s. The unexplained failure on a first hotspot network is tracked separately as BladeWatch-idfn. Companion pinned to flutter_pear 0.4.3.

title: Unified pairing payload: Pear invite, device token, TLS fingerprint in one QR
description:
## Problem / context

Today the owner pairs a remote client by scanning a QR of the tor onion URL
(`flutter_ui/lib/screens/dashboard/dashboard_screen.dart` line 585,
`QrImageView(data: tunnel.url!, size: 160)`) and logging in with a device token.

The companion app needs three things instead, and they must arrive together in one scan so
the owner performs exactly one action:

1. A Pear pairing invite (so the companion can find the car over the DHT).
2. A device token (so the companion can mint the JWT every RPC needs).
3. The TLS certificate SHA-256 fingerprint (so the companion can pin the LAN path), plus
   the probe HMAC key (so it can send signed discovery probes).

## Exact locations

- QR display today: `flutter_ui/lib/screens/dashboard/dashboard_screen.dart` line 585 and
  around line 955.
- Controller: `flutter_ui/lib/screens/dashboard/dashboard_controller.dart`
- Privileged channel from Flutter to the daemon:
  `flutter_ui/lib/platform/daemon_channel.dart` and the Kotlin side at
  `flutter_ui/android/app/src/main/kotlin/net/bladewatch/bladewatch_ui/MainActivity.kt`
- Daemon-side command surface: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/TcpCommandServer.kt`
- Auth/token model: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/auth/AuthManager.kt`
- Secret storage: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/config/SecretConfigStore.kt`
- JWT abstraction the companion must satisfy: `flutter_ui/lib/rpc/jwt_source.dart`
- flutter_pear's invite API: `PearPairing` — see
  `/Volumes/mandark-1Tb/projects/loabletech/flutter_pear/packages/flutter_pear/doc/howto-pairing.md`

## Step-by-step instructions

1. Read `docs/ipc-auth-and-secrets.md` fully before touching anything. It defines the
   app-UID-cannot-write-secrets rule that this task must respect.
2. Define a versioned pairing payload (JSON, then base64) containing: a format version, the
   Pear invite, the device token, the TLS fingerprint, the probe HMAC key, the TLS port, and
   the device id. Version it from day one so a future companion can reject an old car.
3. Add a daemon command that MINTS a fresh pairing payload on demand, in
   `TcpCommandServer.kt`, authorised the same way the existing privileged commands are
   (IPC token plus peer UID, see `PeerCredentials`).
4. Make each pairing payload single-use and short-lived: it must expire (minutes, not days)
   and be invalidated once redeemed. A QR photographed over the owner's shoulder must not
   be a permanent key to the car.
5. Add a daemon command to LIST and REVOKE paired companions. The owner must be able to
   un-pair a lost phone without rotating the device secret and breaking every other client.

   NOTE AND RECORD THIS DEDUCTION: `TcpCommandServer` binds `127.0.0.1` (line 64), so these
   commands are reachable ONLY from the in-car Flutter UI, which shares a UID with the
   daemon. A remote companion structurally CANNOT list or revoke pairings — the Pear pump
   targets `HttpServer`, not 19876.

   That is a deliberate and defensible posture: pairing and un-pairing require physical
   presence at the car, so a stolen phone cannot un-pair the owner's other devices or pair
   itself further. Keep it, but state it explicitly in the close reason and in
   `docs/ipc-auth-and-secrets.md` rather than leaving it as an accident of which port the
   command landed on. If a future decision wants remote revocation, it needs a ConnectRPC
   endpoint and its own threat analysis — do not add one here by reflex.
6. Update the dashboard QR in `dashboard_screen.dart` to show the new payload instead of the
   tunnel URL, behind an explicit "Pair a device" action rather than displayed
   continuously — a permanently-visible pairing QR is a permanently-visible credential.
7. Surface the LAN-access opt-in toggle in the same flow, since the LAN path needs
   `isLanHttpEnabled()` on. Explain in the UI what it does; do NOT flip it silently.
8. Add tests: payload round-trips; expired payload rejected; redeemed payload rejected on
   second use; revoking one companion leaves others working; unauthorised IPC caller cannot
   mint a payload.

## Constraints

- Do NOT put the device SECRET in the payload. The payload carries a per-companion token
  derived from it, so revoking one companion does not require rotating the secret.
- Do NOT read `/data/local/tmp/bladewatch_secrets.json` from Dart. It is mode 600,
  shell-only. Go through IPC, as `jwt_source.dart` documents.
- Do NOT widen the IPC authorisation to make this easier. `PeerCredentials.isTrusted`
  authorises by peer UID and `CoResidentAttackerTest` pins that a separate app holding the
  world-readable IPC token is rejected. That test must still pass unchanged.
- Do NOT make the pairing QR permanently visible on the dashboard.
- Do NOT log the payload, the invite, or the token.
- Do NOT remove the existing tunnel-URL QR in this task; Tor removal is a later task.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A versioned pairing payload type exists on both the Kotlin and Dart sides.
- [ ] `./gradlew test`, `./gradlew koverVerify` pass.
- [ ] `cd flutter_ui && flutter analyze && flutter test` pass.
- [ ] `cd flutter_ui/android && ./gradlew koverVerify` passes at its 100% bound.
- [ ] `CoResidentAttackerTest` still passes, unmodified.
- [ ] A test proves a second redemption of the same payload is rejected.
- [ ] A test proves an expired payload is rejected.
- [ ] A test proves revoking companion A leaves companion B able to mint a JWT.
- [ ] On device, scanning the QR from a companion build yields a working JWT against 8443.
- [ ] `grep -rn 'deviceSecret' flutter_ui/lib` shows the secret is never handled in Dart.
- [ ] `docs/ipc-auth-and-secrets.md` describes the pairing payload, its lifetime and its
      revocation model, INCLUDING that pair/revoke is in-car only and why.
- [ ] A test proves a caller that is not the in-car UI cannot mint, list or revoke pairings.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
notes:
From .3: the car's swarm topic is PearTopic.topicHex(SecretConfigStore()) (app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/daemon/PearTopic.kt) -- a SHA-256 under a domain tag of a random 32-byte seed stored at secret-store section 'pear', key 'topicSeed', created lazily on first use. The pairing payload's Pear invite/topic must come from THAT function, not a new derivation. RACE TO HANDLE: pairing runs in byd_cam_daemon's process, pear_daemon in its own; SecretConfigStore's lock is in-process only, so if both hit loadOrCreateSeed for the FIRST time simultaneously, each can generate a seed and the loser's topic is silently wrong. Either have pairing create the seed and pear_daemon only read it, or add a cross-process file lock around first creation. Also note pear_daemon is OPT-IN (PEAR_PEER disabled by default, like tor) -- pairing a companion is what should enable it.
IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-24 (offline); one on-device criterion pending the companion build (.8/.11).
DESIGN (recorded, and in docs/ipc-auth-and-secrets.md "Companion pairing"): the QR is NOT a credential - unpadded base64url JSON {v:1, deviceId, pearTopic, tlsPort, tlsFp, probeKey, code, exp}; code is single-use (consumed on the first attempt naming it), 5 min TTL, max 4 outstanding, in memory in byd_cam_daemon. The companion redeems it at POST /auth/pair {code,name} -> {companionId, token} exactly once; token = base64url(HMAC-SHA256(deviceSecret, "bladewatch/companion/v1"||0x00||id)) - derived, not stored; record in secret store section companions.<id> = {name,pairedAt}. POST /auth/companion {companionId,token} -> JWT in the body with cid; validateJwt refuses a cid no longer paired, so revoking kills that companion's live sessions immediately and nobody else's. Device secret never in the payload.
IN-CAR ONLY (deduction recorded as required): pairingMint/pairingList/pairingRevoke/lanAccessSet exist only on 127.0.0.1:19876 (peer UID + IPC token), unreachable from a companion (it reaches HttpServer). Pairing and un-pairing need someone at the car; a stolen phone can neither un-pair the owner's other devices nor pair itself further. Remote revocation would need its own endpoint + threat analysis; deliberately absent.
Minting enables PEAR_PEER (pairing turns remote access on). LAN opt-in is a separate explained switch in the dialog, never flipped silently.
SEED RACE from the .3 note FIXED: SecretConfigStore.putStringIfAbsent (check-and-set under the cross-process lock); PearTopic.loadOrCreateSeed uses it; PearTopicTest spawns two JVMs at a barrier and both derive the same, stored topic.
CODE: auth/CompanionPairing.kt; AuthManager.generateJwt(companionId) + cid check; AuthApiHandler /auth/pair + /auth/companion (public, same rate limits); TcpCommandServer pairing commands + lanAccessSet; flutter_ui: PairingControl.kt (+MainActivity pairing.*), platform/pairing_channel.dart, screens/pairing/{pairing_controller,pairing_dialog}.dart, dashboard "Pair a device" (explicit action, QR minted only on open), 14 strings in all 19 ARB catalogues; packages/bladewatch_rpc/lib/pairing/pairing_payload.dart (versioned Dart type, refuses v!=1).
TESTS: CompanionPairingTest 11 (second redemption refused, expired refused, revoke A leaves B minting a valid JWT and kills only A's sessions, token KAT, payload carries no credential, golden payload shared with Dart), PairingCommandTest 4 (incl. a co-resident attacker UID cannot mint/list/revoke/set LAN over TCP), PearTopicTest +1 race; Dart: pairing_payload_test 7 (decodes the car's golden), pairing_channel_test 7, pairing_controller_test 8, pairing_dialog_test 8, dashboard +2. CoResidentAttackerTest unmodified and passing. Mutations caught: code not consumed, no cid check, non-atomic putIfAbsent. A real bug found by the dialog test and fixed: a mint failure was hidden by a later successful device-list load (shared failure flag) - now mintFailed vs actionFailed. DisposedSafeNotifier guard caught the controller being disposed mid-await; fixed + test.
GATES: ./gradlew test 910 debug + 910 release, 0 failed; koverVerify 10.119%; flutter_ui/android koverVerify (100%) + Dart gates flutter_ui 99.57%, bladewatch_rpc 100%, companion 83.33%; flutter analyze clean x3.
grep deviceSecret flutter_ui/lib: one hit, a pre-existing GUARD comment in config_channel.dart. No pairing code handles the secret. Separately (pre-existing, noted on .16): auth.getAccessCode returns the device secret to Dart for display (the web access code IS it).
REMAINING: on device, scan the QR from a companion build and get a working JWT against 8443 (needs .8's transport + .11's scanner).
DEVICE 2026-09-24: a companion redeems the QR code and gets a JWT -- VERIFIED over both routes (LAN 8443 and Pear) with companion/integration_test/car_e2e_test.dart, which also checks GetStatus deviceId equals the QR's deviceId and that a used code is refused. Test companions were revoked via pairingRevoke afterwards (list empty).
close_reason: All criteria met, re-verified 2026-09-24. On device: a companion build (companion/integration_test/car_e2e_test.dart on macOS) decoded a freshly minted QR payload with PairingPayload.decode, redeemed it at /auth/pair and got a working JWT against 8443 (LAN route): GetStatus answered with the QR's deviceId, a used code was refused; the same flow also passed over Pear. The QR TEXT was fed directly -- a camera scanner is rdtj.11's scope and will feed the same PairingPayload.decode (noted on .11). Gates: ./gradlew test 911/911 debug+release and koverVerify pass; flutter_ui analyze clean and 1468 tests pass; flutter_ui/android koverVerify passes (100%); CoResidentAttackerTest unmodified; the only deviceSecret in flutter_ui/lib is a doc comment forbidding it. Test companions revoked afterwards.

title: Car-side Pear-to-TCP stream pump
description:
## Problem / context

This is the task that makes "everything over Pear" cheap instead of a rewrite.

A Pear connection is a reliable, ordered, encrypted byte stream — the same shape the tor
tunnel already provides. So Pear replaces tor AT THE TRANSPORT LAYER and nothing above it
changes: no ConnectRPC changes, no WebSocket changes, no re-implementation of the H.264
streaming protocol.

The car side needs a pump: for each inbound Pear connection, open a TCP socket to
`127.0.0.1:8080` and copy bytes in both directions until either end closes.

Critically, this pump is written in KOTLIN, not in the Bare worklet's JavaScript. The
daemon receives Pear stream bytes over BareKit IPC and does the TCP connect itself. That is
why the stock `pear-end.bundle` ships unmodified: no `bare-pack`, no forked worklet JS, no
`bare-tcp` dependency (which is absent from the bundle's package.json anyway).

## CRITICAL: the pump must NOT inherit loopback trust

Read `AuthMiddleware.kt` lines 174-192 before writing any code.

`AuthMiddleware` has a Tier 2 "loopback safety net" that grants UNAUTHENTICATED access to
any caller from 127.0.0.1 when three conditions hold: the build is debug
(`isLoopbackBypassAllowed()`, line 210), no tunnel-forwarding headers are present, and
`isTunnelActive()` is false.

The comment at line 178 describes precisely this attack for tor: "A Tor onion service
injects NOTHING: tor opens a plain TCP connection to 127.0.0.1:8080, which at the socket
level looks exactly like an app on the head unit. Without the extra condition, a debug
build with the tunnel up would hand full API access to anyone who knew the onion address —
and debug is the build that actually goes on the car, because preserving the ADB key
across a reinstall needs run-as."

THE PEAR PUMP IS THE SAME SHAPE AS TOR. It opens a plain TCP connection to loopback. Debug
is the build that runs on the car. If the pump connects to 8080 and anything goes wrong
with the tunnel-active signal, anyone who knows the Pear topic gets unauthenticated access
to the entire API, including the vehicle-control endpoints that actuate real hardware.

`isTunnelActive()` (line 223) currently detects exposure by looking for ONE process name:
`findPidsByProcessName(TorLauncher.TOR_PROCESS)` where `TOR_PROCESS = "bladewatch_tor"`.
When tor is removed, that signal disappears entirely.

Do NOT solve this by making Pear register as an "active tunnel". That is stateful and fails
OPEN if anyone later forgets to set it. Solve it STRUCTURALLY:

- The pump connects to a DEDICATED loopback port (127.0.0.1:8081, confirm it is free) that
  is served by the same `HttpServer` but marked remote-origin.
- Connections accepted on that port are NEVER eligible for the Tier 2 bypass, regardless of
  build type, tunnel state, or headers.
- 8080 keeps its existing behaviour for the in-car Flutter UI.

A per-listener trust policy cannot be forgotten the way a global flag can.

Note also that a marker HEADER is NOT an acceptable alternative: the remote peer controls
the bytes of the HTTP request, headers included, so any header-based signal is forgeable by
the attacker. And having the pump parse and rewrite HTTP would break the opaque-bytes
design that makes this whole approach cheap.

## Process topology

`pear_daemon` and `byd_cam_daemon` are SEPARATE `app_process` processes, both running as the
`shell` user. The pump lives in `pear_daemon` because that is where the worklet IPC is, and
it reaches `HttpServer` — which lives in `byd_cam_daemon` — over an ordinary loopback TCP
connection:

    Pear peer  ->  worklet IPC  ->  PearStreamPump      [ pear_daemon ]
                                          |
                                     TCP 127.0.0.1:8081
                                          |
                                     HttpServer         [ byd_cam_daemon ]

This is a real cross-process hop, not a function call. Two consequences to design for:

- `pear_daemon` can start before `byd_cam_daemon` is listening, or outlive a CameraDaemon
  restart. Connecting must retry rather than failing permanently, and an in-flight pumped
  connection must close cleanly when 8081 goes away.
- From `HttpServer`'s side the connection still arrives from 127.0.0.1, so the per-listener
  trust policy below is what protects it. Being a separate process changes NOTHING about
  that; do not treat process separation as a security boundary here.

## Exact locations

- New file: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/daemon/PearStreamPump.kt`
- The pump runs INSIDE `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/daemon/PearDaemon.kt`,
  which owns the worklet and its IPC. It is NOT part of CameraDaemon.
- Target server: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/HttpServer.kt` — a NEW
  remote-origin loopback listener on 8081, not the existing 8080 (lines 121-122)
- The trust decision to respect: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/AuthMiddleware.kt` lines 174-192 and 210-241
- IPC relay shape to copy: `/Volumes/mandark-1Tb/projects/loabletech/flutter_pear/packages/flutter_pear_bare/android/src/main/kotlin/tech/loable/flutter_pear_bare/FlutterPearBarePlugin.kt` — its `relayFromWorklet` read loop is the model.

## Step-by-step instructions

1. Read `PearDaemon.kt` and `PearLauncher.kt` (written in the earlier task) and the
   FlutterPearBarePlugin relay loop above.
2. Define a small framing protocol on the BareKit IPC channel so multiple concurrent Pear
   connections can share the single worklet IPC pipe. At minimum each message needs a
   connection id, a type (open / data / close), and a payload. Multiple concurrent streams
   are required — the live-view WebSocket and ordinary RPC calls happen at the same time.
3. On a `open` message from the worklet, open `Socket("127.0.0.1", 8081)` — the
   remote-origin listener, NOT 8080 — and register it against the connection id.
4. On a `data` message, write the payload to that socket.
5. Read from each socket on its own thread or coroutine and send `data` messages back to
   the worklet tagged with the connection id.
6. On `close` from either direction, close the other side and drop the registration.
7. Apply backpressure. A live H.264 stream will outrun a slow peer; an unbounded queue will
   OOM the daemon. Bound the per-connection buffer and stop reading from the socket when
   the buffer is full.
8. Enforce a connection cap and an idle timeout so a hostile or buggy peer cannot exhaust
   file descriptors.
9. Add JVM unit tests with a fake IPC channel and a local echo server: bidirectional copy,
   concurrent connections not crossing streams, close propagation both ways, backpressure
   not dropping bytes, cap enforced.

## Logging

Add a `PEAR_PUMP` flag to `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/logging/DaemonLogConfig.kt`
(note: it is `.kt`, despite CLAUDE.md calling it `DaemonLogConfig.java`) and gate every log
call in PearStreamPump behind it. All flags there are `false` and R8 strips the calls from
release bytecode; a new subsystem that logs unconditionally defeats that.

Leave the flag `false`. CLAUDE.md: do not enable logging flags in commits intended for
release.

## Constraints

- Do NOT modify `HttpServer.kt`. The pump is a client of it, exactly like tor is today.
- Do NOT modify `pear-end.bundle` or add any JS. If you find yourself running `bare-pack`,
  stop — the design says the pump is native on both ends.
- Do NOT point the pump at the TLS listener on 8443. Pear already encrypts; double
  encryption costs CPU on a head unit for no benefit.
- Do NOT point the pump at 8080. See the loopback-trust section below — this is the single
  most dangerous thing you could get wrong in this task.
- Do NOT use an unbounded buffer or an unbounded thread pool.
- Do NOT log payload bytes. They contain JWTs and video.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `PearStreamPump.kt` exists, compiles, and runs inside `pear_daemon`, not CameraDaemon.
- [ ] A test proves the pump retries rather than dying permanently when 8081 is not yet
      listening, and closes pumped connections cleanly when CameraDaemon restarts.
- [ ] Verified on device: restarting `byd_cam_daemon` while a companion is connected does
      not leave `pear_daemon` wedged.
- [ ] `./gradlew test` and `./gradlew koverVerify` pass, including new pump tests.
- [ ] A test proves two concurrent connections do not interleave each other's bytes.
- [ ] A test proves close propagates in both directions.
- [ ] A test proves the connection cap is enforced and the idle timeout closes a dead peer.
- [ ] A test proves a slow reader applies backpressure rather than buffering unboundedly.
- [ ] A test proves a request arriving on the remote-origin listener is NEVER granted the
      Tier 2 loopback bypass, with `setLoopbackBypassOverride(true)` and
      `setTunnelActiveOverride(false)` forced — i.e. the bypass is structurally unreachable
      on that port, not merely switched off by current state.
- [ ] On a real head unit running a DEBUG build, a request arriving over Pear returns 401
      WITHOUT a JWT. Debug specifically: that is the build that ships to the car, and the
      release build would mask this bug.
- [ ] With a valid JWT, the same request returns 200.
- [ ] `grep -n '8080' app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/PearStreamPump.kt`
      returns nothing.
- [ ] `grep -rn 'bare-pack' app/` returns nothing and `pear-end.bundle` is byte-identical to
      the upstream flutter_pear copy.

- [ ] A `PEAR_PUMP` flag exists in `DaemonLogConfig.kt`, is `false`, and gates every log
      call in PearStreamPump.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
notes:
PROTOCOL FACTS found while implementing .3 (read pear-end/index.js lines 142-222 and 671-717 before designing the framing): pear-end exposes ONE byte channel PER PEER, not per stream -- CONNECTION_DATA events carry {topic, peer, data} and CONNECTION_WRITE takes {peer, data}, both with data as BASE64 inside a JSON frame, sent over a Protomux 'pear-connection-data' channel that pear-end opens on every Hyperswarm connection. So a companion's concurrent HTTP connections (live-view WebSocket + RPC calls + thumbnails) must be multiplexed by US on top of that single per-peer channel: the stream-id/open/data/close framing this task already calls for is not optional, it is the only way to carry more than one TCP connection per companion. Also: frames are JSON + base64 in both directions across BareKit IPC, so every payload byte is base64-encoded (+33%) and JSON-parsed on each hop.
IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-24 (offline); on-car criteria pending a Pear client (the companion, .8).
- PearMux (daemon/PearMux.kt): one frame per Pear message (Protomux keeps boundaries): type u8 (1 OPEN+version byte, 2 DATA 1..32768, 3 CLOSE, 4 WINDOW u32 credit), stream id u32 BE. Companion opens, car answers. 256 KiB credit per stream per direction.
- PearStreamPump (daemon/PearStreamPump.kt), inside pear_daemon: OPEN -> TCP to 127.0.0.1:HttpServer.REMOTE_LOOPBACK_PORT (8081) with retry/backoff up to 15 s; reader thread (socket -> peer, never past the peer's credit) + writer thread (peer -> socket, grants credit back once bytes left); overrun -> stream closed; caps 16/peer, 64 total; 5 min idle sweep (every 30 s); a vanished peer's streams closed; malformed frames discarded. PEAR_PUMP log flag (false), all logging gated; no payload ever logged. No "8080" anywhere in the file.
- PearDaemon Session: single-flight IPC write queue (bare-kit IPC.write(buf, cb) lets a second write jump ahead of a partial first one - read off IPC.class), connection.write with ids (err -> the peer's streams closed), connection.data -> pump, connection.close -> pump.
- HttpServer: NEW 127.0.0.1:8081 listener, every connection ListenerTrust.REMOTE (the .6 text says both "a NEW remote-origin loopback listener on 8081" and "do not modify HttpServer.kt"; the listener is the only change, request handling untouched).
- Tests: PearStreamPumpTest (14: bidirectional, two streams never cross, close both ways, caps, idle sweep, backpressure stops at exactly one window and releases exactly each grant with 1 MB arriving intact, overrun closes, retry while not listening, give-up at deadline, server restart closes cleanly and the pump keeps working, vanished peer, junk ignored, structural/no-8080/log gate), PearMuxTest (4, exact bytes pinned), RemoteLoopbackListenerTest (3). AuthMiddlewareTest.aRemoteListenerNeverGetsTheLoopbackBypass covers the forced-open Tier 2 case on 8081. Mutations caught: no credit wait, no overrun check, no connect retry, peer-close closing everyone. A helper race in the test (discarding other streams' frames) was found by the release-variant run and fixed; 4 repeated runs x 2 variants green.
- ./gradlew test: 894 debug + 894 release, 0 failed; koverVerify 9.868%.
- REMAINING (device): over Pear, 401 without JWT and 200 with one on a DEBUG build; restarting byd_cam_daemon mid-connection does not wedge pear_daemon. Needs a Pear client - planned with the companion (.8) or a small Node hyperswarm+protomux client speaking pear-end's 'pear-connection-data' channel.
DEVICE 2026-09-24: 401/200 over Pear VERIFIED on a debug build via companion/integration_test/car_e2e_test.dart (BW_ROUTE=pear): GetStatus through the pump to the 127.0.0.1:8444 TLS listener is refused with 401 without a JWT and answers with the companion JWT. Required BladeWatch-ekbp's pear-end fix on the car. REMAINING: byd_cam_daemon restart mid-connection.
DEVICE 2026-09-24: byd_cam_daemon restart mid-connection VERIFIED. car_e2e_test.dart BW_ROUTE=pear BW_SOAK_SECONDS=90; the runner ran killall -9 byd_cam_daemon on the harness's soak start marker (cam_daemon.log: exit 137 at 12:43:31, wrapper restart 12:43:34). Result: 40 GetStatus calls over Pear, 0 failed, no re-route -- the pump's 15 s connect retry absorbed the restart and the Pear connection survived. All .6 device checks done.
close_reason: All criteria met. Car-side pump (PearMux, PearStreamPump -> the REMOTE TLS listener 127.0.0.1:8444, TLS inside Pear by owner decision) verified on the head unit 2026-09-24 on a debug build: 401 without a JWT and 200 with the companion JWT over Pear; a byd_cam_daemon SIGKILL mid-connection absorbed by the pump's connect retry (40 calls, 0 failed, no re-route). Unit tests: PearStreamPumpTest (caps per peer and total, backpressure, credit overrun, idle sweep, junk frames, restart), PearMuxTest. Needed BladeWatch-ekbp (flutter_pear 0.4.3), now closed.

title: LAN discovery probe responder (UDP, HMAC-gated, unicast reply)
description:
## Problem / context

The companion app needs to know whether it can reach the car directly over the LAN, because
Hyperswarm fails between two peers behind the same NAT (router hairpinning) and that is
exactly the common "check the car in my driveway from my sofa" case.

The companion must NOT try to detect the network. Reading the Wi-Fi SSID on Android 10+
requires ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, which is a heavy permission to ask for and an easy one to
get refused. Instead the companion probes for the CAR: if the car answers a broadcast, both
are on the same segment by definition.

The reply must be UNICAST back to the probe's source address. A multicast reply would force
the companion to hold a `WifiManager.MulticastLock` on Android; a unicast reply to an
already-open `DatagramSocket` needs nothing.

The daemon runs as a shell-UID `app_process` with no Android `Context`, so `NsdManager`
(mDNS) is not available to it. A plain `DatagramSocket` is, which is why this is a UDP
probe and not mDNS.

## Exact locations

- New file: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/LanDiscoveryResponder.kt`
- Start/stop it beside the other servers in
  `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/daemon/CameraDaemon.kt`
- Secret for the probe HMAC: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/config/SecretConfigStore.kt`
- Gate flag: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/config/UnifiedConfigManager.kt` line 612 (`isLanHttpEnabled`)
- The TLS fingerprint the reply carries comes from the TLS-listener task.

## Step-by-step instructions

1. Pick a fixed UDP port for the probe. Do NOT reuse 8080, 8443, 19876 or 19877 — those are
   taken (see `docs/networking-and-tunnels.md`). Document the chosen port in that file.
2. Write `LanDiscoveryResponder`:
   - Binds a `DatagramSocket` on the chosen port, on all interfaces.
   - Receives probe datagrams.
   - Validates the probe: it must carry an HMAC-SHA256 over a nonce plus a timestamp, keyed
     by the pairing secret. Reject anything that fails the HMAC, and reject a timestamp
     outside a small window so a captured probe cannot be replayed indefinitely.

     BEWARE THE HEAD UNIT'S CLOCK. `AuthMiddleware.kt` lines 225-228 document that these
     head units NTP-correct their wall clock shortly after boot and that it can jump
     BACKWARDS — which is exactly when the daemon is starting and when an owner is most
     likely to be probing. A naive `abs(now - probeTs) < window` check will silently reject
     every probe during that skew, and the symptom is "LAN discovery just doesn't work
     sometimes", which is miserable to debug. Handle it explicitly: widen the window, use a
     monotonic nonce cache instead of wall-clock alone, or defer strict checking until the
     clock has settled. Whichever you choose, write down why.
   - On a valid probe, replies UNICAST to `packet.address`/`packet.port` with: the car's LAN
     IP, the TLS port (8443), the TLS certificate SHA-256 fingerprint, and the device id.
   - Signs the reply with the same key so the companion can tell a real car from a spoofer.
3. Gate the whole responder on `isLanHttpEnabled()`. If LAN access is off, do not bind at
   all.
4. Start it from `CameraDaemon` alongside the other servers, and stop it cleanly on daemon
   shutdown.
5. Add JVM unit tests: valid probe is answered; bad HMAC is silently ignored; stale
   timestamp is ignored; responder does not bind when the flag is off.

## Logging

Add a `LAN_DISCOVERY` flag to `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/logging/DaemonLogConfig.kt`
(note: it is `.kt`, despite CLAUDE.md calling it `DaemonLogConfig.java`) and gate every log
call in LanDiscoveryResponder behind it. All flags there are `false` and R8 strips the calls from
release bytecode; a new subsystem that logs unconditionally defeats that.

Leave the flag `false`. CLAUDE.md: do not enable logging flags in commits intended for
release.

## Constraints

- Do NOT answer unsigned probes. An unauthenticated responder announces to every device on
  the network that a BladeWatch car is parked there, which is an information leak about the
  owner's location and vehicle.
- Do NOT broadcast unsolicited announcements. The car answers, it never advertises.
- Do NOT put the device secret, the JWT, or any token in the reply. The reply carries only
  routing information plus a public certificate fingerprint.
- Do NOT use `NsdManager` or any API that needs an Android `Context` — the daemon does not
  have one.
- Do NOT log the HMAC key or the raw probe contents.
- Do NOT enable this by default; it follows the same opt-in flag as LAN HTTP.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `LanDiscoveryResponder.kt` exists, compiles, and is started and stopped by `CameraDaemon`.
- [ ] With `isLanHttpEnabled()` false, the UDP port is not bound (verify with `ss -lun` on the head unit).
- [ ] With it true, a correctly-signed probe broadcast from another machine on the LAN gets
      a unicast reply containing the car's IP, 8443, and the fingerprint.
- [ ] The fingerprint in the reply byte-matches the one the TLS listener actually serves.
- [ ] A probe with a corrupted HMAC gets NO reply. Prove this by sending one.
- [ ] A probe with a timestamp outside the accepted window gets NO reply. Prove this.
- [ ] A test simulates the clock jumping BACKWARDS mid-session and proves valid probes are
      still answered. Document the chosen strategy.
- [ ] `./gradlew test` and `./gradlew koverVerify` pass.
- [ ] The chosen UDP port is documented in `docs/networking-and-tunnels.md` in the Local
      Ports table.

- [ ] A `LAN_DISCOVERY` flag exists in `DaemonLogConfig.kt`, is `false`, and gates every log
      call in LanDiscoveryResponder.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
close_reason:
Done, with one criterion AMENDED by a hardware finding (below). Device checks on the head unit 2026-09-24 from a Mac on the same LAN; probes were signed ON the car by a throwaway checker (the probe key never left the car) and sent from the Mac with a small Python sender.

- LanDiscoveryResponder is started and stopped by CameraDaemon (and gated live on the LAN flag).
- LAN flag OFF: netstat -lun shows no 18443. ON: udp6 :::18443 bound within 5 s. OFF again: unbound.
- The probe key is created lazily by the responder on the first well-formed probe (a forged 256-byte probe with a random HMAC got no reply and created lanDiscovery.probeKey) - by design, the lambda in CameraDaemon.
- Correctly signed probe, UNICAST to the car: reply 182 bytes (< 256, no amplification), magic BWREPLY1, nonce echoed, ip = the car's LAN address, port 8443, fp byte-equal to the fingerprint the TLS listener serves (and to lanTlsInfo), id present.
- Corrupted HMAC (one bit flipped): NO reply. The same probe uncorrupted, sent right after: answered - so a forged packet cannot burn a legitimate nonce.
- Timestamp 25 h in the past: NO reply. 25 h in the future: NO reply. Truncated (100 bytes): NO reply. Exact replay of an answered probe: NO reply.
- Clock-jump test: LanDiscoveryResponderTest simulates the wall clock jumping backwards mid-session and valid probes are still answered. Strategy (documented in the class doc and docs/networking-and-tunnels.md): +/-24 h wall-clock freshness window, replay protection keyed on the MONOTONIC clock.
- ./gradlew test (863, 0 failures) and koverVerify pass. udp/18443 is in the Local Ports table. LAN_DISCOVERY flag exists, false, gates every log call.

AMENDED CRITERION - discovery must be unicast, not broadcast.
"A correctly-signed probe BROADCAST gets a reply" cannot be met on this car: valid probes sent to the subnet-directed broadcast address and to 255.255.255.255 got no reply in six tries, while the same probes sent unicast were answered every time. dumpsys wifi: no MulticastLock held; the Qualcomm firmware filters broadcast/multicast unless one is. The daemon cannot take one (shell uid lacks CHANGE_WIFI_MULTICAST_STATE); holding one from the app process would keep Wi-Fi awake for all multicast through every sentry night; and iOS forbids SENDING broadcast without Apple's multicast entitlement anyway. The responder itself needs no change - it answers unicast. The companion's selector (BladeWatch-rdtj.8, notes appended) must probe the last-known address and then sweep its own /24 by unicast. docs/networking-and-tunnels.md "LAN discovery" records the measurements and the design.

title: TLS listener on 0.0.0.0:8443 with self-signed cert and stable pinned fingerprint
description:
## Problem / context

The companion app will connect directly over the LAN whenever it is on the same network as
the car, because Hyperswarm fails between two peers behind the same NAT (router
hairpinning). That LAN path must not be plain HTTP.

Today every remote byte is inside the tor tunnel and therefore encrypted. A plain-HTTP LAN
path would put the Bearer JWT on the wire in cleartext. A passive sniffer on a shared Wi-Fi
(apartment building, office car park) who captured that token would gain the full API,
including the vehicle-control endpoints that actuate real hardware — windows, trunk,
lights, climate. That is a straight security downgrade from the current state and is not
acceptable.

Fix: a SECOND listener. Loopback stays plain HTTP (it is loopback, and the Pear pump
already rides an encrypted stream); the LAN listener is TLS with a self-signed certificate
whose fingerprint the companion pins at pairing time.

| Bind | Transport | Clients |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `127.0.0.1:8080` | plain HTTP | in-car Flutter UI, Pear stream pump |
| `0.0.0.0:8443` | TLS, self-signed | companion on the same LAN |

## Exact locations

- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/HttpServer.kt`
  - line 121: `val bindHost = if (UnifiedConfigManager.isLanHttpEnabled()) "0.0.0.0" else "127.0.0.1"`
  - line 122: `val socket = ServerSocket(port, 10, InetAddress.getByName(bindHost))`
  - line 865-867: the `/status` response already reports `httpBind`.
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/config/UnifiedConfigManager.kt` line 612:
  `fun isLanHttpEnabled(): Boolean`
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/config/SecretConfigStore.kt` — where the
  keystore password belongs.
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/AuthMiddleware.kt` line 210 —
  `isLoopbackBypassAllowed()` is debug-only. Leave it that way.

## Step-by-step instructions

1. Read `HttpServer.kt` lines 100-200 fully to understand the current accept loop and how
   the accepted socket's streams are consumed. The TLS listener must feed the SAME request
   handling path — an `SSLSocket` is an ordinary `Socket` subclass, so the handler code
   should not need to change at all.
2. Change the existing listener at line 121-122 to ALWAYS bind `127.0.0.1`. The LAN bind
   moves to the new TLS listener.
3. Add certificate generation: on first use, generate a self-signed X.509 certificate and
   keypair, store them in a `KeyStore` file next to the other daemon state, with the
   keystore password in `SecretConfigStore` (mode 600). Regenerate only if missing or
   expired. Certificate validity should be long (10 years) — this is a pinned cert, not a
   CA-chained one, so expiry only creates churn.
4. Expose the certificate's SHA-256 fingerprint through the existing IPC command surface
   (`TcpCommandServer.kt`) so the pairing task can put it in the QR payload. Do NOT expose
   it over unauthenticated HTTP.
5. Add a second accept loop binding `0.0.0.0:8443` via `SSLServerSocketFactory` backed by
   that keystore. Gate it on `isLanHttpEnabled()` — the same opt-in flag.
6. Report the TLS listener's state in `/status` next to the existing `httpBind` field.
7. Add JVM unit tests: fingerprint is stable across restarts; the listener does not bind
   when the flag is off; the keystore password is not readable by the app UID.

## Constraints

- Do NOT make LAN access enabled by default. CLAUDE.md states LAN HTTP is disabled by
  default and must remain opt-in; that invariant survives this change. The pairing flow
  surfaces the toggle to the owner, it does not flip it silently.
- Do NOT weaken `AuthMiddleware`. LAN callers are not loopback and must keep full JWT
  enforcement. Do NOT add 8443 or the LAN interface to any public-path list.
- Introduce the trust policy PER LISTENER, not as a global flag. `HttpServer` is about to
  have three listeners with different trust: 8080 loopback (in-car UI, Tier 2 bypass
  eligible in debug as today), 8081 loopback (Pear pump, NEVER bypass eligible — added by
  the pump task), and 8443 LAN TLS (NEVER bypass eligible). Build the plumbing so each
  accepted socket carries its listener's policy into `AuthMiddleware`, and make the default
  for a new listener be "not bypass eligible". A global "is a tunnel up" flag fails OPEN
  when someone forgets to set it; a per-listener policy cannot be forgotten.
- Do NOT put the keystore password in `bladewatch_config.json` or any world-readable file.
- Do NOT change the WebSocket upgrade handling, the ConnectRPC routing, or any handler.
  This task only adds a second way to arrive at the existing server.
- Do NOT bind the plain-HTTP listener to `0.0.0.0` under any configuration after this
  change. Plaintext must never leave the device.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `grep -n '"0.0.0.0"' app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/HttpServer.kt`
      shows the LAN bind ONLY on the TLS listener, never on the plain one.
- [ ] With `isLanHttpEnabled()` false, `netstat`/`ss` on the head unit shows neither 8443
      bound nor 8080 bound to anything but 127.0.0.1.
- [ ] With it true, 8443 is bound on 0.0.0.0 and 8080 is still 127.0.0.1 only.
- [ ] `curl -k https://<car-ip>:8443/status` from another machine on the LAN returns 401
      without a JWT and 200 with one.
- [ ] `curl http://<car-ip>:8080/status` from another machine on the LAN fails to connect.
- [ ] The SHA-256 fingerprint returned over IPC matches
      `openssl s_client -connect <car-ip>:8443 </dev/null | openssl x509 -fingerprint -sha256`.
- [ ] The fingerprint is unchanged after a daemon restart and after a device reboot.
- [ ] A test proves a request on the 8443 listener is denied without a JWT even with
      `setLoopbackBypassOverride(true)` and `setTunnelActiveOverride(false)` forced.
- [ ] The per-listener trust policy defaults to NOT bypass-eligible for any newly added
      listener. Prove it by adding a throwaway listener in a test and asserting it denies.
- [ ] `./gradlew test` and `./gradlew koverVerify` pass.
- [ ] The keystore password does not appear in logcat or in any world-readable file.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
close_reason:
Done. All acceptance criteria verified; device checks on the head unit 2026-09-24 from a Mac on the same LAN.

- grep '"0.0.0.0"' HttpServer.kt: only in runLanTlsListener (also pinned by LanTlsTest "plain HTTP binds loopback only -- 0_0_0_0 appears solely in the TLS listener").
- LAN flag OFF (the default): netstat on the car shows 8080 LISTEN on ::ffff:127.0.0.1 only, nothing on 8443; from the Mac both 8080 and 8443 refuse.
- LAN flag ON (set through UnifiedConfigManager.setLanHttpEnabled; took effect within 5 s, the recheck interval): 8443 LISTEN on the dual-stack wildcard (:::8443, which covers 0.0.0.0); 8080 still ::ffff:127.0.0.1 only and still unreachable from the Mac.
- From the Mac: curl -k https://<car>:8443/status -> 401 with no JWT, 401 with a garbage JWT, 200 with a valid JWT. Plain http to 8443 -> connection fails. The JWT was minted ON the car by a throwaway checker with a 120 s TTL (the long-lived device secret never left the car) and never printed.
- TLS: TLSv1.3, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, 256-bit EC key; -tls1 and -tls1_1 handshakes refused.
- Fingerprint: openssl s_client | x509 -fingerprint -sha256 from the Mac == the lanTlsInfo IPC reply (queried over the real IPC on 19876 as shell, token read on the car) == SHA-256 of the stored certificate. lanTlsInfo also reported enabled=true, port=8443.
- Fingerprint unchanged after (a) killing byd_cam_daemon (respawned in 7 s, 8443 back in 8 s), (b) the full CLAUDE.md uninstall/reinstall of the service host, (c) a head-unit reboot (adb back in ~44 s; relaunch needed because of BladeWatch-8net). Same fingerprint prefix across all three.
- Tests: AuthMiddlewareTest "aRemoteListenerNeverGetsTheLoopbackBypass" (loopback bypass forced on, tunnel forced off, REMOTE listener still denies) and "aCallerThatDoesNotDeclareItsListenerFailsClosed" (an undeclared listener defaults to REMOTE and denies).
- ./gradlew test (863, 0 failures) and ./gradlew koverVerify (9.054%) pass.
- Keystore password: LanTls builds an in-memory PKCS12 with a random per-process password that is never stored or logged; logcat grep for keystore/pkcs12/storepass: 0. The TLS private key's prefix: 0 hits in logcat, every /data/local/tmp/*.log and the world-readable config (positive control found it in the 600 secret store).
- Restored afterwards: LAN flag back to false, 8443 closed.

title: PearDaemon + PearLauncher: the Pear peer as its own supervised daemon process
description:
## Problem / context

With the BareKit spike proven, BladeWatch needs a real, supervised Pear peer.

THE PEER IS ITS OWN DAEMON PROCESS — `pear_daemon` — exactly like `byd_cam_daemon`,
`sentry_daemon` and `acc_sentry_daemon`. It is NOT a thread inside `CameraDaemon`. Verified
on the head unit 2026-09-23, the existing daemons run as:

    sh -c CLASSPATH=/data/app/net.bladewatch.app-<hash>/base.apk \
      app_process /system/bin --nice-name=sentry_daemon \
      net.bladewatch.app.daemon.SentryDaemon

as the `shell` user, outside the Activity lifecycle. The runtime class is
`net.bladewatch.app.daemon.*` while the source is `com/loabletech/bladewatch/daemon/*` —
the Gradle package rename makes them disagree on purpose.

Its lifecycle must match the tor tunnel it replaces: alive whenever the car is up,
including while parked with the Flutter UI never launched. The peer joins a Hyperswarm
topic so a paired companion can find it from anywhere.

## Exact locations

- Model the LAUNCHER on `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/launcher/TorLauncher.kt`
  (347 lines) — same supervision shape, same logging style, same process-name discipline.
- Model the DAEMON on `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/daemon/SentryDaemon.kt`
  and `CameraDaemon.kt` — same standalone-process shape and shutdown handling.
- New file: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/daemon/PearDaemon.kt` (the process;
  promoted from the spike)
- New file: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/launcher/PearLauncher.kt` (launches
  and supervises it)
- Launch-command construction: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/launcher/AdbDaemonLauncher.kt`
- Register it alongside the other daemons:
  - `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/ui/model/DaemonType.kt`
  - `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/ui/daemon/DaemonStartupManager.kt`
  - `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/ui/daemon/TorController.kt` is the closest
    existing controller to copy for a `PearController`.
- Secret storage: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/config/SecretConfigStore.kt`
- Config: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/config/UnifiedConfigManager.kt`
- Reference for the Worklet/IPC call sequence:
  `/Volumes/mandark-1Tb/projects/loabletech/flutter_pear/packages/flutter_pear_bare/android/src/main/kotlin/tech/loable/flutter_pear_bare/FlutterPearBarePlugin.kt`

## Step-by-step instructions

1. Read `TorLauncher.kt` fully first. Match its structure: start, stop, health check,
   restart-on-crash, and its logging tags.
2. Read the spike's close reason for any PASS WITH CAVEAT runtime requirement and implement
   that requirement here.
3. Promote the spike's `PearDaemon` into a real daemon: bundle extraction, `Worklet` boot,
   `IPC` attach, a clean shutdown path, and a main loop that keeps the process alive.
4. Write `PearLauncher` with:
   - `start()` — launch `pear_daemon` via `app_process --nice-name=pear_daemon`, mirroring
     how `AdbDaemonLauncher` builds the other daemons' commands.
   - A read loop relaying worklet IPC messages to a Kotlin-side dispatcher.
   - `stop()` — `killall -9 pear_daemon`. Use `killall`, NOT `pkill -f`: toybox `pkill -f`
     matches the pattern as a literal substring of every `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`, including
     the adb shell running the command itself, and the bracket trick does not save you.
     CLAUDE.md records this killing an ADB session mid-procedure.
   - Health check and crash detection: `pidof pear_daemon`; restart with backoff exactly as
     `TorLauncher` handles a dead tor process.
4. Derive the swarm topic from the device secret, NOT from a hardcoded string. Read
   `SecretConfigStore.kt` for how secrets are stored and fetched. A hardcoded or
   string-derived topic is a GLOBAL rendezvous — every BladeWatch car worldwide would land
   in the same room. flutter_pear's own API names this hazard `unsafeTopicFromString`.
   Use a SHA-256 of a per-device secret.
5. Persist the peer's key material so the topic survives a daemon restart and a reboot.
   Store it in the secret store (mode 600, shell-only), never in
   `bladewatch_config.json` and never anywhere world-readable.
7. Wire the launcher into `DaemonStartupManager` on the optional-daemon tier (~60s after
   boot), behind a config flag so it can be turned off. Add it to `DaemonType.kt`.
8. Add `pear_daemon` to CLAUDE.md's clean-reinstall daemon-stop block, in the
   `killall -9 byd_cam_daemon sentry_daemon acc_sentry_daemon` line. A daemon missing from
   that list survives an uninstall as a detached `app_process` and blocks the next build
   with a stale lock — which is exactly the failure that block exists to prevent.
9. Add JVM unit tests under `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/launcher/`
   modelled on `TorLauncherCommandTest.kt`, covering the constructed launch command.

## Logging

Add a `PEAR_LAUNCHER` flag to `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/logging/DaemonLogConfig.kt`
(note: it is `.kt`, despite CLAUDE.md calling it `DaemonLogConfig.java`) and gate every log
call in PearLauncher behind it. All flags there are `false` and R8 strips the calls from
release bytecode; a new subsystem that logs unconditionally defeats that.

Leave the flag `false`. CLAUDE.md: do not enable logging flags in commits intended for
release.

## Constraints

- Do NOT hardcode the swarm topic or derive it from a human-readable string.
- Do NOT write the Pear key material to `/data/local/tmp/bladewatch_config.json` or any
  world-readable file. It goes in the secret store, mode 600.
- Do NOT log key material, the topic, or any invite. `SecretRedactor` exists for this.
- Do NOT modify `TorLauncher.kt` in this task. Tor is removed in a later task, on purpose,
  only after the Pear path is proven.
- Do NOT start the worklet from an Activity or require a Context if the spike showed one is
  not needed.
- The daemon process name must survive the kernel's 15-character `comm` cap if you give it
  one — see the `bladewatch_tor` naming note in CLAUDE.md for why that length matters.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `PearDaemon.kt` and `PearLauncher.kt` exist and compile; `./gradlew :app:assembleDebug` succeeds.
- [ ] On the head unit, `ps -A -o PID,USER,ARGS | grep pear_daemon` shows it running as the
      `shell` user, as a SEPARATE process from byd_cam_daemon.
- [ ] `pidof pear_daemon` returns a pid; `killall -9 pear_daemon` stops it.
- [ ] CLAUDE.md's daemon-stop block lists `pear_daemon`.
- [ ] `./gradlew test` passes, including new tests for the launcher.
- [ ] `./gradlew koverVerify` passes and coverage did not drop.
- [ ] On a real head unit, `pear_daemon` stays up for at least 10 minutes with the Flutter
      UI never launched.
- [ ] `killall -9 pear_daemon` causes `PearLauncher` to restart it within its backoff
      window, proven by killing it and showing the restart in logs.
- [ ] The swarm topic is derived from a per-device secret: two different devices produce
      different topics. Prove this, do not assert it.
- [ ] `grep -rn 'unsafeTopicFromString' app/src/main` returns nothing.
- [ ] The Pear key material file is mode 600 and is not readable by the app UID.
- [ ] No key material, topic or invite appears in logcat at any log level.

- [ ] A `PEAR_LAUNCHER` flag exists in `DaemonLogConfig.kt`, is `false`, and gates every log
      call in PearLauncher.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
notes:
## From the spike (BladeWatch-rdtj.2, CLOSED PASS WITH CAVEAT) -- read its close reason first

The spike's PearDaemon.kt already contains working, commented versions of everything below.
Promote it; do not rediscover any of this.

MUST carry into the real daemon, every one:
1. Install a stand-in Application into ActivityThread.mInitialApplication BEFORE
   worklet.start() -- see PearDaemon.installApplicationForBareKit. Without it bare-kit's
   bare_kit__on_thread_enter aborts the process (unchecked currentApplication()). Keep it in
   PearDaemon, NOT in the shared DaemonBootstrap.
2. Worklet + IPC on a thread with a prepared AND pumped Looper (IPC captures
   ALooper_forThread with no null check). Prepare the looper BEFORE DaemonBootstrap.init().
3. Launch with -Djava.library.path=$nativeLibDir:/system/lib64:/vendor/lib64:/product/lib64:/odm/lib64,
   exactly like CameraDaemon in DaemonLauncher.kt. Put $nativeLibDir FIRST, so the APK's own
   libc++_shared.so wins over any firmware copy.
4. fetchBareKit already ships libbare-kit.so AND libc++_shared.so. Keep both.
5. Decide the 12 pear-end addon .so files (currently untracked in
   app/src/main/jniLibs/arm64-v8a/): vendor-and-commit with SHA-256 pins, or fetch from a

6. STORAGE_DIR = /data/local/tmp/pear, chmod 0700, passed as argv[0]. Read the bundle from

## NEW OPERATIONAL HAZARD this task creates -- same class as tor's hs/ directory

Once pairing (.7) exists, /data/local/tmp/pear holds the car's PERMANENT Pear identity
(Corestore's primary key). Deleting it mints a new identity and silently breaks every paired
companion, exactly like deleting /data/local/tmp/tor/hs. So:
- Add it to CLAUDE.md's daemon-stop block warnings ("NEVER widen any rm glob to cover it").
- Never delete it in PearLauncher.stop() or any hard-reset path; add a test asserting that,
  modelled on the tests TorLauncher has for its hs dir.
- pear-end creates pear-corestore inside it as 0777. The parent's 0700 is the ONLY
  protection. Never loosen it, and assert the mode in a test.

## Measured cost to budget for

112 MB PSS / 52 MB private dirty on the head unit (7.8 GB total, 4.4 GB available); 0.0%
CPU when idle; boot-to-attach.info reply about 3 s.

- PEAR_LAUNCHER flag: added to DaemonLogConfig (false, in ANY_LOGGING_ENABLED, tag "PearLauncher"). PearLauncher previously had NO flag -- all its log calls now go through one gated log() helper. New test "every log call goes through the PEAR_LAUNCHER gate" (source scan: logManager only inside the helper; flag must ship false). Mutation-proven: a planted direct logManager call failed it (expected 3 but was 4).

ON THE HEAD UNIT
- Enabled PEAR_PEER via UnifiedConfigManager.setDaemonEnabled: the service host health check launched pear_daemon 6 s later, as user shell, separate process from byd_cam_daemon (own PID/PPID), with the launch shape from PearLauncher.launchCommand.

- 10-minute soak on the relaunched process: ELAPSED 10:02, 8 s total CPU (mostly startup), 0.0% CPU at the end sample, PSS ~115 MB (RSS 224 MB, 168 MB shared). Flutter UI never launched (pidof net.bladewatch.flutter empty). (The first process was killed at 9:26 - the soak was redone rather than rounded up.)
- Key material: /data/local/tmp/bladewatch_secrets.json is -rw------- shell:shell; run-as net.bladewatch.app cannot read it ("app uid denied") nor list /data/local/tmp/pear (drwx------ shell:shell).
- Logs: a throwaway on-car checker (scratchpad only, removed afterwards) derived the topic exactly as PearTopic does and counted occurrences of topic, topic seed, probe key, TLS private key and device secret in logcat, every /data/local/tmp/*.log and the world-readable config: all 0, three times (after first launch, after LAN enable, after reboot). Positive control on the secrets file found each stored secret (so the zeros are real). Values were never printed.
- Survived: daemon restart, full CLAUDE.md uninstall/reinstall (BladeWatch-10u6) and a head-unit reboot; after the post-reboot relaunch all four daemons (camera, sentry, acc_sentry, pear) were up within 70 s.

BUGS FOUND AND FIXED ALONG THE WAY
1. SecretConfigStore lost-update race (new with this task: pear_daemon is a SECOND process writing the secret store). mutateRoot was an unlocked read-modify-write with a fixed temp name, so two first-run writes could drop each other's section - the auth secret, TLS identity, probe key or topic seed - which silently unpairs companions. Fix: exclusive fcntl lock on a sidecar file created 600 atomically (world-readable would let any co-resident app take a shared lock and block every secret write), inside a JVM-wide monitor (FileLock is per process). Unopenable lock file -> returns false like writeRootMap (AuthManagerTest contract). New SecretConfigStoreCrossProcessTest spawns two real JVMs behind a start barrier (300 writes each) and checks every key survives, plus lock-file perms. Mutation-proven: without the file lock a child's write failed outright. On the car the lock file exists as -rw------- shell:shell.
2. pear_daemon ran the service host's PermissionGranter pass on every start: 17.75 s of pm grant calls (30 granted, 113 skipped) before the worklet could boot. DaemonBootstrap.init(grantPermissions = false) for PearDaemon only; CameraDaemon keeps it (BYD HAL needs it).
