Mutation-test every one: change the comparison to `<=`, flip the gate to run after the probes, and remove the gate entirely. Each mutation must fail at least one test. A guard that cannot fail is worse than no guard.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A sub-30 kWh known nominal capacity yields PHEV even when both fuel HAL signals are at sentinel.
- [ ] An unknown (0) capacity changes nothing versus today's behaviour.
- [ ] A capacity of 30.0 or above changes nothing versus today's behaviour.
- [ ] `getNominalCapacityKwh()` throwing leaves the method behaving exactly as today.
- [ ] The 30.0 threshold is a named constant, not a repeated literal.
- [ ] New tests exist and all three listed mutations are caught.
- [ ] `./gradlew test koverVerify assembleDebug` passes.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
close_reason: Extracted the drivetrain decision into a pure package-visible decideDrivetrain() and put the capacity gate ahead of the fuel-HAL probes. A known sub-30 kWh pack now resolves to PHEV before the warm-up sentinels can conclude BEV and cache it for 60s. Capacity is read best-effort via knownNominalKwh(); a throwing or uninitialised VehicleDataMonitor leaves behaviour exactly as before. Threshold is the named constant PHEV_MAX_NOMINAL_KWH, documented as inherited from Overdrive and not re-derived on this car, with a pointer to the duplicate rule in VehicleDataMonitor.isPhevVehicle. 9 tests; all three specified mutations (loosened boundary, demoted gate, deleted gate) verified failing.

title: Port Overdrive PHEV support: drivetrain detection hardening + fuel-aware trips
description:
Port Overdrive's PHEV/hybrid support into BladeWatch: harden drivetrain detection, and make trips account for the FUEL leg when the car is a PHEV.

## Why

BladeWatch already collects PHEV telemetry and already knows how to detect a PHEV, but nothing in `trips/` consumes either. On a PHEV the recorded trip is therefore wrong in a way that looks plausible: the electric leg is costed and the petrol leg is silently free, so `tripCost` under-reports and `energyPerKm` describes only part of the journey.

Overdrive (upstream, MIT, cloned for reference at `/tmp/overdrive-eval`) solved this over roughly v12 to v36. This epic ports that work.

## What BladeWatch has today (verified 2026-09-15, do not re-derive)

- `byd/BydDataCollector.java:1786` `computeIsPhev()` — the fuel-HAL half of the detector, with the same "0 is not real" guard as Overdrive. `isBevFuelSentinel(int)` at line 1853.
- `monitor/VehicleDataMonitor.java:300` `getNominalCapacityKwh()`, and `isPhevVehicle(double)` at line 314 which already carries the sub-30 kWh rule, but only as a startup FALLBACK.
- `byd/BydVehicleData.java` carries `totalFuelCon` (line 60), `fuelRangeKm` (64), `fuelPercent` (66), `totalElecCon` (59), `oilLevel` (180), `engineCode` (181).
- A full `trips/` package with a SQL store using additive `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` migrations (`TripDatabase.java:274-284`).

## What is missing

- The capacity PRE-gate in `computeIsPhev` — Overdrive added it because the fuel HAL returns BMS sentinels during warm-up, which latches a false BEV verdict for 60s.
- Every fuel field on `TripRecord` (`fuelPctStart/End`, `fuelConStart/End`, `litresUsed`, `fuelPricePerL`, `fuelCost`, `electricCost`).
- The metered-energy tier (`elecConStart/End`), so short trips currently report a flat 0 kWh.

## Scope boundary

Detection + trip accounting + the API surface that exposes it. Explicitly NOT in scope: a SoH/degradation estimator (BladeWatch has none by decision — `VehicleDataMonitor:296` says so and callers treat the pack as healthy), and any BYD vehicle-control change.

## Open question for the owner

Is the car actually a PHEV? If the fleet is BEV-only, every child here still runs correctly (the fuel fields simply stay at their unavailable sentinels) but delivers no visible value. Do not block on this — the code must be correct either way, and a PHEV owner installing the same build must get correct trips.
close_reason: All 10 children delivered. BladeWatch now detects PHEVs reliably (capacity gate ahead of the warm-up-prone fuel HAL), records the petrol leg on every trip, and costs both legs. Shipped: 10 TripRecord fields, 10 persisted columns with an additive migration, capture at both trip boundaries gated on drivetrain, a two-tier energy cascade that also fixes short-trip accounting on BEVs, fuel price and tank capacity config, dual-leg cost, API and proto exposure at new field numbers, fuel consumption learning with range prediction, and docs across four files. ~60 tests, every one mutation-verified. BEV behaviour is provably unchanged: tripCost is pinned against an independently reproduced legacy formula across five input sets. Core data model (TripRecord, TripConfig, RangeEstimate) and all new code are Kotlin; the remaining large Java files in the blast radius are being converted separately. STILL OPEN FOR THE OWNER: whether the car is actually a PHEV. Everything is correct on a BEV - the fuel fields simply stay at -1 - but the fuel leg and the range prediction deliver nothing visible on a BEV-only fleet.

title: Wire fisheye dewarp into the AI path, mosaic tiles only
description:
## Problem

Children 2 and 3 produced a tested dewarp transform and a tested inverse mapping, but nothing calls them. This task wires them into the AI path - the ONLY task in this epic that touches the live pipeline.

## Where

app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/surveillance/SurveillanceEngineGpu.java, the aiExecutor lambda containing the primary detector call at approximately line 1790:

    java.util.List<net.bladewatch.app.ai.Detection> detections = detectorSnap.detect(
            cropData, qW, qH, aiConfidence, detectPerson, detectCar, false, detectBike, minObjectSize);

The variable quadrant is already in scope. Line numbers WILL have shifted - search for the call rather than trusting them.

## Scope limit - this is the part most likely to be got wrong

Dewarp applies ONLY to full-tile mosaic crops. It must NOT apply to foveated crops.

Overdrive's class doc explains why: foveated crops are re-centred sub-windows of the panorama, so their crop centre is NOT the lens axis, and a tile-centred radial model is geometrically wrong there. Applying it would move boxes in the wrong direction.

At the call site there are two crop paths, at approximately lines 1667-1702:

- Foveated: cropOnGlThread(quadrant, centroidX, centroidY), after which qW and qH are set to FoveatedCropper.CROP_SIZE (640).
- Mosaic: cropFromMosaic(mosaicRgb, quadrant, qW, qH), after which qW and qH are THUMBNAIL_WIDTH/2 and THUMBNAIL_HEIGHT/2 (320 x 240). Note the foveated branch FALLS BACK to the mosaic crop when cropOnGlThread returns null - that fallback IS a mosaic tile and must be treated as one.

Do NOT infer the path from qW == 640. Add an explicit boolean, for example fromMosaicTile, set to false in the foveated success branch and true in both the fallback and the legacy else branch. An explicit flag is the point: a future change to CROP_SIZE must not silently re-enable dewarp on foveated crops.

## What to do

1. Add the boolean described above, set correctly in all three branches.
2. Immediately before the detect() call:

    byte[] detectorInput = cropData;
    byte[] dewarped = fromMosaicTile ? FisheyeDewarp.dewarpForDetector(cropData, qW, qH, quadrant) : null;
    if (dewarped != null) detectorInput = dewarped;

   Pass detectorInput to detect() instead of cropData. Note the null contract from child 2: null means "not dewarped", so the original bytes are used.
3. Immediately after detect() returns, and BEFORE any other code touches the list:

    if (dewarped != null) {
        detections = FisheyeDewarp.mapDetectionsToSource(detections, qW, qH, quadrant);
    }

   This must sit before the motion-overlap filter, before DetectionBaseline, before ActorTracker, before ThumbnailBuffer.observe - everything downstream must see original crop space.
4. Leave cropData itself untouched. ThumbnailBuffer and the tracker consume it and must keep seeing the warped pixels.

## Threading

Overdrive's class doc records that this is called on the AI executor only, matching YoloDetector's single-lane discipline, and that the shared scratch buffer is safe only because of it. BladeWatch dispatches AI through the same single aiExecutor lane. CONFIRM that before relying on it - if the crop is ever handed to another thread, the shared scratch buffer in child 2 becomes a data race.

## Constraints

- Do NOT dewarp the recording, the stream, the thumbnail, or anything the tracker sees. Detector input only.
- Do NOT change detect()'s signature.
- Do NOT reorder any existing downstream stage.
- Do NOT add a config key or setting.
- If a crop is neither foveated nor a mosaic tile in some path you discover, leave it undewarped and say so in the close notes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An explicit boolean distinguishes mosaic tiles from foveated crops, set correctly in all three branches including the foveated fallback.
- [ ] Dewarp is applied only when that boolean is true.
- [ ] mapDetectionsToSource is called before any downstream consumer of the detection list. Verify by reading the code path, and state in the close notes which stages you checked.
- [ ] cropData is byte-identical after the change - the thumbnail and tracker still see warped pixels.
- [ ] With QUADRANT_STRENGTH all zeros the pipeline behaves byte-identically to before this task - verify by running the surveillance tests with a temporarily zeroed array.
- [ ] A guard test pins that dewarp is not applied to a 640x640 foveated crop.
- [ ] ./gradlew test koverVerify assembleDebug passes.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
close_reason:
Wired in, mosaic tiles only. This was the only task in the epic touching the live pipeline.

THE FLAG. Added a final boolean fromMosaicTile beside the existing final cropData, set explicitly in ALL THREE branches: false in the foveated success path, true in the legacy mosaic path, and true in the foveated FALLBACK - the one that is easy to miss, because it sits inside the foveated branch but produces a real 320x240 tile. Deliberately NOT inferred from qW == FoveatedCropper.CROP_SIZE: that works today and breaks silently the day CROP_SIZE changes or a third crop path appears.

THE WIRING. Before detect(), dewarpForDetector runs only when fromMosaicTile is true; a null return means this quadrant is not dewarped, so the original bytes go to the detector. Immediately after detect() and before anything reads the list, mapDetectionsToSource brings the boxes back to warped space. cropData is untouched and stays final, so ThumbnailBuffer and the tracker still see the original warped pixels.

ORDER VERIFIED by reading the path, as the acceptance criteria asked. detect() then mapDetectionsToSource then the motion-overlap filter, which is the first consumer, then DetectionBaseline, ActorTracker, CrossQuadrantTracker and ThumbnailBuffer - all downstream of the mapping.

SCOPE, AND AN OPEN QUESTION I AM RECORDING RATHER THAN ASSUMING AWAY. Dewarp is on the live detection path only. The three DetectionBaseline seeding and refresh call sites also run YOLO over full mosaic tiles and are NOT dewarped. I checked Overdrive before deciding: it wires this in exactly one place too, so the scope matches. But the asymmetry is real - the baseline records what is normally present, and dewarped live detection finds MORE than undewarped baseline seeding does, so an object the baseline never saw is not suppressed and could in principle ADD a false positive, the one thing DETECTION-INVARIANTS says a change here must not do. Two things mitigate it and neither is proof: boxes reach the baseline mapped back into its own warped space so they still MATCH, and a newly-found static object is independently handled by ActorTracker static/everMoved logic. Documented at the call site and added to BladeWatch-3dg8 as a required measurement - that task must now record FALSE POSITIVES before and after, not just detection counts.

GUARD TEST. New FisheyeDewarpWiringTest.kt reads the engine source as data (the class is ~4,000 lines and needs GL, a camera and TFLite to instantiate) and pins five properties: the flag exists, every branch assigns it, dewarp is gated on it, cropData is never replaced, and the mapping precedes the motion-overlap filter BY POSITION IN THE FILE. Mutation tested: removing the foveated gate fails the third; moving the mapping after the motion filter fails the fifth.

Also confirmed the wiring guard still passes with all strengths zeroed, since the wiring is correct independently of the constants.

Gate: ./gradlew test koverVerify assembleDebug BUILD SUCCESSFUL.

title: Port the detection back-mapping from dewarped to source space
description:
## Problem

Once the detector runs on a DEWARPED crop (BladeWatch-cxjn child 2), the boxes YOLO returns are in dewarped coordinate space. Every downstream consumer in BladeWatch - the motion-overlap filter, DetectionBaseline, ActorTracker, CrossQuadrantTracker, ThumbnailBuffer - expects boxes in the ORIGINAL warped crop space. This task ports the inverse mapping so the coordinate space seen downstream never changes.

This is a pure function. Do not wire anything; that is child 4.

## Why a naive corner mapping is wrong

The transform is RADIAL. A box's extreme point after mapping can lie at an edge MIDPOINT, not only at a corner - a straight edge bows outward under barrel distortion. Mapping only the 4 corners therefore under-covers the object.

Overdrive maps 8 points - the 4 corners PLUS the 4 edge midpoints - and takes the bounding box of the mapped set. Port that. The forward sampling map is used (the same one the pixels used), not an analytic inverse.

## Source to port

/tmp/overdrive-eval/app/src/main/java/com/overdrive/app/surveillance/FisheyeDewarp.java, method mapDetectionsToSource, lines 160-218.

## BladeWatch type differences - read this before copying

Overdrive's Detection is a Java class with getters: d.getX(), d.getY(), d.getW(), d.getH(), d.getClassId(), d.getConfidence(), and a 6-arg constructor.

BladeWatch's is a KOTLIN DATA CLASS at app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/ai/YoloDetector.kt line 25:

    data class Detection(
        val classId: Int,
        val confidence: Float,
        val x: Int,
        val y: Int,
        val w: Int,
        val h: Int
    )

From Java, the accessors are getClassId(), getConfidence(), getX(), getY(), getW(), getH() - Kotlin generates those - and the constructor arg ORDER is (classId, confidence, x, y, w, h). Overdrive's constructor call is new Detection(classId, confidence, bx, by, bw, bh), which happens to match. CONFIRM the order against the data class before trusting it; swapping confidence and classId would compile and be silently wrong.

Note the package: net.bladewatch.app.ai.Detection (the applicationId namespace), even though the file lives under com/loabletech/bladewatch/. See any existing usage in SurveillanceEngineGpu.java for the exact import.

## The transform, stated so you can test it

For each of the 8 sample points (px, py) of a box:

    nx  = (px / w) * 2 - 1
    nya = ((py / h) * 2 - 1) * ASPECT
    r2  = nx*nx + nya*nya
    inv = 1 / (1 + k1*r2 + k2*r2*r2)
    sxp = ((nx * inv * zoom) * 0.5 + 0.5) * w
    syp = (((nya * inv * zoom) / ASPECT) * 0.5 + 0.5) * h

with k1, k2, zoom, ASPECT exactly as in child 2. Take min/max over the 8 mapped points, round, and clamp into [0, w-1] / [0, h-1] with a non-negative width and height.

## What to do, test-first

1. Extend FisheyeDewarpTest.java (or add MapDetectionsToSourceTest.java) FIRST with:
   - Strength 0 returns the SAME list instance or an equal list, unchanged - identity.
   - A null or empty list returns without throwing.
   - Non-geometric fields survive: classId and confidence are preserved exactly for every detection, and list ORDER is preserved.
   - A box centred on the tile centre maps to approximately itself (radial transform is identity at r=0).
   - An off-centre box moves TOWARD the centre, because dewarping expands the centre outward so the inverse pulls inward. Assert the direction of movement, not an exact pixel.
   - Mapped boxes are always within the crop bounds, and w and h are never negative - test with a box touching the tile edge.
   - The 8-point property: construct a wide, short box spanning the tile horizontally and assert its mapped height is GREATER than what mapping only the 4 corners would give. This is the test that actually pins the edge-midpoint behaviour; write a 4-corner helper in the test to compare against.
2. Then implement mapDetectionsToSource to pass.

## Failure policy

Any exception returns the ORIGINAL list, unmapped. The original's comment is explicit: better an unmapped box than a dropped one. Never return null, never drop entries.

## Constraints

- Pure function. No Android imports, no logging that requires a Context.
- Do NOT modify the Detection data class.
- Do NOT wire this into SurveillanceEngineGpu in this task.
- Preserve list order and size exactly - downstream code indexes into it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every test listed above exists and passes, including the 8-point versus 4-corner comparison.
- [ ] Mutation check: temporarily reduce the sample set to the 4 corners and confirm the 8-point test fails; restore afterwards.
- [ ] classId, confidence and list order are asserted preserved.
- [ ] The failure path returns the original list - prove it with a test that forces an exception path if reachable, or document why it is not.
- [ ] Nothing outside FisheyeDewarp.java and its test is modified.
- [ ] ./gradlew test koverVerify assembleDebug passes.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
close_reason:
Done, test-first, in Kotlin. Wrote FisheyeDewarpMappingTest.kt before the implementation, then added mapDetectionsToSource to FisheyeDewarp.kt to pass it.

WHAT IT DOES. Maps YOLO's boxes from dewarped crop space back to the original warped space using the same forward sampling transform the pixels used, evaluated at the four corners PLUS the four edge midpoints, taking the bounding box of the mapped set. Eight points rather than four because the transform is radial: a straight edge bows, so a box's extreme can sit at an edge midpoint, and a corners-only mapping clips the subject out of its own box. Order and size are preserved because downstream code indexes the list positionally. Fails open by returning the ORIGINAL list, never null and never a dropped entry.

TYPE CHECK THE TASK ASKED FOR. Confirmed against the data class rather than assumed: BladeWatch's Detection is Kotlin, constructed as (classId, confidence, x, y, w, h), which happens to match Overdrive's Java constructor order. Being Kotlin-to-Kotlin now, properties are accessed directly (d.x, d.classId) rather than through generated getters.

SEVEN TESTS, each pinning something a plausible mistake would break: identity on a non-dewarped quadrant, null and empty handled, classId/confidence/order preserved, a centred box staying put, bounds and non-negative extents at all four edges and both slivers, the 8-point versus 4-corner height comparison, and a ROUND TRIP.

The round trip is the one that matters most and it is not in the original: paint a marker at a known source position, dewarp the image, locate the marker in dewarped space, feed that back as a detection, and require it to map home within a few pixels. Every other test checks a function against the formula; this one checks the two halves of the feature against EACH OTHER. A consistent sign error in both would pass everything else and still put boxes in the wrong place.

MUTATION TESTED, three ways, each caught by the test written for it: dropping the edge midpoints fails the 8-point test; replacing classId and confidence with constants fails the preservation test; and inverting the transform in the mapping alone - dividing where it should multiply, so the mapping no longer matches the pixels - fails the round trip.

Gate: ./gradlew test koverVerify assembleDebug BUILD SUCCESSFUL. Nothing outside FisheyeDewarp.kt and its two test classes was modified; the Detection data class is untouched.

title: Port the fisheye dewarp transform as a pure, tested class
description:
## Problem

BladeWatch has no fisheye dewarp. This task ports the transform ONLY - a pure function, no Android types, no pipeline wiring - so it can be developed and proven test-first before anything touches the live AI path. Wiring is BladeWatch-cxjn child 4.

## Source to port

/tmp/overdrive-eval/app/src/main/java/com/overdrive/app/surveillance/FisheyeDewarp.java (222 lines). If the clone is gone, re-clone with:

    git clone https://github.com/yash-srivastava/Overdrive-release /tmp/overdrive-eval

Read the whole class doc before writing code - it records why the constants are what they are.

## The maths, stated so you can test it without reading the original

Division-model dewarp. For each OUTPUT pixel, sample the SOURCE at a radially-scaled position:

    k1   = 0.30 * strength
    k2   = 0.10 * strength
    ASPECT = 0.75                       (tile h/w = 240/320)
    a2   = ASPECT * ASPECT
    zoom = 1 + k1*a2 + k2*a2*a2         (keeps corners at the tile edge)

    for output pixel (x, y):
      nx  = ((x + 0.5) / w) * 2 - 1
      ny  = ((y + 0.5) / h) * 2 - 1
      nya = ny * ASPECT
      r2  = nx*nx + nya*nya
      inv = 1 / (1 + k1*r2 + k2*r2*r2)
      sx  = nx * inv * zoom
      sy  = (nya * inv * zoom) / ASPECT
      srcX = clamp((int)((sx*0.5 + 0.5) * w), 0, w-1)
      srcY = clamp((int)((sy*0.5 + 0.5) * h), 0, h-1)
      lut[y*w + x] = srcY*w + srcX

Strength 0 gives k1=k2=0, inv=1, zoom=1, so the LUT is the identity - byte-identical output.

## Per-quadrant strengths

    private static final float[] QUADRANT_STRENGTH = {0f, 0.5f, 0f, 0.5f};

Indexed by MotionPipelineV2.QUADRANT_NAMES = {"front", "right", "rear", "left"}, so front=0, right=0.5, rear=0, left=0.5. The two mirror cameras are dewarped; front and rear are not, because Overdrive's test footage had no subjects in those tiles and 0 is byte-identical to today.

BEFORE relying on this indexing, read BladeWatch-cxjn child 1. FoveatedCropper.java contains a comment that misstates the quadrant order; the array above is correct.

## What to do, test-first

1. Write app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/surveillance/FisheyeDewarpTest.java FIRST, covering at minimum:
   - strengthFor() returns 0 for quadrants 0 and 2, 0.5 for 1 and 3, and 0 for out-of-range indices including negatives.
   - Strength 0 is EXACT identity: a generated RGB buffer dewarped at a strength-0 quadrant comes back null (see the null contract below) - assert the caller therefore uses the original bytes.
   - The LUT is a pure function of (strength, w, h): building it twice gives equal arrays.
   - Every LUT entry is in range [0, w*h).
   - The centre pixel maps to itself (r2=0 at the exact centre of an odd-sized tile, or within one pixel for even sizes).
   - The transform is symmetric about both axes: the source offset for (x,y) mirrors that for (w-1-x, y).
   - A malformed input (null buffer, or rgb.length < w*h*3) returns null rather than throwing.
2. Then write app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/surveillance/FisheyeDewarp.java to pass them.
3. Keep the LUT cached per (strength, w, h) behind a lock, as the original does - it is rebuilt only if dimensions change.
4. Keep the reusable output scratch buffer. Overdrive's own audit note records that allocating 230 KB per side-cam inference was about 0.92 MB/s of large-object GC churn at the 250 ms cadence, firing precisely while recording.

## The null contract - keep it

dewarpForDetector returns null when the quadrant is not dewarped, rather than a copy of the input. The original's doc says this makes "no change" impossible to confuse with a copy. Preserve that; the caller in child 4 depends on it.

## Constraints

- Package-private class, like the original. Nothing outside the surveillance package should see it.
- No Android imports. This must be unit-testable on the JVM with no Robolectric.
- Do NOT add a user-facing setting, a config key, or a UI slider. See the epic: the constants describe the lens, not a preference.
- Do NOT wire it into SurveillanceEngineGpu in this task.
- Retain Overdrive's MIT copyright notice in the file header.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] FisheyeDewarpTest.java exists and every test above is present and passing.
- [ ] Mutation check: temporarily change QUADRANT_STRENGTH to all zeros and confirm at least one test fails; restore afterwards. A guard that cannot fail is worse than no guard.
- [ ] FisheyeDewarp.java compiles, is package-private, and imports nothing from android.*.
- [ ] The file header records the MIT attribution to Yash Srivastava.
- [ ] Nothing outside the new class and its test is modified.
- [ ] ./gradlew test koverVerify assembleDebug passes.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
notes:
REDONE IN KOTLIN at the developer's instruction, replacing the Java version this issue was originally closed with. FisheyeDewarp.java and FisheyeDewarpTest.java were deleted; FisheyeDewarp.kt and FisheyeDewarpTest.kt replace them. Precedent for both exists - SurveillanceConfigManager.kt sits in the same main package, and there are four Kotlin test classes already.

One interop consequence worth recording: Kotlin cannot express package-private, and the caller (SurveillanceEngineGpu) is Java. So it is an object with @JvmStatic members rather than a package-private final class. That makes it module-public instead of package-private - a deliberate, documented loosening, noted in the class doc so nobody mistakes it for API.

All 11 tests kept and passing. The three mutations still behave: zeroing the strengths is caught, swapping Q2/Q3 is caught, and inverting the correction is caught by magnificationFallsOffWithRadius.

Gate: ./gradlew test koverVerify assembleDebug BUILD SUCCESSFUL.
close_reason:
Done, test-first. Wrote FisheyeDewarpTest.java before the implementation and confirmed it failed to compile, then wrote FisheyeDewarp.java to pass it.

DELIVERED: app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/surveillance/FisheyeDewarp.java - package-private, no android.* imports, MIT attribution to Yash Srivastava in the header. Division-model dewarp with a LUT cached per (strength, w, h) under a lock, a reusable output scratch buffer, and the null-not-a-copy contract preserved so the caller can tell unchanged from changed. QUADRANT_STRENGTH is {0, 0.5, 0, 0.5} indexed by MotionPipelineV2.QUADRANT_NAMES, so only the two mirror cameras are dewarped.

TESTS: 11 cases covering quadrant indexing including out-of-range and negative, the null contract, fail-open on malformed input, determinism, in-bounds sampling, vertical symmetry, an approximately fixed centre, outward sampling, LUT rebuild on a size change in both directions, and the radial profile.

MUTATION TESTING FOUND A GAP IN MY OWN SUITE, which is the main thing worth recording. Three mutations were tried. Zeroing all strengths: caught. Swapping Q2/Q3 - the exact trap BladeWatch-7elj was filed for: caught. But INVERTING the correction, replacing inv = 1/(1 + k1*r2 + k2*r4) with inv = (1 + k1*r2 + k2*r4), PASSED everything. Both models sample further from the centre than the output pixel, so samples-outward cannot distinguish them; the correction was deepening the barrel distortion rather than removing it and every test was happy. Added magnificationFallsOffWithRadius, which pins the radial PROFILE - magnification must be strongest at the centre and fall off - and that mutation is now caught. Probes are deliberately kept clear of the tile edge because clamping flattens the ratio and hides the inversion.

ALSO A BUG IN MY FIRST TEST FIXTURE, found by a genuine red: the gradient encodes source x and y in single BYTES, but the live tile is 320 wide, so source x=306 read back as 50 and the symmetry assertion compared nonsense. Coordinate-decoding tests now use 200x150, which keeps the same 0.75 aspect the transform actually depends on. Size and null-contract tests still use 320x240.

Gate: ./gradlew test koverVerify assembleDebug BUILD SUCCESSFUL. Nothing outside the new class and its test was modified.

title: Fix the misleading quadrant-order comment in FoveatedCropper
description:
## Problem

app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/surveillance/FoveatedCropper.java lines 36-60 contain a comment block where someone reasoned out the quadrant-to-mosaic mapping in the file. Its conclusion is CORRECT but it twice states the underlying array wrongly, and the next task in this epic assigns per-quadrant constants by index. An implementer who trusts the comment will dewarp the wrong cameras and the bug will be invisible - the feature will simply underperform.

## The facts

The real array, at app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/surveillance/MotionPipelineV2.java line 27:

    public static final String[] QUADRANT_NAMES = {"front", "right", "rear", "left"};

So Q0=front, Q1=right, Q2=rear, Q3=left. Overdrive's MotionPipelineV2.java line 54 has the identical array, so the two projects agree and Overdrive's constants port across unchanged.

The comment in FoveatedCropper says, twice (around lines 44 and 56):

    But QUADRANT_NAMES = ["front", "right", "left", "rear"]

That swaps Q2 and Q3 and is wrong. The block's own final line - "So: Q0=TL=Front, Q1=TR=Right, Q2=BL=Rear, Q3=BR=Left" - is right and contradicts it. The comment also contains stray working-out ("Wait -", "Actually from the fragment shader", "Let's just use...") that reads as unresolved when it is in fact resolved.

## What to do

1. Open FoveatedCropper.java and read lines 30-62 in full.
2. Rewrite that comment block so it states the mapping once, correctly, and cites MotionPipelineV2.QUADRANT_NAMES as the source of truth. Keep the strip-offset table and the fragment-shader derivation - both are useful. Remove the self-contradiction and the thinking-aloud.
3. Do NOT change any code in this file. This task is comment-only. If you find yourself editing a statement, stop - that belongs in a different issue.

## Constraints

- Comment text only. No behaviour change, no renames, no reordering.
- Do not "fix" MotionPipelineV2.QUADRANT_NAMES to match the comment. The array is correct; the comment is wrong.
- Leave the strip offsets alone. They were derived from the fragment shader and are not in question.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] FoveatedCropper.java no longer contains the string ["front", "right", "left", "rear"] in any form.
- [ ] The comment names MotionPipelineV2.QUADRANT_NAMES as the source of truth and states Q0=front, Q1=right, Q2=rear, Q3=left once.
- [ ] git diff for this task shows changes to comment lines only - no line of executable code differs.
- [ ] ./gradlew test koverVerify assembleDebug passes.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
close_reason: Comment-only fix, verified. The header block in FoveatedCropper.java stated QUADRANT_NAMES with Q2 and Q3 swapped, twice, alongside a correct conclusion that contradicted it plus stray working-out (Wait, Actually, Lets just use). Rewrote it to state the mapping once - Q0 front TL 0.75, Q1 right TR 0.50, Q2 rear BL 0.00, Q3 left BR 0.25 - naming MotionPipelineV2.QUADRANT_NAMES as the source of truth and keeping both independent derivations (fragment shader gridPos and runAiOnQuadrant startX/startY) because they corroborate the table. Verified against the CODE rather than any comment: the QUADRANT_STRIP_OFFSET_X array at line 148 and its own inline comment were already correct, so only the header was wrong. Added a cautionary note for the next task in the epic explaining why a per-quadrant constant keyed off the wrong order is the expensive kind of error - it applies to the wrong camera, compiles cleanly, and shows up only as the feature underperforming. Deliberately DESCRIBED the old wrong ordering rather than quoting the literal array, so the incorrect string appears nowhere in the file and cannot be found by grep - the acceptance criterion said in any form. Confirmed comment-only: git diff shows 20 insertions and 19 deletions, every one a comment line, no executable line differs. Gate: ./gradlew test koverVerify assembleDebug BUILD SUCCESSFUL.

title: Remote Tor traffic starves the in-car UI: both share one 32-thread HTTP pool
description:
## Symptom

Owner, 2026-09-15: the IN-CAR Flutter UI becomes unresponsive while the Tor tunnel is on,
and is responsive again the moment the tunnel is switched off. Repeatable.

## What the measurements say

This is NOT a Flutter bug and not a CPU shortage.

    dumpsys gfxinfo net.bladewatch.flutter
      Total frames rendered: 257   ... and 257 again 10 s later  -> NOTHING is repainting
      Janky frames: 114 (44.36%)
      50th 18 ms | 90th 101 ms | 95th 150 ms | 99th 600 ms

Zero frames drawn over ten seconds rules out an animation or render loop. The jank profile
is the signature of a UI thread that is BLOCKED WAITING, not one that is busy. Meanwhile the
head unit had 497% of 800% idle, so the machine was not saturated either.

With the tunnel up and a remote browser watching live video, the camera/encode stack carried
the extra load: mm-qcamera-daemon ~41%, byd_cam_daemon ~40%, media.codec ~25%.

## Mechanism

The in-car UI and every remote browser share ONE HTTP server and ONE thread pool.

- flutter_ui/lib/rpc/connect_client.dart:43 - the in-car UI speaks ConnectRPC to
  http://127.0.0.1:8080, the same server the onion service fronts.
- HttpServer.java:58 - Executors.newFixedThreadPool(32), fixed.
- Every response sends Connection: close (see BladeWatch-67h8), so each request occupies a
  thread for a whole connection lifecycle rather than reusing one.
- Over Tor a single request costs 1.4-2.2 s of round trip, measured, and up to 9.9 s cold.
- The /ws H.264 stream holds one of those 32 threads for the ENTIRE viewing session.

So a remote SPA load - dozens of assets, each on its own connection, each seconds long -
plus a live stream can occupy a large share of the pool for sustained periods. The in-car
UI's RPC calls then queue behind traffic arriving through a six-hop anonymity network. The
Dart side awaits those calls, frames go late, and the panel feels dead.

Corroborating detail: netstat on the head unit showed one ESTABLISHED connection to 8080
and a PILE of TIME_WAIT sockets - exactly the churn Connection: close produces.

## Why this matters more than it looks

The in-car UI is the safety-relevant surface. A remote viewer on a slow link should never be
able to degrade the driver's own screen. Today the coupling is direct and unbounded.

## Options, roughly in order of value

1. Do not let remote traffic starve local traffic. Either a separate small pool reserved for
   loopback/in-car callers, or a bounded queue per client class. The in-car UI is loopback
   and trivially identifiable - AuthMiddleware already distinguishes it.
2. Keep-alive (BladeWatch-67h8) - fewer connections means fewer thread-seconds per page.
3. Do not let /ws consume a general pool thread for its whole lifetime; hand streaming off
   to its own executor so a viewer cannot occupy general capacity indefinitely.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With a remote client loading the SPA over the onion AND a live stream running, the
      in-car UI's RPC latency stays within a stated bound. Measure before and after and
      record both numbers here.
- [ ] gfxinfo for the Flutter app shows the janky-frame percentage materially reduced under
      that same load.
- [ ] A remote client cannot exhaust the pool: verify with several concurrent slow clients.
- [ ] Live video over the onion still works.
- [ ] ./gradlew test koverVerify assembleDebug passes.

Do not make mistakes. Measure the BEFORE numbers on the head unit with the tunnel up and a
real remote client attached, not on loopback - loopback hides the latency that causes this
entirely. Read HttpServer's request loop and the /ws upgrade path fully before changing the
threading. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
close_reason:
FIXED the unbounded half, and CORRECTING a wrong claim I made when filing this.

WHAT SHIPPED

H.264 WebSocket streaming now runs on its own executor (streamPool, cached, daemon threads
named http-stream) instead of the 32-thread request pool. That was the unbounded case:
streamH264ToWebSocket sets setSoTimeout(0) and blocks for the whole viewing session, so on
the request pool each viewer PERMANENTLY removed a worker that the in-car UI's RPCs also
queue on. Ordinary requests are bounded by their 15 s socket timeout; a stream was bounded
by nothing.

A trap this nearly shipped with: handleClient ends in finally { client.close(); }. Handing
the socket to the stream pool and returning would have closed it immediately, killing every
live view the instant it started - while the pool-isolation tests still passed. Ownership is
now tracked explicitly (socketHandedOff), handleWebSocketUpgrade returns whether ownership
actually transferred, and a FAILED handshake deliberately returns false so that socket is
still closed rather than leaked. Both properties are pinned by tests.

VERIFIED ON THE HEAD UNIT after deploying:
  /ws upgrade still returns HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
  http-stream threads: 0 idle -> 1 while a stream is held open
So the handshake is intact, the socket survives the hand-off, and the stream is demonstrably
off the request pool.

CORRECTION - option 1 as I wrote it is NOT POSSIBLE

I said "the in-car UI is loopback and trivially identifiable - AuthMiddleware already
distinguishes it". That is wrong, and it is wrong for the same reason the security fix
earlier in this epic was needed: TOR CONNECTS TO 127.0.0.1:8080 TOO. Onion traffic is
indistinguishable from in-car traffic at the socket level - that is precisely why
AuthMiddleware had to stop trusting loopback and start checking whether a tunnel process is
running. It does not identify a connection's origin and cannot.

So reserving capacity "for loopback callers" would reserve it for remote clients as well.
Any real implementation needs a different discriminator - a header carrying the IPC token
(which never leaves the device, so a remote client cannot obtain it), or resolving the peer
port through /proc/net/tcp to the owning process. Both are more invasive than they sounded.

CORRECTION - keep-alive may not help this, and could hurt

BladeWatch-67h8 is still worth doing for LATENCY: ~1.4 s of Tor round trip per request is
paid because every response says Connection: close. But for POOL OCCUPANCY it is not
obviously a win and may be a loss: with a thread-per-connection model, keep-alive means
fewer connections each holding a worker for LONGER, across multiple requests. Do not land it
expecting it to fix starvation; measure occupancy before and after.

WHAT REMAINS

With streams moved off, the worst case on the request pool is now bounded: concurrent slow
Tor requests, each capped at the 15 s socket timeout. That is far better than unbounded, but
32 workers shared between the driver's screen and the public internet is still a coupling
worth removing. Reopen or file a follow-up if the in-car UI is still degraded under a real
remote load - and measure it with gfxinfo rather than by feel.

title: Settings: Tor Tunnel row shows Waiting/off while tor is running
description:
## Problem

On Settings > Services, the Tor Tunnel row reports "Waiting" with the switch OFF while tor
is actually RUNNING. Observed on the head unit 2026-09-15: the row said "Waiting", the
header said "3 of 4 running", and at that same moment tor was alive as pid 21015 and had
reached "Bootstrapped 50%". The Dashboard chip on the same device read "4/4 Running".

## Cause

Two things compound:

1. The switch binds to LIVENESS, not to the stored setting:
   flutter_ui/lib/screens/settings/settings_daemons_screen.dart, the Switch has
   value: row.running, where row.running comes from daemon.processStatus.
2. The screen loads ONCE and never refreshes. SettingsDaemonsScreen.initState calls
   controller.load() and there is no timer, no stream and no refresh on resume.
   SettingsDaemonsController.toggle() calls load() immediately after the IPC returns.

Enabling the tunnel only RECORDS INTENT - TcpCommandServer's daemon_set_enabled writes the
flag and does not launch anything. DaemonStartupManager's health check does the launch on
its next cycle, and tor then needs up to another minute to bootstrap (61 s measured on this
device). So load(), running a fraction of a second after the toggle, always observes
running=false and the switch springs back to off. It then stays wrong until the user leaves
the screen and returns.

## Why it matters more now than it did with the previous tunnel

The switch reads as "the toggle did not work". A user's natural response is to toggle it
again, which disables the tunnel - daemon_set_enabled with enabled=false also KILLS the
running process - so trying twice actively turns off the thing they just turned on.

## Suggested fix

Bind the switch to the RECORDED INTENT and show liveness in the status line instead, where
"Waiting" / "Running" already lives and where a lag is honest rather than misleading. That
needs the enabled flag exposed over IPC; daemonStatus currently returns liveness only, so
either extend it or add a daemon_get_enabled. Then refresh the rows while the screen is
visible so "Waiting" becomes "Running" on its own.

Optimistically flipping the switch and leaving it is NOT enough on its own - if the launch
fails the switch would lie in the other direction.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Enabling the tunnel leaves the switch ON immediately and it stays on.
- [ ] The status line moves Waiting -> Running by itself once tor starts, with no
      navigation away and back.
- [ ] Disabling still both records the intent and stops the process.
- [ ] A launch that fails is visibly distinguishable from one still in progress.
- [ ] Widget tests cover: toggle-on keeps the switch on while running=false; the status
      line updates on refresh; toggle-off turns it off.
- [ ] cd flutter_ui && flutter analyze && flutter test passes, and
      cd flutter_ui/android && ./gradlew koverVerify passes.

Do not make mistakes. Read settings_daemons_controller.dart, settings_daemons_screen.dart
and TcpCommandServer's daemon_set_enabled handler fully before editing. Do not make the
switch merely optimistic. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
close_reason:
Fixed. The daemonStatus IPC command now reports the user's ENABLED INTENT alongside process liveness, and the Settings switch binds to intent instead of liveness.

Root cause as filed: enabling only records intent - the health check launches on its next cycle and tor then needs up to a minute to bootstrap - so load(), running a fraction of a second after the toggle, always saw running=false and the switch sprang back to off. The second tap a user would naturally make then DISABLED the tunnel, because the disable path also kills the process.

Changes: TcpCommandServer reports an 'enabled' map (toggleable daemons only; an unreadable config fails to 'not enabled' without taking the command down). DaemonChannel.daemonStatus() returns running and enabled, falling back to liveness if an older daemon omits the field so a mismatched pair degrades to the OLD behaviour rather than something worse. DaemonRowState gains enabled and pending. The screen binds toggleable switches to enabled, shows 'Starting Tor tunnel...' in the warning colour for the pending window, and finally REFRESHES - it previously called load() once from initState and never again, which is why a tunnel that came up 30 s later stayed 'Waiting' until you navigated away and back.

Covered by four new widget tests and five new JVM tests; the switch binding was mutation-checked RED against the old code.

title: Daemon controllers kill their own ADB shell: pkill -f / pgrep -f self-match
description:
## Problem

Several daemon control paths kill or probe processes with "pkill -9 -f" / "pgrep -f".
On this head unit that is broken, and it fails SILENTLY.

toybox matches the -f pattern as a literal SUBSTRING of every /proc/<pid>/cmdline. Every
one of these commands is delivered as "adb shell <script>", so the ADB shell's own cmdline
IS the script, pattern included. The command therefore matches itself.

Measured on the head unit 2026-09-15, with a marker string matching NO process at all:

    $ adb shell "echo start; pkill -9 -f 'bwprobe_marker_xyz'; echo SHOULD PRINT"
    start
    (exit 137 - SIGKILL; the second echo never ran)

    $ adb shell "pgrep -f 'bladewatch_tor'"       # no tor process existed
    5187                                          # the probing shell's own pid

So a "pkill -9 -f" kills the shell and every statement after it never runs, and a
"pgrep -f" answers "running" unconditionally.

The bracket trick does NOT rescue pkill/pgrep. It works for grep because grep takes a
REGEX, so start_[c]am_daemon does not match the literal text start_[c]am_daemon sitting in
the shell's cmdline. pkill -f takes no regex, so it finds the bracketed literal too.

## What is already fixed (do not redo)

BladeWatch-3lbz.6 fixed TorLauncher.stopCommand, TorLauncher.isRunningCommand and
DaemonHardReset.hardResetCommand, and removed two dead helpers from AdbShellExecutor. Those
are covered by tests in TorLauncherCommandTest and DaemonHardResetCommandTest.

## What is still broken (this issue)

All pre-existing, none of it touched by the Tor migration:

- app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/ui/daemon/CameraDaemonController.kt
  lines ~75, ~79, ~129, ~133
- app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/ui/daemon/AccSentryDaemonController.kt
  lines ~41, ~76 ("pkill -9 -f 'acc_sentry'")
- app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/ui/daemon/SentryDaemonController.kt
  lines ~26, ~27 (pkill) and ~32 ("pgrep -f 'SentryDaemon|AccSentryDaemon' | head -1")
- app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/launcher/DaemonLauncher.kt line ~1395
- app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/ui/model/PresetCommand.kt lines ~36, ~39, ~44
  and its Flutter twin flutter_ui/lib/screens/diagnostics/adb_console_models.dart
  lines ~21, ~24, ~29 (these two are user-facing ADB console presets - a user tapping
  "Kill Sentry" kills their own ADB session instead)

## How to fix

Prefer killall, which matches comm OR basename(argv[0]) - both "sh" for the ADB shell, so
it cannot match itself. SPELL NAMES IN FULL. CLAUDE.md used to say acc_sentry_daemon had to
be truncated to acc_sentry_daem because the kernel caps /proc/<pid>/comm at 15 chars; the
cap is real but the conclusion was wrong, and the truncated spelling matches NOTHING.
These daemons launch with --nice-name, so argv[0] is the full name while comm is "main".
Measured on the head unit 2026-09-15:

    pidof acc_sentry_daemon -> 4571
    pidof acc_sentry_daem   -> (nothing)
    pidof main              -> 2851 3102 4571      (comm for all three is "main")

That correction is already in CLAUDE.md.

Where a cmdline match is genuinely required - the watchdog SCRIPTS run as
"sh /data/local/tmp/start_cam_daemon.sh", so argv[0] and comm are both "sh" and killall
cannot single them out - use the ps + grep -E bracket-trick loop, which IS safe because
grep takes a regex. DaemonHardReset.hardResetCommand has a worked example, including the
trap that any OTHER clause in the same command mentioning the literal name re-arms the
self-match (that is why its rm globs start_*.sh instead of naming the scripts).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No "pkill -f" or "pgrep -f" remains in app/src/main or flutter_ui/lib.
- [ ] Each replacement is verified ON THE HEAD UNIT to (a) leave the ADB shell alive and
      (b) actually kill/find its target. Dry-run first by replacing kill/killall with echo.
- [ ] Killing a daemon from the Diagnostics ADB console no longer kills the console's own
      session.
- [ ] Commands are extracted as pure functions (as TorLauncher/DaemonHardReset now do) and
      covered by unit tests asserting no "-f" form, RED-checked by mutation.
- [ ] ./gradlew test koverVerify assembleDebug, cd flutter_ui && flutter analyze && flutter
      test, and cd flutter_ui/android && ./gradlew koverVerify all pass.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing, and read
DaemonHardReset.hardResetCommand first - it documents every trap. Verify on the real head
unit, not by reasoning: this whole class of bug is invisible in a unit test and silent at
runtime. Do NOT delete /data/local/tmp/tor/hs at any point; it is the car's permanent onion
identity. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
close_reason:
Fixed across all six sites, with a repo-wide guard so it cannot come back.

New DaemonKillCommands centralises the three safe primitives: killByName (killall, which matches comm/argv[0] - both 'sh' for the issuing shell, so it cannot self-match), killMatchingCmdline (ps + grep -E with a bracketed regex, for the watchdog scripts that all run as 'sh' and cannot be told apart by name), and isRunningByName (pidof).

Fixed: CameraDaemonController (both kill blocks), SentryDaemonController (kill and check), AccSentryDaemonController, DaemonLauncher.verifyDaemonRunning, PresetCommands.ALL and its Flutter twin adb_console_models.dart - the last two being the user-facing Diagnostics console, where tapping 'Kill Sentry' killed the user's own session.

TWO bugs were hiding in SentryDaemonController, not one. Besides self-killing, 'pkill -f SentryDaemon' matched the wrong process entirely: app_process overwrites argv[0] with --nice-name, so the Java class name only appears in the launching sh -c. Measured on the head unit:
  new: pidof sentry_daemon      -> 24945   (the daemon)
  old: pgrep -f SentryDaemon    -> 24942   (the launching sh)
                                   28862   (the probing shell itself)
It never once matched the daemon.

Also corrected a related wrong belief: pgrep WITHOUT -f consults comm only, which is 'main' for every app_process daemon here, so it reports them all dead. pidof consults comm OR basename(argv[0]). That is why pidof is used rather than pgrep.

Verified on the car non-destructively: the rebuilt camera sweep reaches 'done' with exit 0 (the old one died at its first clause), selects the watchdog script and not its own shell, and killall -0 matches byd_cam_daemon, sentry_daemon and acc_sentry_daemon while failing on a bogus name.

New NoSelfMatchingProcessCommandsTest scans app/src/main/java, flutter_ui/lib and the Flutter Kotlin tree for pkill -f / pgrep -f in executable lines (comments may still explain the trap), with the scanned dirs declared as Gradle test inputs so it cannot go UP-TO-DATE when it matters.

title: Tor tunnel does not auto-start on the boot path (no ADB fallback branch)
description:
## What happens

`DaemonStartupManager.relaunchDaemon(type)` (around line 496 of
`app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/ui/daemon/DaemonStartupManager.kt`) prefers
`daemonsViewModel.startDaemon(type)`, and falls back to an ADB-only launch when the
ViewModel is null — the boot path. That fallback is a `when (type)` with branches for
CAMERA_DAEMON, SENTRY_DAEMON and ACC_SENTRY_DAEMON only. The tunnel falls through to
`else`, which just logs "no ADB fallback for …".

So when the health check decides the tunnel should be running and no ViewModel exists,
nothing starts it.

Observed on the head unit on 2026-09-15 during BladeWatch-3lbz.7: with
`daemons.TOR_TUNNEL = true` in `/data/local/tmp/bladewatch_config.json` and the service
host freshly installed and running, the tunnel never launched. `isOptionalDaemonEnabled`
correctly returned true (the health check reads the shared config), so the decision was
right and only the execution was missing. Confirmed by launching tor by hand with
`TorLauncher`'s exact commands, after which everything downstream worked.

## This is PRE-EXISTING, not a regression from the Tor migration

The `when` had no branch for the previous tunnel either — the `else` arm predates
BladeWatch-3lbz. Nobody hit it because the tunnel was disabled on this device
(`{"ZROK_TUNNEL": false}` in the shared config), so the boot path was never exercised.
The Tor work renamed the enum; it did not remove a branch.

## Why it matters more now

The Tor tunnel is the ONLY remote access path, and its whole appeal is that the address is
permanent so a saved QR code keeps working. If the tunnel does not come back on its own
after a reboot, the user has to open the in-car UI to restore remote access — which
defeats the point for a parked car they are not standing next to.

## What to do

1. Add a `DaemonType.TOR_TUNNEL ->` branch to that `when`, launching through `TorLauncher`
   the same way `startTorOnBoot()` already does (same file, ~line 302). That method is the
   model; do not duplicate its body, factor it.
2. Work out whether `daemonsViewModel` is genuinely null on the boot path or was merely
   null in this test because `MainActivity` backgrounds itself immediately
   (`moveTaskToBack(true)`). If it is normally non-null, this branch is defence in depth
   rather than the actual fix, and the real cause is elsewhere — say which in the notes.
3. TDD: the existing suite has no coverage of `relaunchDaemon`'s fallback at all. Add a
   test that the tunnel type reaches a launch rather than the `else` arm, and watch it fail
   first.
4. Verify on the head unit: enable the tunnel, reboot, and confirm it comes back with the
   SAME onion address and without opening the UI. Note that BladeWatch-3lbz.7 could not
   verify reboot persistence for this reason.

## Constraints

- Do not weaken the health check's "only restart optional daemons the user enabled" rule.
- Do not log the onion address.
- Logging flags are off in release-shaped builds, which is why this failed silently — if
  you add a log line here, make sure the failure is still detectable without it.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced file fully before editing. Verify the build
compiles and the acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop
and ask rather than guessing.
close_reason:
Fixed, and the root cause was larger than this issue described.

1. The missing branch, as filed. relaunchDaemon now has a DaemonType.TOR_TUNNEL arm
   calling startTorOnBoot(), which drives TorLauncher directly and needs no ViewModel.
   The when is now exhaustive over all four DaemonType values.

2. The bigger half, found while reviewing the staged diff: TorLauncher.isTunnelRunning
   used "pgrep -f bladewatch_tor", and toybox pgrep -f matches the pattern as a substring
   of every process cmdline -- including the ADB shell running the probe, whose cmdline IS
   the probe. So the probe answered "running" unconditionally.

   Measured on the head unit 2026-09-15 with NO tor process anywhere:
     pgrep -f bladewatch_tor -> 5187   (the probing shell's own pid)
     pgrep    bladewatch_tor -> (nothing, correct)

   That made startTunnelFromPreferences take the "Tor already running, skipping start"
   branch every time, so the tunnel never started on the WITH-ViewModel path either --
   which is the normal path, not the boot fallback. restartTunnelIfEnabled was wedged the
   same way, and TorController.refreshTunnelUrl would republish a remembered onion URL
   while tor was dead, which its own doc comment promised could not happen.

   Fixed by dropping -f (TorLauncher.isRunningCommand). Verified end to end on the car
   against the real tor binary: pgrep says yes while tor runs, no once it is killed.

Covered by TorLauncherCommandTest "liveness probe matches by process name, never by full
command line", proven RED against the previous code by mutation.

title: Synthesise the Electro evaluations into a ranked shortlist
description:
## Your scope: synthesis and shortlist

You run LAST, after the catalogue and all six domain evaluations are closed. Turn six
documents into one decision the developer can act on. Do not re-do the evaluations; if
one is thin, contradicts another, or leans on a Low-confidence row, say so and name it.

## What to do

1. Read all six evaluation documents in `docs/evaluations/` plus the catalogue.
2. Write `docs/evaluations/electro-integration-shortlist.md` containing:
   - A single ranked table of every feature recommended Build or Adapt, sorted by value
     per unit of effort. Columns: feature, domain, confidence, effort, what it gives
     the user in one clause, main risk.
   - A "Blocked" section grouping everything ruled out, by reason (needs a backend
     BladeWatch does not have, BYD Cloud gone, not on DiLink v3, unsafe, already
     implemented, paid infrastructure). One line each. This section is as valuable as
     the recommendations: it stops the same features being re-proposed in six months.
   - A "Top 5" with a paragraph each: why it is worth doing, what it depends on, and
     the first concrete step.
   - An "Open questions for the developer" section listing every genuine fork in the
     road the evaluations could not settle without crossing the research limits.
3. CROSS-REFERENCE THE OVERDRIVE EPIC. Both epics evaluate automations, remote audio
   and deterrent overlays. Where a feature appears in both, say which source is the
   better starting point and why - Overdrive's code is MIT-licensed and readable, while
   Electro's is closed, so for anything both products have, Overdrive is almost always
   the better base and Electro's value is in showing what the UI should feel like. If
   the Overdrive shortlist already exists, reconcile against it explicitly rather than
   producing a second, competing ranking.
4. Flag any row whose confidence is Low but whose effort is L. Building a week of work
   on a guess about a competitor's UI string is the specific failure this epic must not
   produce.

## Constraints

- Still EVALUATION. Do not write feature code.
- Do NOT file implementation issues yet. The developer picks from the shortlist first;
  implementation issues get written against their decision afterwards, with the full
  task template CLAUDE.md requires. State that at the end of the document.
- Do not pad the ranking. If only three things are worth building, the table has three
  rows and says so.
- Do not copy Electro's copy, assets or branding into the document.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `docs/evaluations/electro-integration-shortlist.md` exists with the ranked table,
      the Blocked section grouped by reason, a Top 5 with reasoning, and open questions.
- [ ] Every domain document is represented; none silently dropped.
- [ ] Overlaps with the Overdrive epic are reconciled, with a stated preference for the
      better starting point in each case.
- [ ] Every Low-confidence, high-effort row is flagged as such.
- [ ] The document ends by stating that implementation issues come after the
      developer's decision.
- [ ] No other file is created or modified; nothing staged or committed.

## Shared context - read this before anything else

Electro (https://electro.app.br/en/) is a commercial BYD companion product. It is NOT
open source and it is NOT a fork relative of BladeWatch - unlike Overdrive, there is no
code to read. You are evaluating a competitor's feature set from its public surface and
deciding what is worth building independently.

### What Electro is, established on 2026-09-14

- A React PWA (Vite, Mantine UI, Leaflet maps, i18next, Recharts) served from
  electro.app.br, installable to the home screen, plus a SEPARATE car-side APK that the
  phone pairs to by scanning a QR code shown in the car.
- Backed by a server: `/api/*` answers 401 without credentials. Sign-in is via Google.
- A paid product: there are `/subscription` routes, subscription expiry dates, promo
  codes, CPF-on-invoice (Brazilian tax ID) and a WhatsApp flow to book a remote
  installation with a technician. It also has a `/closed-beta` route.
- Localised into at least English, Portuguese (BR), Spanish, Italian, French, German,
  Polish, Turkish and Korean. Portuguese is clearly the primary language.

Routes visible in the JavaScript bundle, which are the app's feature map:

    /app/status   /dashboard   /trips   /charging-history   /live-cam   /sentry
    /dashcam      /seats       /logs    /mobile-data-usage  /automations
    /integrations /settings    /notifications  /car-apk  /subscription
    /changelog    /remote-log  /login   /closed-beta        /usb

### How to research it, and the hard limits on that

ALLOWED, and sufficient:

- The public marketing and documentation pages under https://electro.app.br/en/.
- The published JavaScript bundle, which embeds the full translated UI copy. This is
  the richest source by far - the translation strings enumerate nearly every feature,
  setting and error state in the product. Fetch
  `https://electro.app.br/assets/index-<hash>.js` (the hash changes; read it from the
  page's script tag) and extract quoted strings. The catalogue task does this once and
  publishes the result, so the other tasks do not each re-download 3.8 MB.
- The `/changelog` page, and any public demo videos, screenshots or user forum posts.

NOT ALLOWED, and not necessary for this evaluation:

- Do NOT create an account, sign in, subscribe, pay for anything, or use a closed-beta
  invite.
- Do NOT call, probe, fuzz or scrape their `/api/*` backend. It is authenticated; do
  not attempt to get past that.
- Do NOT download, install, decompile or unpack their car APK.
- Do NOT copy their code, assets, icons, screenshots, branding, or their translated
  UI copy into BladeWatch. We are taking FEATURE IDEAS, which is fair; taking their
  text and artwork is infringement, and BladeWatch is a public open-source repository
  where it would be obvious.
- Do not reproduce long verbatim quotations of their copy in the evaluation document
  either. Summarise in your own words. Short phrases as evidence are fine.

If you find yourself wanting to do any of the above to answer a question, the correct
outcome is to record the question as unanswered in the document's open-questions
section.

## The filters that decide whether a feature can even be copied

Apply these FIRST. Most of this epic's value is an honest "not portable" with a reason.

1. THEY HAVE A BACKEND. BladeWatch DOES NOT. Electro has a server, accounts, Google
   sign-in and a subscription. BladeWatch is local-first: a daemon on the head unit, a
   Flutter UI in the car, an Angular web UI for remote browsers, and a tunnel (zrok
   today, Tor soon) that exposes the car's own authenticated web server. There is no
   BladeWatch server and none is planned. For EVERY feature ask: can this work with
   only the head unit and the tunnel? Anything that needs a always-available cloud
   relay - push while the car is offline, cross-device account state, a shared hazard
   or location database - is blocked unless you can describe a purely local equivalent.
   Say which, concretely.
2. BYD CLOUD IS GONE FROM BLADEWATCH. The whole `byd/cloud/` package was deleted in
   commit 61b4d7f. `VehicleCommandRouter.Path` is now `{SDK, NONE}`, and Lock, Unlock,
   Flash, FindCar, SetBatteryHeat and the charging schedule resolve to NOT_SUPPORTED.
   Electro appears to do things while the car is off, which usually means a cloud path.
   Anything that needs it is blocked; do not propose restoring the cloud client.
3. HARDWARE. BladeWatch targets DiLink v3 ONLY: arm64-v8a, Android 10 / API 29, NOT
   rooted (no su, ro.secure=1, ro.build.type=user). Electro supports a range of BYD
   models and head units. A control that exists on their supported car may have no
   local SDK method on a DiLink v3 unit - check `docs/byd-integrations.md` and the
   reflection-based manager pattern before assuming.
4. UI IS A REIMPLEMENTATION, NEVER A COPY. Electro's UI is React/Mantine. BladeWatch's
   in-car UI is Flutter and its remote UI is Angular. Layout and interaction IDEAS
   transfer; nothing else does. Size accordingly, and say whether a feature needs the
   in-car UI, the remote web UI, or both.
5. PHYSICAL SAFETY. BYD vehicle control APIs actuate real hardware. CLAUDE.md requires
   conservative treatment. Anything that moves a window, seat, sunroof or brake needs a
   safety paragraph.
6. LEGAL AND ETHICAL. Feature ideas are not protected; their code, copy, assets and
   trade marks are. Never imply BladeWatch is affiliated with Electro.

## What BladeWatch already has

Read `docs/features.md` before writing a single line - its sections are Recording,

description:
## Your scope: ADAS and vehicle modes

Electro exposes controls that change how the car DRIVES. This is the highest-risk
domain in the epic and the evaluation must be correspondingly conservative.

Confirmed from the strings on 2026-09-14, to verify and extend from the catalogue:

- Control AEB (automatic emergency braking) - explicitly named in several locales.
- Control emergency lane keeping / lane-departure assistance.
- Control the smart speed limit function.
- Active suspension mode, and switching it.
- Current drive mode reporting, and current gear selector position.
- ADAS warning surfacing, including a note in their own UI that on ADAS-equipped cars a
  system rectangle is drawn on the instrument cluster while the app is open and cannot
  be removed.

  system. Any feature that can disable it, from a phone, possibly while the car is
  moving, can contribute to a collision. For each control state plainly: what is the
  worst realistic outcome of it firing at the wrong moment, and what interlock would be
  mandatory (parked only, ACC off, speed zero, an explicit confirmation, a
  re-enable-on-restart guarantee). If you cannot describe an interlock you would trust
  with your own car, the recommendation is Skip and that is a perfectly good result.

  through the reflection pattern described in CLAUDE.md. A control that exists on
  Electro's supported models may simply not exist here.

  low-risk and possibly already present in BladeWatch's telemetry. Changing them is

title: Synthesise the Overdrive evaluations into a ranked shortlist
description:
## Your scope: synthesis and shortlist

You run LAST, after the catalogue and all eight domain evaluations are closed. Your job
is to turn eight separate documents into one decision the developer can actually make.
Do not re-do the evaluations; if one is thin or contradicts another, say so and name
the issue rather than quietly patching over it.

## What to do

1. Read all eight evaluation documents in `docs/evaluations/` plus the catalogue.
2. Write `docs/evaluations/overdrive-integration-shortlist.md` containing:
   - A single ranked table of every feature recommended Port or Adapt across all
     domains, sorted by value per unit of effort. Columns: feature, domain, effort,
     what it gives the user in one clause, main risk.
   - A "Blocked" section grouping everything ruled out, by reason (BYD Cloud gone,
     DiLink 4/5 only, needs a removed daemon, needs privilege BladeWatch lacks, unsafe,
     already implemented). One line each. This section is as valuable as the
     recommendations - it stops the same features being re-proposed in six months.
   - A "Top 5" with a paragraph each: why it is worth doing, what it depends on, and
     the first concrete step.
   - An "Open questions for the developer" section listing every genuine fork in the
     road the evaluations could not settle.
3. Where two domains overlap (toast/dialog appears in both automations and remote
   communication; AI-generated automations appear in both automations and
   ai-assistant), reconcile them into one row and note the overlap.
4. Flag any evaluation you believe is wrong or under-researched, with the specific
   claim you doubt. You are the last reader before a decision gets made on this
   material; a polite synthesis of a bad input is worse than saying it is bad.

## Constraints

- Still EVALUATION. Do not write feature code.
- Do NOT file implementation issues yet. The developer picks from the shortlist first;
  once they have, implementation issues get written against their decision, with the
  full task template CLAUDE.md requires. State that at the end of the document so the
  next agent does not jump the gun.
- Do not pad the ranking to make it look thorough. If only four things are worth
  doing, the table has four rows and says so. A short honest shortlist is the goal.
- Record the MIT attribution obligation for everything in the Port/Adapt table.

      table, the Blocked section grouped by reason, a Top 5 with reasoning, and open
      questions.

- [ ] Cross-domain overlaps are reconciled into single rows.

      developer's decision.

  this domain.

- Seat occupancy automation triggers (v36.4).

Every feature labelled cloud-only, local-SDK or either with evidence; DiLink v3 availability checked against BladeWatch source per feature rather than assumed; every actuating feature has a safety paragraph with an interlock proposal or a Skip; the ADAS diagnostics idea is assessed and recommended as the cheapest first step. Two findings dominate. First, Overdrive's own AdasBlindSpotProbe says the eight blind-spot ALERT registers have never been confirmed on a car and that the shipped code reads six fabricated ids - so the ADAS trigger features are an unfinished investigation, not a feature to port; the read-only probe and its adasFieldInventory dump are the thing worth taking, and BladeWatch cannot get the same data today because its ADAS reads log at DEBUG and R8 strips them in release. Second, and outside the task's list: BladeWatch has NO motion interlock anywhere - a repo-wide search finds no gear or speed check in VehicleCommandRouter, VehicleControlApiHandler or VehicleServiceImpl - while it already actuates windows, seats, climate and the tailgate motor. Charging schedule and remote wake-up are cloud-only and Skipped.
