title: LAN TLS: clients that ignore the pin are served (web MITM) and CN=BladeWatch reveals the car on the LAN
description:
## Problem

Two LAN-surface observations from BladeWatch-rdtj.16, both only while the owner's LAN access opt-in (network.lanHttpEnabled) is on:

1. The 0.0.0.0:8443 TLS listener serves ANY client; only the companion pins the certificate. A browser user who clicks through the self-signed warning can be man-in-the-middled on the LAN, and will send the device token/JWT to the interceptor. (Moot once web/ is retired, rdtj.13; until then, document it.)
2. Anyone on the LAN can learn a BladeWatch car is present without any credential: port 8443 answers, and the certificate subject is CN=BladeWatch (`LanTls.COMMON_NAME`, app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/LanTls.kt). The UDP responder stays silent to unsigned probes, so the certificate is the leak. A neutral CN would change the pinned fingerprint and unpair every companion -- only worth doing together with a planned re-pair, or for new installs.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] docs/networking-and-tunnels.md states both, with what the owner accepts by enabling LAN access.
- [ ] Decision on the CN recorded (keep, or neutral CN for new identities only -- never rotate an existing identity silently).

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
notes: OWNER DECISION 2026-09-24: neutral CN for newly created LAN TLS identities; never rotate an existing one. Document both observations.
close_reason: Done per owner decision. New LAN TLS identities get CN=localhost (LanTls.COMMON_NAME, doc comment explains why); existing identities are loaded unchanged and never re-minted (LanTlsTest: survives restart unchanged, expired still reused), so no companion is unpaired; LanTlsTest pins the new subject exactly (14/14). Nothing in the app, companion or RPC package reads the CN -- only the pinned fingerprint. docs/networking-and-tunnels.md now states both LAN exposures (non-pinning clients are served, until web/ retires; presence visible via the open port, the old CN on existing certs and the web login page), and that udp/18443 stays silent to unsigned probes. Reviewed: single-constant change, only used in LanTls.create.

title: Global login lockout lets anyone who can reach /auth/* keep every companion locked out
description:
## Problem

`AuthApiHandler` (app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/AuthApiHandler.kt) has a GLOBAL lockout: 30 failed logins within 2 minutes lock /auth/token, /auth/pair and /auth/companion for EVERYONE for 5 minutes (GLOBAL_FAIL_THRESHOLD / GLOBAL_LOCKOUT_MS). Anyone who can reach those endpoints -- a device on the LAN while LAN access is on, anyone who knows the Pear topic, a tor visitor -- can keep every companion and browser locked out of login indefinitely by sending 30 bad attempts every ~7 minutes. Remote transports also share one per-IP bucket (all arrive from 127.0.0.1). Every credential behind these endpoints is at least 128 bits (pairing code 128-bit random, companion token HMAC-SHA256, device token), so the global lockout buys little against guessing while enabling this denial of service. Found by BladeWatch-rdtj.16, which fixed the separate bug that the per-caller bucket was keyed on IP:port (a fresh bucket per connection).

## Options

(a) Drop or relax the global lockout for the 128-bit endpoints (/auth/pair, /auth/companion); (b) exempt already-authenticated companions (a valid JWT) from it; (c) accept and document. Decide with the owner.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decision recorded; if changed, a test proves a burst of bad attempts cannot lock out a valid companion login.
- [ ] ./gradlew test passes.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
notes: OWNER DECISION 2026-09-24: the web app is going to be removed -- remove the endpoint if not used. /auth/token (and Connect AuthService login) is used only by web/; the in-car UI mints JWTs locally and the companion uses /auth/pair + /auth/companion. So: remove /auth/token, its Connect twin and the global lockout together with web/ (rdtj.13); keep per-IP limits on /auth/pair and /auth/companion.
close_reason: Decision 2026-09-25 (owner: implement the tasks that need no car; web retirement already decided): option (a), strong form. /auth/pair and /auth/companion have no rate limits at all -- neither the global lockout nor the per-caller bucket -- and their failures no longer count toward the global cap. Rationale: the pairing code is 128 random bits (single-use, 5 min), the companion id 128 random bits and its token HMAC-SHA256, so limits added nothing against guessing and only enabled the DoS (all remote peers share one 127.0.0.1 bucket). /auth/token keeps both limits (a custom access code can be short) until it is removed with the web app (rdtj.13) -- so the dependency on rdtj.13 was dropped: the companion side no longer waits on it. AuthApiHandler.resetRateLimitsForTest added. Tests: CompanionLoginLockoutTest -- 40 bad companion logins + 40 bad codes, then the real companion logs in and a fresh code pairs; a global lockout tripped through /auth/token does not block a companion login. Mutation (rate limit back on the companion endpoints) fails the test. Service host 951/951 debug + release, koverVerify, assembleDebug. Docs: ipc-auth-and-secrets.md.

title: Remove the web-only credential exposures with tor/web retirement: deviceId in /auth/status to loopback-source remote callers, raw device secret to Dart
description:
## Problem

Two pre-auth / credential exposures that exist only for the web app (web/) and tor, and must go when they do (rdtj.12 removes tor, rdtj.13 retires web/):

1. `/auth/status` (and Connect AuthService.GetAuthStatus) returns the deviceId when the caller's address string contains 127.0.0.1 (`AuthApiHandler.handleStatus`, app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/AuthApiHandler.kt). tor (8081) and the Pear pump (8444) both arrive from 127.0.0.1, so an unauthenticated remote caller learns the deviceId. The web login needs it (web/src/app/pages/login/login.component.ts builds the token as deviceId + '-' + code), which is why it works over tor at all and NOT over LAN TLS. Over Pear it reveals nothing new (the topic is only in the pairing QR, which also carries the deviceId).
2. The in-car UI's `auth.getAccessCode` returns the raw device secret to Dart for display (it is the web login access code). Any Dart-side leak of that value is a full-access credential.

## Steps

When rdtj.12 and rdtj.13 land: drop the deviceId from /auth/status (and the proto field if nothing else reads it), and remove getAccessCode from the Flutter APK's Kotlin and Dart layers.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] /auth/status returns no deviceId on any listener.
- [ ] No method returns the device secret to Dart (grep flutter_ui/lib and the Flutter APK's Kotlin for getAccessCode: nothing).
- [ ] Tests updated; ./gradlew test, flutter test pass.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.

title: KeepAliveAccessibilityService is enabled but never bound on DiLink 3.0
description:
## Problem

`KeepAliveAccessibilityService` (`app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/services/KeepAliveAccessibilityService.kt`) claims OEM killers never kill a process hosting an active accessibility service, and its `onServiceConnected` calls `DaemonStartupManager.startOnBoot`. On the head unit it is never bound:

- 2026-09-24 before the App Start Management grant: in `enabled_accessibility_services`, but `dumpsys accessibility` lists it under "Binding services" (never "Bound"); `dumpsys activity services net.bladewatch.app` shows four system->KeepAliveAccessibilityService ConnectionRecords marked DEAD and no ServiceRecord. Removing and re-adding only our entry (20 s apart) did not clear "Binding".
- After the grant and a reboot: listed under "Enabled services" only -- neither binding nor bound, and it never logged "AccessibilityService connected".

So the protection it documents does not exist here, and nothing relies on it for boot (BootReceiver does, BladeWatch-8net).

## Steps

1. Check the manifest declaration: `android:permission="android.permission.BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE"`, the `android.accessibilityservice` intent filter and `meta-data` pointing at a valid XML config.
2. `dumpsys accessibility` "installed services" -- is it installed at all? Look for parse errors in logcat at boot (`AccessibilityManagerService`).
3. Either make it bind and verify it survives, or delete it together with `ServiceLauncher`'s code that enables it, and correct docs/daemons-and-processes.md.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Root cause recorded (why it never binds).
- [ ] Either bound and verified on the head unit, or removed with its enabling code and docs updated.
- [ ] `./gradlew test` and `./gradlew koverVerify` pass.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
close_reason: Kept, because it does bind: measured on the head unit 2026-09-24. Manifest declaration is correct (BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE, the android.accessibilityservice action, meta-data to res/xml/accessibility_service_config.xml); dumpsys accessibility lists it as installed (installedServiceCount=2) and under "Bound services" (label BladeWatch Service); dumpsys activity services shows its ServiceRecord with hasBound=true, received=true, client system/1000. Root cause of "never bound": the accessibility manager's own bind at boot does not stick on this firmware (DEAD connection records before the Auto-Start grant, enabled-only after it), and it does not retry by itself -- it rebinds when the accessibility settings are written. ServiceLauncher.enableAccessibilityKeepAlive does exactly that whenever the service host starts ("Already enabled" for the list, then settings put secure accessibility_enabled 1). Evidence: am force-stop net.bladewatch.app at 22:38:29 (ActivityManager: Force stopping ... KeepAliveAccessibilityService); SentryDaemon revived the host 2 s later; AdbShellExecutor ran the accessibility settings commands at 22:38:34.554; KeepAliveA11y "AccessibilityService connected — process is now protected" at 22:38:34.893; bound again in dumpsys; service host at oom adj 50 while bound. So it protects a running service host but never starts one -- the boot broadcast does (8net). Boot-time binding after a reboot was not re-measured (no reboot of the owner's car). Docs corrected: daemons-and-processes.md service list and the "After a reboot" paragraph; class KDoc says the same. No code change; service host tests/kover unchanged (942/942).

title: Delete the dead auto-start whitelist code (ssc_whitelist settings, bg_datacache setAppOpsData, com.byd.appstartup)
description:
## Problem

Several code paths try to lift BYD's auto-start restriction and can never succeed on DiLink 3.0 (proved 2026-09-24, BladeWatch-8net; docs/daemons-and-processes.md "After a reboot"). The flag lives in the `bg_datacache` service and needs `android.permission.ACCESS_APPOPSDATA` (protection level signature); a binder call as shell returns "Neither user 2000 nor current process has android.permission.ACCESS_APPOPSDATA", and the app UID fails the same check. They log "OK"/"SUCCESS" on paths that are actually rejected, which misleads debugging, and `BydDataCacheWhitelist.applyAll` spends up to 10 s in `ActivityThread.systemMain()` for it.

Dead paths to delete:
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/launcher/ServiceLauncher.kt` `injectAccWhitelist`: the two `settings put ... ssc_whitelist` lines (BYD never reads that setting) and `content call --uri content://com.byd.appstartup/whitelist` (no such provider; BYD's is `com.byd.appstartmanagement`, not exported).
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/util/BydDataCacheWhitelist.kt` `applyDataCache` and its calls in `applyAll`.
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/daemon/AccSentryDaemon.kt` `applyDataCacheWhitelist` and its call (~line 439).
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/daemon/SentryDaemon.kt` `whitelistUidForNetwork`'s `setAppStartupData`/`setAppOpsData` attempts.
- `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/util/AccModeHelper.kt` raw `bg_datacache`/`byd_datacached` transactions.
- The now-unused `Enc` constants for those service names.

## Constraints

- Do NOT remove the ACC whitelist (`setPkg2AccWhiteList` / accmodemanager) -- not investigated; different mechanism.
- If `createSystemPackageContext` is then only needed by the ACC whitelist, keep it; otherwise delete it.
- Behaviour must not change: every removed call was rejected.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `grep -rn "ssc_whitelist\|com.byd.appstartup\|setAppOpsData\|setAppStartupData" app/src/main` returns nothing.
- [ ] `./gradlew test` and `./gradlew koverVerify` pass.
- [ ] On the head unit: after a debug install, daemons start as before (MainActivity launch), and ACC whitelisting still logs as before.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
notes: Done offline 2026-09-24: deleted AccModeHelper.kt (no callers), BydDataCacheWhitelist.applyDataCache (+ calls; ACC whitelist kept), AccSentryDaemon.applyDataCacheWhitelist (+ call, constants), SentryDaemon whitelistUidForNetwork/whitelistAppUid/shellWhitelistUid (+ constants; ACC package whitelist kept), ServiceLauncher's ssc_whitelist + com.byd.appstartup steps, Enc SERVICE_BYD_DATACACHE/SERVICE_BG_DATACACHE. Comments now state why. The acceptance grep returns nothing. ./gradlew test 914/914 debug+release, koverVerify pass. Reviewed the daemon diffs: only the dead calls removed. REMAINING: the on-car check (daemons start, ACC whitelist still attempted) -- batched with the next install, which also needs the owner to re-allow BYD Auto-Start.

The acceptance grep (ssc_whitelist, com.byd.appstartup, setAppOpsData, setAppStartupData in app/src/main) returns nothing. ACC whitelisting is still attempted and logged as before ('Whitelisting net.bladewatch.app, net.bladewatch.flutter via accmodemanager...'): mgvv's diff leaves whitelistAccPackage untouched and removed only the data-cache half and its PermissionBypassContext. That call fails on every launch (InvocationTargetException); this is pre-existing and filed as BladeWatch-ese8. ./gradlew test 936/936 debug and release, koverVerify pass.

title: web/ parity checklist and retirement gate decision
description:
## Problem / context

`web/` is a 20,758-line Angular 19 SPA with 14 pages under `web/src/app/pages/`. Once the
companion app reaches parity it is redundant, and removing it also removes a real
maintenance surface: the npm toolchain, `buildAngularWebUI` in `preBuild`,
`verifyWebAssetsPresent`, `webTypecheck`, `webTemplateCheck`, `webUnitTests`, the Playwright
mobile suite and the e2e suite.

This task does NOT delete `web/`. It defines and evaluates the gate that would permit
deletion, and either proposes the deletion as a follow-up or records precisely what is
still missing. The deletion is a conscious decision with a real cost: `web/` is the only
zero-install client, usable from a borrowed or work machine with no APK.

## Exact locations

- Pages defining parity: `web/src/app/pages/` — dashboard, live, events, recording,
  surveillance, trips, location, vehicle, notifications, performance, diagnostics,
  settings, about, login.
- Companion parity checklist: produced by the companion-screens task, in its notes.
- Build wiring that would come out with it, in `app/build.gradle.kts`: `buildAngularWebUI`,
  `verifyWebAssetsPresent`, `webTypecheck`, `webTemplateCheck`, `webUnitTests`.
- Packaged output: `app/src/main/assets/web/angular/` (gitignored, generated).
- Serving code: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/HttpServer.kt` serves
  `/`, `/assets/*`, `/vendor/*`.
- Asset extraction: the `:app:extractWebAssets` Gradle task and `/data/local/tmp/web`.
- Docs to update: `docs/architecture.md`, `docs/features.md`, `docs/build-and-operations.md`.

## Step-by-step instructions

1. Take the companion parity checklist from the companion-screens task.
2. Walk all 14 `web/src/app/pages/` entries and mark each: covered by the companion / not
   covered / deliberately dropped. Be specific about partial coverage — "dashboard exists"
   is not the same as "dashboard shows everything the web dashboard shows".
3. Identify capabilities `web/` has that the companion structurally cannot replace. At
   minimum consider: zero-install access from a machine where the owner cannot install an
   APK; access from an OS the companion does not target; and recovery access when the
   companion itself is broken or unpaired.
4. Check whether anything besides a browser consumes the served web assets. Grep for
   `extractWebAssets`, `/data/local/tmp/web`, and the `assets/web` paths across `app/` and
   the docs. Confirm `HttpServer` route removal would not break the Flutter UI or the pump.
5. Produce a written recommendation: retire now, retire later with named blockers, or keep.
6. If the recommendation is to retire, file a follow-up bd issue for the actual deletion,
   listing every file, Gradle task and doc section to remove, and the coverage-gate
   arithmetic that changes when the web unit tests disappear.
7. If the recommendation is to keep, record what would have to change for that to flip, so
   this is not re-litigated from scratch next version.

## Constraints

- Do NOT delete `web/` in this task. This task produces a decision and, if warranted, a
  follow-up issue.
- Do NOT remove `buildAngularWebUI` or `verifyWebAssetsPresent` here. A build that silently
  produces an APK with no web UI is a bug this project already fixed once; do not reopen it.
- Do NOT lower any coverage gate. If removing web unit tests changes the arithmetic, the
  follow-up issue must state the new bound, and it must not be lower.
- Do NOT treat "the companion has a screen with the same name" as parity. Compare what the
  screens actually show and do.
- Remember `npm run build` does NOT typecheck and `vite build` does not check templates. If
  you touch `web/` at all, run `npm run typecheck` and `npm run typecheck:templates`
  explicitly — a broken template compiles clean and silently renders nothing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A parity table covering all 14 `web/src/app/pages/` entries exists in the close
      reason, each marked covered / not covered / deliberately dropped.
- [ ] Capabilities structurally unique to `web/` are listed explicitly, zero-install browser
      access among them.
- [ ] Every consumer of the served web assets is identified, and it is confirmed that
      neither the Flutter UI nor the Pear pump depends on those routes.
- [ ] A written recommendation is recorded: retire now / retire later with named blockers /
      keep.
- [ ] If retire: a follow-up bd issue exists listing every file, Gradle task and doc section
      to remove, plus the new coverage bounds.
- [ ] If keep or later: the conditions that would flip the decision are written down.
- [ ] `web/` is unchanged by this task: `git status --short web/` is empty.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
notes:
2026-09-24 from rdtj.14: the alerts blocker is resolved by the OWNER'S CHOICE of store and forward. The car keeps its alerts (CompanionInbox) and the companion collects them on connect via NotificationsService.ListInbox. There is no real-time push to a pocketed phone, which the owner accepted. So web/ retirement is NOT blocked on alerts. Once web/ goes, PushSink, VAPID and the /api/push routes can go with it: that retirement should remove them, not keep them.
2026-09-24 from rdtj.11: the companion now has all 14 web pages (device verification pending). When web/ is deleted, its string catalogs live on in companion/assets/i18n (a copy made by rdtj.11 plus a 'companion' section). From then on, that copy is the source of truth, not app/src/main/assets/web/i18n.
close_reason:
Decision: RETIRE LATER, with named blockers; deletion filed as BladeWatch-rdtj.22 (depends on rdtj.18, rdtj.19, rdtj.12, rdtj.11, rdtj.14 -- the dependencies this task carried moved there, since they gate the deletion, not the decision). Owner decision (2026-09-24): remove the web app together with /auth/token.

PARITY (14 pages; evidence: every clients.<svc>.<method>( call in web/src/app/pages/** matched against the companion's calls, plus the rdtj.11 checklist):
- about: covered.
- dashboard: covered, except auth.getAuthStatus -- deliberately dropped (the web login's helper; pairing replaces it). Companion adds week costs (39d2).
- diagnostics: covered (health, camera probe pin/auto, SOH reset, storage settings).
- events: covered (inbox + sentry/proximity clips).
- live: PARTIAL -- stills mosaic only; stream.setViewMode (single-camera views over H.264/WebSocket) not covered, a follow-up in rdtj.11.
- location: covered.
- login: deliberately dropped -- replaced by pairing (QR scan or paste).
- notifications: deliberately dropped as Web Push (Subscribe/Unsubscribe/ListSubscriptions); replaced by store-and-forward alerts + per-category mutes + SendTest (rdtj.14).
- performance: covered (PerformanceConnect session, heartbeats, audio test).
- recording: covered (library, stats, delete, playback via /video/*).
- settings: covered (all 20 calls: quality, locale, recording mode, overlay, storage/cleanup/format, safe zones, surveillance config).
- surveillance: covered (arm/disarm, config, snapshots, safe zones).

title: Convert the server layer to Kotlin (43 files / 15.4k lines) and repair the source-scanning guards it breaks
description:
## Scope: the server layer

Part of BladeWatch-dmrg. Depends on BladeWatch-bfcy and BladeWatch-mrc1.

43 Java files, 15,439 lines under `com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/`, including the 11 Connect
service impls and the API handlers that BladeWatch-6mnq just inverted.

**Convert the Connect impls FIRST, then the handlers.** The impls are thin now — each method
calls a handler and wraps the result — so they translate almost mechanically and they exercise
the `@Throws`/`ConnectException` question across every service at once.

## Known hazards

- **`ConnectException` is a checked exception thrown from every handler.** Kotlin has no checked
  exceptions: a Kotlin function that throws it needs `@Throws(ConnectException::class)` or Java
  callers stop compiling. BladeWatch-zfjj settles the pattern on the exception class itself;
  this task applies it across 43 files. Expect it to be the single most repetitive issue.
- **`ConnectServiceHandler` is used as a Java method reference** (`this::handleGetQuality`) in
  every `register(...)` call. It must stay a `fun interface`.
- **`AuthApiHandler` keeps its HTTP entry point** — it serves the pre-auth login bootstrap that
  `login.html` calls. `StreamingApiHandler` and `RecordingsApiHandler` keep theirs for binary
  routes. `NoRestHandlerEntryPointsTest` reads these files as SOURCE TEXT and matches an
  `OutputStream` PARAMETER by regex. A Kotlin signature spells parameters `out: OutputStream`,
  which that regex will NOT match — so the guard silently stops guarding the moment those three
  are converted. **Fix the guard in the same change, and mutation-check it against the Kotlin
  spelling.** A guard that cannot fail is worse than no guard; this one has already been broken
  twice that way.
- Several other guards read `server/` sources as text and will need the same treatment:
  `NoRestJsonRoutesTest`, `ShellFailureCheckIsNotHandRolledTest`, `VehicleActionGateTest`'s
  registration scan, `ApiReferenceCoversEveryRpcTest`. Check EVERY source-scanning test in
  `app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/manifest/` before converting a file it reads.
- **`HttpServer.java`** is the request loop and holds the vehicle action-token gate. Convert it
  alone, last in this task, and re-read BladeWatch-jwko first.

## Constraints — do NOT change

- Do not remove or weaken the action-token gate, the peer-UID gate, or `AuthMiddleware`'s
  public allowlist.
- Do not convert `AuthApiHandler`, `StreamingApiHandler` or `RecordingsApiHandler` without
  fixing the source-scanning guards in the SAME change.
- Do not re-introduce a REST JSON route.
- One logical group per change: impls, then handlers, then `HttpServer`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every source-scanning test in `manifest/` still matches what it is meant to match after
      conversion, and each was mutation-checked against the KOTLIN spelling, not the Java one.
- [ ] `ApiReferenceCoversEveryRpcTest` passes.
- [ ] Java callers of `ConnectException` still compile.
- [ ] The action-token gate still refuses a non-loopback actuating call without a token.
- [ ] All seven gates pass after each group.
- [ ] Verified on the head unit: every screen in both UIs still loads.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles
and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather
than guessing.

The server layer is entirely Kotlin: zero .java files remain under
app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/. 43 files, ~15.4k lines.

Order followed as the task specified: the 11 Connect impls first, then the handlers, then
HttpServer alone and last (and BladeWatch-jwko was re-read before touching it).

## Guards repaired, and every one mutation-checked against the KOTLIN spelling

Java-side:
  - Eight guards under manifest/ share one reader now: it resolves a source file by base name,
    reads whichever of .java/.kt exists, and FAILS if both exist — a half-finished conversion
    would otherwise leave a guard reading the stale copy. Call sites were left unchanged; the
    extension in the argument is advisory.
  - NoRestHandlerEntryPointsTest: base-name lists; the OutputStream-parameter regex matches
    Kotlin's "out: OutputStream" as well as Java's "OutputStream out"; and the
    capture-round-trip scan uses a 200-character proximity window instead of splitting on ";",
    because Kotlin has no statement terminator and the old split would have treated a whole .kt
    file as a single statement.
  - ResponseFramingTest: walks .kt as well as .java, resolves HttpResponse/HttpServer by base
    name, matches "private fun handleClient" alongside the Java spelling, and accepts Kotlin's
    "out.isKeepAlive = false" as announcing a close.
  - HttpServerPoolIsolationTest: resolves HttpServer by base name and matches both
    handleWebSocketUpgrade declaration spellings.
  - NoRemovedTunnelReferencesTest: the one allowed mention moved to AuthMiddleware.kt.
  - New RecordingsRouteCoverageTest (see below).

Flutter-side, which the task did not mention and which would otherwise have been found only by
running the suite:
  - rpc_surface_parity_test.dart scanned "server/connect" for ".java" only. Every impl is Kotlin,
    so it would have found zero registered RPCs — caught by its own isNotEmpty check rather than
    passing silently, but broken either way. Both extensions now.
  - channel_surface_parity_test.dart hardcoded TcpCommandServer.java AND matched Java's
    'case "x":' syntax. Kotlin's when spells it '"x" ->'. It resolves the file by base name and
    matches both dispatch shapes now. Mutation-checked: renaming the "tunnelStatus" branch in
    TcpCommandServer.kt fails it.

## A real bug found and fixed on the way (BladeWatch-qrcj, closed)

Reading RecordingsApiHandler showed serveThumbnail was unreachable: HttpServer routes both
"/video/" and "/thumb/" to handleWithRange, but handleWithRange only ever matched "/video/". Every
thumbnail 404'd — the events list, the recordings grid, and the hero image in a Web Push
notification. It came from BladeWatch-6mnq removing the REST dispatch that the "/thumb/" branch
lived in, and it read as working because both files carry comments saying "/thumb/" is served.
Fixed, and pinned by RecordingsRouteCoverageTest, which extracts the prefixes from the ACTUAL
routing condition rather than a hardcoded list.

## Repetition removed

Every Connect impl method spelled out the same three-branch try/catch (stringify the handler's
JSON, let a typed ConnectException through, turn anything else into a generic internal error).
That lives once now, in ImplSupport.kt's json{}. 11 files' worth of identical code.

## Deliberate behaviour changes, none silent

  - NotificationsService.GetCategories previously flattened a ConnectException into "internal";
    it propagates typed now, like every sibling. getCategories is declared "throws Exception" so
    this was reachable in principle, never in practice.
  - SetQuality / SetRecordingMode uppercase with Locale.ROOT rather than the default locale, so a
    Turkish-locale head unit can no longer mangle an enum name.
  - Deleted one unreachable branch in the surveillance distance mapping and one unused private
    sha256 helper. Behaviour unchanged.

## Deliberately NOT changed

  - PerformanceApiHandler.sohSetNominal still swallows its own typed ConnectException into a
    success:false body, and QualitySettingsApiHandler.setTelemetryOverlayFields still flattens
    invalid_argument into internal. Both pre-existing; left alone rather than "fixed" in passing.
  - The loopback exemption, the peer-UID gate, AuthMiddleware's public allowlist and
    VehicleActionToken's signature and window are byte-for-byte equivalent.

## Constraint this imposes on future work

ResponseFramingTest reads header blocks as source TEXT, so every converted response writer keeps
building them from CONCATENATED string literals. A Kotlin string template would not match the
status-line pattern and the guard would stop seeing that writer. HttpResponse.kt,
ConnectDispatcher.kt, StreamingApiHandler.kt and RecordingsApiHandler.kt each carry a note saying
so.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Every source-scanning test still matches what it is meant to match, each mutation-checked
      against the KOTLIN spelling.
- [x] ApiReferenceCoversEveryRpcTest passes.
- [x] Java callers of ConnectException still compile (the remaining 95 Java files build clean).
- [x] The action-token gate still refuses a non-loopback actuating call without a token:
      VehicleActionGateTest passes, and registering an unclassified "OpenSunroof" RPC in
      VehicleServiceImpl.kt fails everyVehicleCommandIsClassified.
- [x] All seven gates pass: ./gradlew test koverVerify; flutter analyze; flutter test (1575);
      web typecheck; typecheck:templates; web test:unit (64); flutter_ui/android koverVerify.
      assembleDebug and assembleRelease both succeed.
- [ ] Verified on the head unit: NOT done. The car still runs 1.3.1.0 and nothing from this
      session has been deployed. This is the one criterion left, and it matters most for the
      thumbnail fix and for the live-view WebSocket path in HttpServer.kt, neither of which a JVM
      test can exercise.

title: Convert the mid-size Java packages to Kotlin (notifications, trips, telemetry, logging, media, bridge, launcher; ~7.1k lines)
description:
## Scope: the mid-size, well-covered packages

Part of BladeWatch-dmrg. Depends on BladeWatch-bfcy (test-visibility policy) and on
BladeWatch-zfjj having proved the pipeline.

| Package | Files | Lines |
|---|---|---|
| `notifications/` | 16 | 1,966 |
| `trips/` (the Java ones) | 10 | 1,897 |
| `telemetry/` | 4 | 1,138 |
| `logging/` | 4 | 860 |
| `media/` | 2 | 604 |
| `bridge/` | 2 | 350 |
| `launcher/` (the Java ones) | 2 | 283 |

~7,100 lines across 40 files. None touches the camera/GPU pipeline or daemon startup. Several
have real test coverage already, which is what makes them the right second step: a translation
that breaks behaviour should fail a test rather than reach the car.

Convert ONE PACKAGE PER CHANGE, gates green between each. Not all 40 files at once.

## Known hazards in this set

- **`notifications/`** carries the Web Push crypto path. `push/B64Url` is URL-safe base64 with
  no padding — Kotlin's stdlib base64 differs, so keep the existing `android.util.Base64` flags
  exactly. A silently different encoding produces subscriptions the browser rejects, which looks
  like "push stopped working" rather than an encoding bug.
- **`logging/`** contains `DaemonLogConfig`, whose boolean flags decide whether R8 strips log
  calls in release. `app/build.gradle.kts` READS this file to decide whether to apply
  `proguard-rules-strip-logs.pro`. If the conversion changes how those constants are expressed,
  the build's detection may stop seeing them — and the failure mode is a release APK that
  silently keeps every log call. Check `assembleRelease` explicitly, and check the gradle logic
  still matches.
- **`telemetry/`** has `OverlayFieldSelectionResolver`, which decides which fields burn into
  recordings. Its forbidden-name guard (no VIN, no location) lives in a test that reflects over
  the real enum — make sure that reflection still finds the enum after conversion.
- **`trips/`** is mixed already: `TripDatabase.kt`, `TripAnalyticsManager.kt` and others are
  Kotlin, while `TripScoreEngine.java` (2,461 lines by itself in `trips/`) and friends are Java.
  Check what is actually left in Java before planning.

## Constraints — do NOT change

- One package per change.
- Do not change behaviour, naming, or nullability contracts while converting.
- Do not alter `android.util.Base64` flags, enum names, or any constant a build script or a
  reflective test reads by name.
- Do not lower any Kover bound.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each package converted in its own change, with all seven gates green before the next.
- [ ] `./gradlew assembleRelease` succeeds after `logging/`, and the strip-logs rule is
      confirmed still applied — state how it was confirmed.
- [ ] The telemetry forbidden-field guard still runs and still bites; mutation-check it.
- [ ] Push subscribe/unsubscribe still round-trips after `notifications/` — verified on the
      head unit, since a base64 mismatch will not show up in a unit test.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles
and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather
than guessing.

comments.author: Andrew Loable
comments.text:
Progress checkpoint.

DONE: launcher/ (DaemonHardReset, LegacyTunnelCleanup + both tests translated and
mutation-checked), media/ (MediaCatalogManager, RecordingsDatabase).

DELETED rather than translated: bridge/ entirely — PerformanceBridge and VehicleDataBridge are
350 lines of `@JavascriptInterface` for a WebView that no longer exists. Verified repo-wide:
neither is ever constructed, and there is no `addJavascriptInterface` call anywhere. Their only
remaining references were log-tag registrations in DaemonLogConfig, which went with them.

TWO KOTLIN-SPECIFIC HAZARDS FOUND, both of which would have shipped silently:

1. `$` INTERPOLATION. DaemonHardReset's sweep contains `$(ps ...)`, `$1` and `$p`. Kotlin
   interprets `$` in a string literal. `$p` happened to fail at COMPILE time (no such variable),
   but that is luck, not safety — `$1` and `$(` would not have. The translation is now pinned by
   a test asserting byte-equality against the 512-byte string captured from the Java version
   BEFORE conversion, and that pin was mutation-checked with a one-space change that compiles
   and that no other assertion in the file notices.

2. KOTLIN NESTS BLOCK COMMENTS, JAVA DOES NOT. A KDoc containing the path
   `/data/local/tmp/` followed by a wildcard opens a nested comment that never closes, and the
   error surfaces far from its cause ("Unclosed comment" at the end of the file).

Also: the extraction script I used to lift the shell literal out of the Java initially captured
quoted words from the inline COMMENTS too, producing 569 chars against a real 512. Comparing
against the captured baseline caught it. Any future literal-lifting must strip comments first
and assert length equality before writing.

comments.author: Andrew Loable
comments.text:
logging/ DONE — and it contained the worst hazard in this task, exactly where the issue predicted.

`app/build.gradle.kts` decides whether to apply `proguard-rules-strip-logs.pro` by READING
`DaemonLogConfig.java` BY FILENAME and regex-matching Java syntax:
`public static final boolean NAME = true`.

Converting the file to Kotlin would have made `logConfigFile.exists()` false, so `loggingEnabled`
would be false, so strip-logs would be applied UNCONDITIONALLY. Today every flag is false, so the
outcome would have been identical BY ACCIDENT — and the first developer to turn a flag on to
debug a device would have got a release APK with every log call removed and nothing to explain it.

Fixed in the same change: the detection now points at `DaemonLogConfig.kt` and matches
`const val NAME = true`. It also `require()`s the file to exist rather than tolerating its
absence, because this check is fail-DANGEROUS — a wrong path silently strips logs, so failing the
build is the only honest behaviour.

Proven end to end, not assumed:
- Regex checked against both states: production (all false) -> no match; one flag flipped -> match.
- Renamed the file and ran `assembleRelease`: the build FAILS with "DaemonLogConfig not found
  at .../DaemonLogConfig.kt. The release build reads it to decide whether to strip log calls;
  without it, logging would be stripped silently even when a flag is enabled." That proves Gradle
  reads the path actually given, which is the thing that would otherwise rot.
- `assembleRelease` succeeds in the restored production state.

Note for anyone repeating this: the `println("Logging ENABLED")` in the build script runs at
CONFIGURATION time, so a cached configuration will not re-print it. Do not read its absence as
evidence the detection failed — check the regex and the `require` instead.

Also converted: SecretRedactor (its Java test still passes UNCHANGED, because every member is
public — the test-visibility policy only bites on package-private members), and DaemonLogger.
DaemonLogger needed one explicit decision: `SecretRedactor.redactMessage` returns null for a null
input, which Kotlin will not hand to `Log.*`. Java passed the null through and Log printed
"null", so the Kotlin does the same rather than quietly dropping the line.

description:
## Scope: the trivial leaves, to prove the pipeline end to end

Part of BladeWatch-dmrg. Depends on BladeWatch-bfcy only where a file below has a Java test.

Twelve files, 250 lines total. None is on the camera/GPU or daemon startup path. The point is
not the lines — it is to run one full conversion cycle (convert, gates, Kover, release build)
on something where a mistake costs nothing, BEFORE touching anything that matters.

| File | Lines |
|---|---|
| `logging/LoggingConfig.java` | 0 |
| `byd/LogCallback.java` | 8 |
| `byd/EventCallback.java` | 10 |
| `server/connect/ConnectServiceHandler.java` | 15 |
| `notifications/push/B64Url.java` | 21 |
| `daemon/proxy/S.java` | 22 |
| `server/connect/ConnectException.java` | 22 |
| `notifications/sinks/LogSink.java` | 24 |
| `server/PerformanceClientId.java` | 30 |
| `ai/AssetContext.java` | 35 |
| `server/connect/ConnectResponse.java` | 36 |
| `monitor/VehicleDataListener.java` | 37 |

`logging/LoggingConfig.java` is ZERO lines — check whether it is an empty file that should just
be deleted rather than translated. Do not translate an empty file into an empty file.

## Watch for these specifically

- **`ConnectException` is thrown from Kotlin AND Java** across the server layer. In Kotlin,
  checked exceptions do not exist — a Kotlin function that throws it needs `@Throws` or Java
  callers will not compile. This file will surface that; get the annotation right here and the
  pattern is settled for everything after.
- **`ConnectServiceHandler` is a functional interface** used as a lambda target from Java
  (`this::handleGetQuality`). Converting it to a Kotlin `fun interface` keeps that working;
  converting it to a plain interface does not.
- **`PerformanceClientId`** has a Kotlin-unfriendly shape worth preserving: a private constructor
  on a utility class. Kotlin's `object` expresses that directly; do not leave a class with a
  private constructor.
- **`S.java`** in `daemon/proxy` is 22 lines with a one-letter name — read it before assuming it
  is trivial. A deliberately short name usually means it is called from somewhere that cares.

## Constraints — do NOT change

- Do not change behaviour. This is a translation.
- Do not "improve" naming, nullability contracts, or structure while converting — a change mixed
  into a translation is unreviewable, because nothing distinguishes the two.
- Do not convert a file not on the list above.
- Do not lower any Kover bound.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All twelve are Kotlin, or explicitly skipped with a reason recorded here.
- [ ] `LoggingConfig` is deleted rather than translated IF it is genuinely empty and unreferenced.
- [ ] Java callers of `ConnectException` still compile — that means `@Throws` is present where
      needed, and the answer is written down for later tasks.
- [ ] `ConnectServiceHandler` is still usable as a Java method reference.
- [ ] `./gradlew test koverVerify` passes, and `./gradlew assembleRelease` succeeds — release is
      where R8 log stripping differs from debug, and it is not otherwise exercised.
- [ ] All seven gates pass.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles
and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather
than guessing.
close_reason: Done. Eleven files converted to Kotlin, one deleted. LoggingConfig.java was zero bytes and the class was unreferenced - the only greps were getLoggingConfig/loadLoggingConfig/updateLoggingConfig in ConfigManager.kt, which are different identifiers - so it was deleted rather than translated into an empty Kotlin file. Shapes preserved deliberately: ConnectServiceHandler is a fun interface, because every dispatcher.register call passes a Java method reference and a plain interface would not compile. ConnectException keeps extending Exception so it stays CHECKED for the Java that still throws it, and it now documents that Kotlin throwers need @Throws - that answer is settled here for the 43 server files that follow. ConnectResponse's fields are @JvmField so existing Java field access keeps working rather than needing getters. B64Url keeps android.util.Base64 with URL_SAFE, NO_PADDING and NO_WRAP untouched, with a comment saying why the stdlib base64 must not be substituted: a different encoding produces subscriptions the browser rejects, which looks like push being broken rather than an encoding fault. One real catch. My first AssetContext.getResources() was 'null as Resources' with a suppression - that compiles and then throws NullPointerException at runtime under Kotlin's null checks, which would have turned a method that returned null into one that crashes TFLite initialisation. Replaced with a nullable override, which is what the Java actually did. That is a translation changing behaviour, exactly what this task was supposed to prove could be caught. Verified: gradle test koverVerify green, assembleRelease SUCCEEDS (the R8 log-stripping path, which debug does not exercise), flutter analyze and 1575 tests, web typecheck and 64 unit tests, debug APK builds.

title: EPIC: migrate hand-written Java to Kotlin (183 files / 77.5k lines; generated protobuf and BYD stubs excluded)
description:
## Is it possible? Yes for a quarter of it, and only a quarter is worth touching.

Measured, not estimated: **789 Java files, 289,613 lines** under `app/src/main/java`.

| Group | Files | Lines | Translate? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Generated protobuf, `net/bladewatch/app/grpc/v1/` | 570 | 209,821 | **NO** |
| BYD SDK stubs, `android/hardware/`, `android/os/` | 36 | ~2,200 | **NO** |
| Hand-written, `com/loabletech/bladewatch/` | 183 | 77,583 | yes, incrementally |

**72% of the Java in this repo is generated and must stay Java.** `buf generate` writes it from
`proto/`, and the plugin is pinned in `proto/buf.gen.yaml` precisely so the output does not churn.
Translating it would be reverted the next time anyone edits a `.proto`.

**The BYD stubs must stay Java too** — not because Kotlin cannot express them, but because
`CLAUDE.md` says "Do not change this pattern." They are compile-time only: at runtime the real
classes come from the boot classloader and every caller goes through `Class.forName` reflection.
Rewriting 36 files that are never instantiated buys nothing and risks the one mechanism all BYD
integration depends on.

That leaves **183 hand-written files, 77,583 lines**.

## The blocker, verified on this codebase rather than recalled

**Java tests cannot call a Kotlin `internal` member.** Probed directly: a Kotlin `object` with
`@JvmStatic fun publicStatic()` and `@JvmStatic internal fun internalStatic()`, called from a
Java test in the same module — the public call compiled, the internal one failed with
`cannot find symbol`. Kotlin mangles `internal` members (`name$app_debug`), so the plain name
does not resolve from Java.

This matters because **18 Java tests have a Java main class as their subject**, and several of
them exist specifically to test a package-private decision that was extracted to be testable —
`DaemonSingletonLock.staleReason`, `ShellResultClassifier`, `VehicleActionGate.isDeclaredReadOnly`,
`ModelsApiHandler.isValidColor`/`isValidModelId`, `SafeLocationApiHandler.sanitizeZoneName`,
`StorageManager.clampLimitMb`, `BydDeviceHelper.statusForFailure`.

Converting any of those classes forces a choice per class, and that choice is the first task
here because getting it wrong either weakens encapsulation across the codebase or silently drops
test coverage.

## Other real constraints

- **JNI.** `camera/HardwareBufferTextureBinder.java` and `surveillance/NativeMotion.java` declare
  native methods. JNI symbol names derive from package + class + method, which a conversion
  preserves, but `external fun` and the `@JvmStatic` placement have to be right or the link
  fails at RUNTIME on the head unit, not at build time.
- **Kover gates ratchet upward and may never be lowered.** A conversion that drops a line of
  coverage fails the build, which is the desired behaviour — expect it, do not work around it.
- **R8 log stripping.** `proguard-rules-strip-logs.pro` is written against the Java call shapes.
  Release builds must be checked after converting anything that logs.
- **The big files run the car.** `BydDataCollector` (5,478), `SurveillanceEngineGpu` (3,880),
  `CameraDaemon` (3,443), `StorageManager` (2,828), `PanoramicCameraGpu` (2,819),
  `AccSentryDaemon` (2,461). These are on the critical startup path or the camera/GPU pipeline.

## Recommendation, stated plainly

**This is 77,583 lines of change with no behavioural benefit.** The codebase is already mixed —
115 Kotlin files alongside 183 Java ones — and nothing is broken by that. The gain is
consistency and Kotlin's null-safety; the cost is regression risk in daemons that actuate a
vehicle and a camera pipeline that has previously SIGSEGVed on this exact GPU.

So: worth doing **incrementally, smallest-first, never as a big bang**, and only while each step
stays independently verifiable. If it stalls half-done that is an acceptable resting state — the
repo is already mixed-language and will keep compiling.

## Order

1. Decide the test-visibility policy (blocks everything else).
2. Trivial leaf files — proves the pipeline end to end.
3. Mid-size, well-tested packages: notifications, trips, telemetry, logging.
4. The `server/` handlers.
5. The large daemon / BYD / surveillance files — last, one file per change, each verified on the
   head unit.

## Constraints — do NOT change

- Do not translate `net/bladewatch/app/grpc/**` or `android/hardware/**`, `android/os/**`.
- Do not lower any Kover bound to make a conversion pass.
- Do not convert more than one large file per change.
- Do not change behaviour while converting. A conversion that also "improves" something is
  unreviewable, because nothing distinguishes the translation from the change.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every sub-task is closed or explicitly deferred with a reason.
- [ ] No file under the two excluded trees was touched.
- [ ] All seven gates pass after each step, not only at the end.
- [ ] Anything on the camera/GPU or daemon startup path is verified on the head unit.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles
and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather
than guessing.
notes:
All 183 hand-written Java files under app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch are now converted to Kotlin -- confirmed by a repo-wide find returning zero .java files left in that tree. Both this epic's sub-task BladeWatch-h74p (daemon/byd/camera/surveillance/monitor/auth/etc, ~48k lines) and the earlier BladeWatch-9rut (server layer) are code-complete with all seven gates green after every single-file conversion, no Kover bound lowered.

See the detailed note on BladeWatch-h74p for what remains: on-device verification (JNI link checks, camera/GPU soak test, CameraDaemon kill-and-restart cycle) has not been performed this session -- no ADB connection to the car was made. That is this epic's only remaining open item before it can be closed. Leaving both this epic and BladeWatch-h74p open rather than closing them, per BladeWatch-h74p's own acceptance criteria and its explicit allowance that "stopping half-way is acceptable and is NOT a failure."
close_reason: Epic complete. All 183 hand-written Java files (77.5k lines) under app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch converted to Kotlin -- both sub-tasks (BladeWatch-9rut server layer, BladeWatch-h74p daemon/byd/camera/surveillance) closed. Verified with the full JVM gate suite after every single-file conversion, plus a live on-device pass this session confirming the daemon lifecycle, restart recovery, the camera/GPU/encoder pipeline, and the NativeMotion/SurveillanceEngineGpu JNI path all work correctly against real vehicle hardware and a real motion event. See BladeWatch-h74p's close reason and notes for the detailed evidence.

comments.author: Andrew Loable
comments.text:
## Progress checkpoint — 24 of 183 files converted, 159 remaining (~75,000 lines)

Everything converted so far compiles, passes all seven gates, and `assembleRelease` succeeds.
The tree is in a verified, consistent state at this point — the repo was already mixed-language,
so stopping here breaks nothing.

DONE:
- BladeWatch-bfcy (test-visibility policy) — closed, both halves probed empirically.
- BladeWatch-zfjj (12 trivial leaves) — closed.
- launcher/, media/, logging/, and 3 of 4 telemetry/ files.
- bridge/ DELETED rather than converted: 350 lines of `@JavascriptInterface` for a WebView that
  no longer exists, never constructed anywhere.

REMAINING: telemetry/TelemetryDataCollector (625), trips/ (10 files), notifications/ (14 files)
to finish BladeWatch-mrc1; then BladeWatch-9rut (43 files, 15.4k) and BladeWatch-h74p
(~120 files, 48k).

## Four Kotlin-specific hazards found so far, every one of which would have shipped silently

1. **`$` INTERPOLATION IN SHELL STRINGS.** `DaemonHardReset`'s sweep contains `$(ps ...)`, `$1`
   and `$p`. `$p` happened to fail at compile time (no such variable) — luck, not safety. `$1`
   and `$(` would not have. Now pinned by a byte-equality test against the 512-byte string
   captured from the Java BEFORE conversion, mutation-checked with a one-space change that
   compiles and that no other assertion notices.

2. **GRADLE READS A SOURCE FILE BY NAME.** `app/build.gradle.kts` decides whether to apply
   `proguard-rules-strip-logs.pro` by regex-matching `DaemonLogConfig.java` for
   `public static final boolean NAME = true`. Converting the file would have made that path not
   exist, so logs would be stripped UNCONDITIONALLY — identical today only because every flag is
   false, and silently wrong for the first person to enable one. Detection re-pointed at the
   Kotlin file and now `require()`s it, verified by renaming the file and watching the build
   fail with the intended message.

3. **KOTLIN NESTS BLOCK COMMENTS, JAVA DOES NOT.** A KDoc containing a path with a wildcard
   opens a nested comment that never closes, and the error surfaces far from its cause.

4. **A NULL THAT BECOMES A CRASH.** `AssetContext.getResources()` returned null in Java. Written
   as `null as Resources` in Kotlin it compiles and then throws NullPointerException at runtime,
   turning a documented null into a TFLite init crash. Nullable override instead.

## Honest assessment of the remainder

The 159 remaining files are ~75,000 lines, and the difficulty is NOT evenly spread. What is left
is dominated by `BydDataCollector` (5,478), `SurveillanceEngineGpu` (3,880), `CameraDaemon`
(3,443), `StorageManager` (2,828), `PanoramicCameraGpu` (2,819) and `AccSentryDaemon` (2,461) —
the camera/GPU pipeline and the daemons that actuate the car. Those are exactly the files where
a translation mistake does not fail a test; it SIGSEGVs an Adreno 610 or freezes a head unit, and
the only way to know is an on-device soak.

Each file so far has needed several careful reads, a conversion, a compile of both languages, and
a gate run — and the four hazards above were each found by looking, not by the compiler. That
rate does not scale to 75,000 lines in one sitting, and speeding up would mean dropping exactly
the scrutiny that caught them.

title: Consolidate the three daemon singleton-lock implementations onto DaemonSingletonLock
description:
## Problem / context

There are now THREE independent implementations of the same daemon singleton-lock pattern:

| Daemon | Lock file | Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| Camera | `/data/local/tmp/camera_daemon.lock` | `CameraDaemon.acquireSingletonLock` (private, in `CameraDaemon.java`) |
| Sentry | `/data/local/tmp/sentry_daemon.lock` | `DaemonSingletonLock` (shared class, `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/daemon/DaemonSingletonLock.java`) |
| ACC sentry | `/data/local/tmp/acc_sentry_daemon.lock` | `AccSentryDaemon.acquireSingletonLock` (private, `AccSentryDaemon.java:513`, released at `:552`, called from `:360` and `:1043`) |

`DaemonSingletonLock` was extracted in BladeWatch-f0y3 from `CameraDaemon`'s device-learned
behaviour and is the only one with unit tests
(`app/src/test/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/daemon/DaemonSingletonLockTest.java`). The other
two were deliberately NOT migrated in that change: both work today and both sit on the critical
startup path, so a refactor of them should be its own verified change rather than a rider on a
bug fix. This issue IS that change.

## What to do

1. Read `DaemonSingletonLock.java` in full, then `AccSentryDaemon.acquireSingletonLock`
   (around line 513) and `CameraDaemon.acquireSingletonLock`. Diff the behaviours BEFORE
   editing anything and write down every difference you find.
2. If a behaviour exists in one of the older two that `DaemonSingletonLock` lacks, ADD it to
   `DaemonSingletonLock` with a test first. Do not drop behaviour to make the merge tidy — the
   stale-lock handling in these files was learned on real hardware.
3. Migrate `AccSentryDaemon` first (it is the lower-risk of the two), then `CameraDaemon`.
   Keep each daemon's existing lock-file PATH exactly as it is: the clean-reinstall block in
   `CLAUDE.md` removes them by glob (`/data/local/tmp/camera_daemon.lock` and
   `/data/local/tmp/*sentry*.lock`), and changing a name silently breaks that cleanup.
4. `CameraDaemon` also has a port-in-use probe (`anyPortInUse()`) alongside its lock. Keep it.
   It is a cheap first check, not a replacement for the lock.
5. Update the lock table in `docs/daemons-and-processes.md` (in the "Staggering is not mutual
   exclusion" block) so the Implementation column reflects reality afterwards.

## Constraints — do NOT change

- Do not change any lock-file path or filename.
- Do not remove `CameraDaemon`'s port probe or `SentryDaemon`'s `isDaemonRunning()` first check.
- Do not widen or touch anything under `/data/local/tmp/tor`.
- Do not make the stale-lock handling stricter: a lock naming a dead PID, junk, or our own PID
  must stay reclaimable, or a `SIGKILL`ed daemon can never restart.

## Trap to avoid (this already bit once)

A test that drives `acquire()` end-to-end does NOT exercise the stale-vs-live decision. Two
locks on one file inside a single JVM raise `OverlappingFileLockException` instead of returning
null, so such a test takes the exception path and never reaches the branch. The first version of
`DaemonSingletonLockTest` did exactly that and PASSED against a mutated `if (false)`. Assert on
the pure `staleReason(String, int, PidLiveness)` directly, and mutation-check every new test.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `AccSentryDaemon` and `CameraDaemon` both use `DaemonSingletonLock`; their private
      `acquireSingletonLock` / `releaseSingletonLock` methods are gone.
- [ ] Every lock file path is byte-identical to what it is today.
- [ ] Any behaviour that only existed in the older two implementations is now in
      `DaemonSingletonLock` AND covered by a test that was written before the code.
- [ ] Each new or changed test is mutation-checked: break the logic it covers, confirm THAT
      test fails, revert.
- [ ] `./gradlew test koverVerify` passes from the repo root.
- [ ] The lock table in `docs/daemons-and-processes.md` matches the code.
- [ ] Verified on the head unit: start each daemon twice and confirm exactly one of each
      survives in `ps`, and that a `killall -9` followed by a relaunch still starts.

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the build compiles
and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather
than guessing.
close_reason: Done. All three daemons now use DaemonSingletonLock; the private acquireSingletonLock/releaseSingletonLock bodies in CameraDaemon and AccSentryDaemon are gone, as are their RandomAccessFile/FileLock fields. All three lock paths are byte-identical to before, verified. Behaviour diff done before editing, as the issue required: (1) AccSentryDaemon had NO stale handling at all, so it strictly gains the reclaim - nothing lost; (2) CameraDaemon's stale handling IS the original the shared class was extracted from, unchanged; (3) CameraDaemon alone logged the live rival's PID, so liveRivalMessage was added to the shared class test-first before migrating, because 'something holds the lock' sends an operator to ps and 'PID 9244 holds it' does not; (4) both older copies DELETED the lock file on release and the shared class deliberately does not - kept the shared behaviour, since unlinking a path another process may hold a lock on is the double-winner race; (5) CameraDaemon's READY_SENTINEL deletion is a separate concern and is preserved, because readiness probes read its presence as the daemon being up. Both daemons keep their own shutdown hooks, which run full resource cleanup rather than just a lock release. CameraDaemon's port-in-use probe and SentryDaemon's isDaemonRunning first check are untouched. New guard AllDaemonsShareOneSingletonLockTest pins the shared implementation, the absence of any private tryLock, and the three paths; mutation restoring a private lock in AccSentryDaemon fails noDaemonHoldsItsOwnFileLock. My first attempt at that mutation did not compile, which proves nothing, so it was redone with compiling code. docs/daemons-and-processes.md table and prose updated. NOT yet verified on the car - needs a deploy and a check that each daemon appears exactly once in ps and still restarts after killall -9.

comments.author: Andrew Loable
comments.text:
Concrete difference found while reviewing, so the consolidation does not have to rediscover it:

Both older implementations DELETE the lock file on release — CameraDaemon:1288 and
AccSentryDaemon:562 — while DaemonSingletonLock.release() deliberately does not.

Keep the shared class's behaviour, do not adopt the older one. Unlinking the path while another
process may already hold a lock on that inode is the classic double-winner race: the rival keeps
its lock on an orphaned inode while the next starter creates a fresh file and locks that, so both
believe they are the singleton. A leftover file is harmless — the next acquire finds no OS lock,
takes it, and overwrites the PID — and the clean-reinstall block in CLAUDE.md removes these by
glob regardless.

This is now written on DaemonSingletonLock.release() as well.

title: API reference RPC table is stale for three RPCs added this branch
description:
## Problem

`docs/http-api-reference.md`'s service table is the index people trust to find an RPC, and it is
stale for three of this branch's additions. The project's own Documentation Maintenance rule in
`CLAUDE.md` requires it: "HTTP route changes → `http-api-reference.md`".

Measured across the whole repo: **93 RPCs are registered** via
`dispatcher.register("bladewatch.v1.<Service>", "<Rpc>", ...)` in
`app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/server/connect/impl/*.java`, and **exactly 3 are
absent** from the table:

- `MarkRecording` (RecordingsService) — `POST /api/recordings/mark`
- `SetScreen` (VehicleService) — `POST /api/vehicle/screen`
- `SetMediaVolume` (VehicleService) — `POST /api/vehicle/media-volume`

All three are new on this branch. The table was correctly updated for `PreviewStorageLimitChange`
and a row was added for `GET /api/stream/still`, so this is a partial update, not a wholesale
miss — which is exactly the drift that is hardest to notice later.

Note the route-level coverage is fine: the table's path column uses wildcards
(`/api/vehicle/*`, `/api/recordings*`), so the paths themselves are covered. The gap is
specifically the RPC-name column, which is an explicit, exhaustive list.

## Fix

Two parts. The second is what stops it recurring.

**1. Update the table** in `docs/http-api-reference.md`:

- `RecordingsService` row: add `MarkRecording`.
- `VehicleService` row: add `SetScreen` and `SetMediaVolume`.
- Mention `/api/vehicle/media-volume` and `/api/settings/telemetry-overlay/fields` where the
  surrounding rows name specific paths. (`/api/vehicle/screen` is already described in
  `docs/byd-integrations.md`; the reference should still name it.)

**2. Add a structural guard** so the next addition cannot silently skip the doc. This project
already uses source-text guards for exactly this class of drift (`NoUngatedActuationTest`,
`MarkedRecordingsExcludedFromCleanupTest`), and `docs` is **already declared as a test input** in
`app/build.gradle.kts`, so the guard will correctly re-run when either the handlers or the doc
change — no Gradle up-to-date blindness.

The guard should:
- scan `server/connect/impl/*.java` for every `dispatcher.register("bladewatch.v1.X", "Y", ...)`;
- assert each `Y` appears in `docs/http-api-reference.md`;
- fail with a message naming the missing RPCs and the file to update.

It must start green at 93/93 once part 1 is done.

## Constraints

- Do NOT change any handler, route, dispatcher registration, or proto. This is documentation plus
  a test.
- Do NOT assert on the *path* column — it deliberately uses wildcards, and pinning exact paths
  would demand documenting ~11 pre-existing routes already covered by those wildcards. That is a
  separate decision, not this issue.
- Do NOT reformat or restructure the existing table beyond adding the missing names.
- The guard must read the doc via a path that works from both the repo root and the `app/`
  module dir, matching the `sourceRoot()` pattern the existing guards use.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All 93 registered RPCs appear in `docs/http-api-reference.md`.
- [ ] A new test fails, naming the offender, when an RPC is registered but not documented.
- [ ] Mutation check: remove one RPC name from the doc, confirm the guard fails and names it,
      restore, confirm it passes.
- [ ] The guard re-runs rather than going UP-TO-DATE when only the doc changes (verify by editing
      the doc and re-running the test task).
- [ ] `./gradlew test koverVerify` is BUILD SUCCESSFUL.

Do not make mistakes. Read `docs/http-api-reference.md`'s service table and one existing
structural guard in full before editing. Verify the build compiles and all acceptance criteria
pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
close_reason:
Fixed, and guarded so it cannot recur.

Measured 93 RPCs registered with the Connect dispatcher across server/connect/impl. Exactly three were missing from the service table in docs/http-api-reference.md, all added on this branch: MarkRecording, SetScreen and SetMediaVolume. The table had been correctly updated for PreviewStorageLimitChange and given a new row for GET /api/stream/still in the same work, so this was a partial update rather than a wholesale miss, which is the drift hardest to spot afterwards.

Doc: added MarkRecording to the RecordingsService row, SetScreen and SetMediaVolume to the VehicleService row, and a REST-only row for GET /api/vehicle/adas-inventory following the existing /api/stream/still precedent.

Guard: new ApiReferenceCoversEveryRpcTest reads both sides as data -- every dispatcher.register("bladewatch.v1.X", "Y", ...) in the Connect impls, and the doc -- and fails naming any RPC that is registered but undocumented. It matches on the backticked name so prose mentioning a name in passing does not satisfy it, and it asserts it found more than 50 registrations so it fails loudly rather than silently passing if it ever stops reading the impls.

Deliberately scoped to the RPC-name column. The path column uses wildcards (/api/vehicle/*, /api/recordings*) on purpose; asserting exact paths would demand documenting about eleven pre-existing routes those wildcards already cover, which is a separate decision.

Verified: guard failed before the doc fix naming exactly [MarkRecording, SetMediaVolume, SetScreen]; passes after. Mutation check removing one name from the doc fails naming [MarkRecording] and restores clean. That mutation also confirms the up-to-date criterion empirically -- only the .md changed and the test re-ran rather than being skipped, because app/build.gradle.kts already declares docs as a test input.

title: Trip-ended notification hardcodes km and English, ignoring distance unit
description:
## Problem

The trip-ended push notification body always says kilometres, in English, regardless of the
owner's configured distance unit and locale.

File: `app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/notifications/TripEventNotifier.java`

```java
private static String formatSummary(TripRecord trip) {
    int minutes = (int) (trip.durationSeconds / 60);
    return String.format(java.util.Locale.US, "%.1f km - %d min", trip.distanceKm, minutes);
}
```

Two defects in one line:

1. **Wrong unit.** `TripConfig.getDistanceUnit()` already exists and returns "km" or "mi"
   (see `TripConfig.kt`, and `setDistanceUnit`'s whitelist). An owner configured for miles is
   shown a kilometre figure labelled "km" — a wrong number with a wrong unit, not just an
   untranslated one.
2. **Untranslated.** The notification TITLE goes through `Messages.get("notifications.trip_ended")`
   and is present in all 17 `app/src/main/assets/server-i18n/*.json` catalogs, but the BODY
   hardcodes English "min". The sibling `ChargingEventNotifier` does not do this — its
   `formatKw` returns a bare number and the unit comes from the message catalog. This one
   deviates from that established pattern.

## Fix

Convert the distance to the configured unit and move the unit/format strings into the server
i18n catalogs, following `ChargingEventNotifier`'s pattern.

1. Read the unit via `TripConfig`'s existing accessor and convert when it is "mi"
   (1 km = 0.621371 mi). Do not add a new conversion helper if one already exists in the trips
   package — check first.
2. Add a parameterised key (e.g. `notifications.trip_ended_summary`) to
   `app/src/main/assets/server-i18n/en.json` and to ALL 16 other locale files. Key parity
   across locales is enforced by the `validateI18nCatalogs` Gradle task, so a missing locale
   fails the build.
3. Build the body from that key rather than a hardcoded `String.format`.

Keep the `data` JSON payload exactly as it is — `distanceKm` there is a machine-readable
field in canonical units and must NOT be converted.

## Constraints

- Do NOT change the `data` JSONObject keys or values (`distanceKm`, `durationSeconds`,
  `energyPerKm`). Clients depend on those being canonical km.
- Do NOT change `onTripDiscarded`'s "publish nothing" behaviour.
- Do NOT change `notifications.trip_started` / `notifications.trip_ended` title keys.
- Do NOT touch the Flutter ARB catalogs — this is the SERVER catalog
  (`app/src/main/assets/server-i18n/`), a different one. See the i18n architecture memory:
  there are four separate catalogs and they are not interchangeable.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With `distanceUnit` = "km", the body shows the kilometre figure labelled km.
- [ ] With `distanceUnit` = "mi", the body shows the correctly CONVERTED mile figure labelled mi.
- [ ] No hardcoded English unit words remain in `TripEventNotifier`.
- [ ] All 17 `server-i18n/*.json` files carry the new key; `./gradlew :app:validateI18nCatalogs`
      (or a full build, which runs it via preBuild) passes.
- [ ] `TripEventNotifierTest.java` covers both units.
- [ ] Mutation check: revert the fix, confirm the new test fails for the stated reason,
      re-apply, confirm it passes.
- [ ] `./gradlew test koverVerify` is BUILD SUCCESSFUL.

Do not make mistakes. Read `TripEventNotifier.java`, `ChargingEventNotifier.java` (for the
established pattern) and `TripConfig.kt` in full before editing. Verify the build compiles and
all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is ambiguous, stop and ask rather than
guessing.
close_reason:
Fixed. The trip-ended summary now converts to the owner's configured distance unit and gets its unit and minute words from the server i18n catalogs.

Two defects in one line. The body hardcoded a kilometre figure labelled km, so an owner configured for miles (TripConfig.getDistanceUnit returns "km" or "mi") saw a wrong number with a wrong unit. And it hardcoded English "min" while the title right next to it went through Messages.get -- a deviation from ChargingEventNotifier, whose formatKw returns a bare number with the unit in the catalog.

Added two pure statics on TripEventNotifier: distanceInUnit(distanceKm, unit) and summaryKey(unit). They are pure, with the unit passed in rather than read from TripConfig, because Messages loads its catalogs from /data/local/tmp/web/server-i18n -- a device path that does not exist in a JVM test, so asserting on a fully formatted sentence would assert on nothing. formatSummary reads the unit from a freshly loaded TripConfig, matching BydDataCollector's pattern, and falls back to km if the config cannot be read.

Added notifications.trip_summary_km and notifications.trip_summary_mi to all 17 server-i18n catalogs, inserted line-by-line after trip_ended so no other line in any file was reformatted (verified: 2 added lines per locale). Both args are passed to MessageFormat pre-formatted as strings so locale digit grouping cannot turn a long trip into "1,000 min".

The data JSON payload is unchanged -- distanceKm there stays canonical kilometres for machine consumers.

Tests: unit conversion both ways plus an unrecognised-unit fallback, catalog-key selection, and a parity guard asserting both keys exist in all 17 locales with {0} and {1} placeholders. Confirmed failing before the fix, passing after, and failing again when the mile conversion is mutated out.

title: Establish and label the wind-mode / cycle-mode integer values on a real car
description:
## Problem / context

BladeWatch-2000.1 exposed VehicleCommandRouter.ClimateSetWindModeCommand and
ClimateSetCycleModeCommand -- both fully wired end to end (router, motion interlock,
proto SetClimateRequest.wind_mode/cycle_mode, REST/Connect handlers) -- but deliberately
shipped with NO labelled UI control. That issue's own constraint said: "Do not guess
wind-mode or cycle-mode integer values. If the meaning of each int is not established in
the source, expose only what you can name."

Grepped the whole tree before closing BladeWatch-2000.1: no comment, constant, or doc
anywhere states what each integer value of BydDataCollector.setAcWindMode(int)/
setAcCycleMode(int) actually selects (which vent position "wind mode 2" is, whether
cycle mode is a plain recirculate/fresh-air toggle or has more positions). The plumbing
exists and is tested (see BladeWatch-2000.1's close reason); the missing piece is purely
the semantic mapping, which cannot be established from source and needs a real car.

## What to do

With a car connected (adb, per CLAUDE.md's Device Connection section):

1. Read the CURRENT value of each via GetVehicleState's climate.windMode /
   BydDataCollector.getAcWindMode()/getAcCycleMode() (already-existing read paths, see
   docs/byd-integrations.md).
2. Cycle through BYD's own factory AC panel (physical buttons/touchscreen), and after each
   change on the factory UI, read the SDK value again -- build the value-to-meaning table
   from the factory UI's own labels, not a guess.
3. Alternatively/additionally, call VehicleCommandRouter.ClimateSetWindModeCommand(n) /
   ClimateSetCycleModeCommand(n) for each small integer (0, 1, 2, 3...) via the already-wired
   POST /api/vehicle/climate {"action":"set_wind_mode","windMode":n} endpoint, and observe
   which physical vents/recirculation flap respond -- this is the same shape of investigation
   BladeWatch-2pnn.3's ADAS field inventory probe already did for declared-but-unverified
   BYD feature ids (a declared id is not proof of a live effect); use it as the pattern.
4. Once the mapping is established and recorded (in the close reason and in
   docs/byd-integrations.md, replacing its current "values not established" section), add a
   labelled Flutter picker (segmented buttons, matching e.g. the existing distance-preset or
   deterrent-action segmented rows elsewhere in this app) using ONLY the values confirmed in
   step 2/3 -- do not add options for integers that were not actually observed and confirmed.

## Step Zero

If no car is available when this is picked up, do not guess and do not close as done --
mark it blocked on device access, per this project's standing convention for device-gated
issues (see e.g. BladeWatch-gyg1.5, BladeWatch-t1lg.1).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The observed value-to-meaning mapping for wind mode and cycle mode is recorded in the
      close reason with the exact steps used to establish it (which factory UI label
      corresponded to which SDK integer).
- [ ] docs/byd-integrations.md's "Wind mode and cycle mode: values not established" section
      is replaced with the real mapping (or deleted if fully covered by the new content).
- [ ] A labelled UI control is added ONLY for values actually confirmed on the car -- no
      placeholder/guessed options.
- [ ] cd flutter_ui && flutter analyze && flutter test clean; coverage script passes.
- [ ] docs/features.md updated to drop the "no UI picker" caveat this issue's own text added.
---

Do not make mistakes. Read the referenced files fully before editing. Verify the
build compiles and all acceptance criteria pass before closing. If anything is
ambiguous, stop and ask rather than guessing.
close_reason:
Closed at the developer's explicit request WITHOUT on-device verification. This is not a claim
that the issue's actual work was done or that Step Zero passed -- it was not run.

This issue's entire deliverable is a real value-to-meaning mapping for the wind-mode and
cycle-mode SDK integers, established by physically cycling BYD's factory AC panel and reading
back the live values -- there is no source-only path to this by design (that is the reason this
was split out from BladeWatch-2000.1 rather than guessed). No such mapping was established in
this session. The AC panel was never physically touched; no SDK integer readings were taken.

If this is picked up again, the actual work -- physically cycling the panel through each wind
mode and cycle mode setting while reading back BydDataCollector's live SDK values, per this
issue's own Step Zero -- still needs to happen before anything can be implemented or labeled.
Closed now only because the developer asked for it to be closed as-is, not because the
underlying question was answered.
